item.title: Waypoint-1.5：跑在消费级显卡上的实时交互式视频世界模型 ｜ Waypoint-1.5: A Real-Time Video World Model for Consumer Hardware
item.description:
一句话：用 10 万小时按键鼠标对齐的游戏录像训练，在消费级显卡上实时生成可玩画面。

要点：

  • 预训练数据是 10 万小时、与键盘鼠标输入逐帧对齐的多游戏视频
  • 提出区分 rendered FPS、latent FPS 与 control rate 三类指标，不拿画面帧率冒充交互性
  • 给出两个分辨率变体，覆盖从桌面独显到轻薄本的消费级硬件谱系

为什么值得看：评估 AI 原生引擎时，「画面帧率」和「控制响应率」是两件事，这套指标拆法可以直接拿来做验收口径。

中文摘要：Waypoint-1.5 把交互式世界模型（iWM）当成一个工程系统来写：它必须在严格延迟与吞吐约束下响应高密度用户输入。模型预训练于 10 万小时、与键盘鼠标控制对齐的多游戏视频，可按完整键鼠输入条件生成可玩画面，并提供两个分辨率变体以覆盖不同档位消费级显卡。论文给出一套评估语言：把渲染帧率、潜空间帧率与控制率分开度量，再以延迟和吞吐刻画交互性；同时完整交代了数据管线、网络结构、训练方法与运行时系统，最后讨论了这类模型特有的安全与伦理问题。对做生成式玩法的团队，这是一份难得的「全链路怎么搭」的公开说明。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

Waypoint-1.5: A Real-Time Video World Model for Consumer Hardware

Abstract

We present Waypoint-1.5, a real-time diffusion world model for interactive video generation on consumer-grade hardware. Unlike general video diffusion models, interactive world models (iWMs) must respond to dense user controls under strict latency and throughput constraints. Waypoint-1.5 is pre-trained on 100,000 hours of diverse, control-aligned video game data across hundreds of games, and generates playable video conditioned on full keyboard and mouse input. The model includes two resolution variants that run across a wide spectrum of consumer hardware. To characterize this unique setting, we distinguish rendered FPS, latent FPS, and control rate. We describe the data pipeline, architecture, training methodology, and runtime system behind Waypoint-1.5. We evaluate interactivity through latency and throughput. We conclude with a discussion of the safety and ethical considerations unique to iWMs.

1 Introduction

Neural networks are now capable of synthesizing coherent visual dynamics across space and time, as recent progress in generative video models has demonstrated. Impressive results in visual quality, temporal consistency, and prompt adherence have been achieved by systems including WAN ([22]), Hunyuan Video ([12]), LTX-Video ([9]), and comparable models. These models, however, are built mainly for offline text-guided video generation. Accordingly, prompt adherence, visual fidelity, and temporal coherence serve as the natural evaluation axes, measured by metrics such as VideoBench ([14]) and FVD ([21]). What this form of video generation does not offer is interactivity: users cannot actively steer the environment in real time through low-latency actions like keyboard and mouse inputs, but must instead rely on static text prompts.

Action-conditioned video world models on the other hand offer a solution to this problem. Systems at the frontier of this area: Sora ([5]), Genie ([3]), Hunyuan-GameCraft ([12]) among others, [24][15][19][20][16][1] have shown that coherent visual scenes and interactive worlds can be generated in direct response to user input. Such results suggest a future in which learned world models underpin interactive entertainment, simulation, and embodied AI.

However, there is a large hurdle to cross between research demonstrations and deployment in real-world systems. A large chunk of the existing video world models require enterprise level inference infrastructure (e.g H200s, B200s), yet cannot achieve high FPS or long-horizon rollouts with sufficient action adherence. In order for video world models to become a practical tool in domains such as game development, creative applications, immersive entertainment, and physical AI (e.g robotics, self-driving), it is critical that they must run on consumer grade hardware (e.g RTX 4090).

With this problem in mind, we present Waypoint-1.5, a video world model built from the ground up for real-time inference on consumer GPUs. Our model comprises a single-stream causal Diffusion Transformer (DiT) trained in the latent space of a distilled autoencoder, with design choices centered around the latency and throughput requirements for real-time interactive generation on consumer hardware. Our training methodology includes causal diffusion forcing pretraining, NorMuon optimization, and sequence packing to maximize GPU utilization. Together, these choices allow Waypoint-1.5 to excel and run in real time on a wide range of consumer GPUs (see Section 8).

In this technical report, we describe the model architecture (Section 2), pretraining methodology and input conditioning (Section 3), post-training distillation (Section 4), inference system (Section 5), autoencoder design (Section 6), data pipeline (Section 7), evaluation (Section 8), and safety considerations (Section 9).

2 Architecture

Waypoint-1.5 uses a a 1.28 billion parameter Diffusion Transformer model that processes all video latent frames in a clip as a unified sequence of tokens as a single-stream in contrast to dual-stream or cross-attention-based video DiTs that maintain separate pathways for conditioning and content. The training pipeline and overall architecture are illustrated in Figure 2.

2.1 Spatial Tokenization

We use TAEHV-1.5 to encode video frames into latents which compresses spatially by 16× and temporally by 4×. A 512×1024 frame, for example, yields a 32×64 latent, while a 256×512 frame yields a 16×32 latent. Each latent has 32 channels.

2.2 Frame-Causal Attention with KV Caching

We use factorized spatiotemporal attention wherein within each latent, tokens may attend bidirectionally to all other tokens. Across latents, a causal mask is applied using FlexAttention, which enables efficient and temporally autoregressive generation.

To balance short-term local context with long-range temporal coherence, we use a two-level attention hierarchy:

  • •

    Local window: each frame densely attends to the preceding 16 frames.

  • •

    Global dilated window: every 4th block also attends to a set of evenly-spaced frames within a 128-frame context window, using a pinned dilation factor of 8. This sparse global attention efficiently covers long-range context without quadratic memory growth.

    • Static Rolling KV Cache.

    During inference, a static ring-buffer KV-cache stores the key-value representations of past fully denoised frames. Noisy intermediate frames during multi-step denoising are not cached. The cache is pre-allocated to a fixed capacity to prevent unbounded VRAM growth: for local attention layers, a dense ring of 16 frames is maintained, with the oldest frame evicted when a new one is committed. Every 4th block uses global dilated attention with a 128-frame ring and a fixed dilation of 8, meaning new frames evict older ones at regular intervals rather than simply discarding the oldest.

    2.3 Grouped Query Attention

    In order to reduce the KV memory footprint and memory bandwidth, we use Grouped Query Attention (GQA) [2] with 32 query heads and 16 key-value heads (2:1 ratio). This halves the KV memory footprint relative to standard multi-head attention.

    2.4 WAN-Style AdaLN Noise Conditioning

    We perform noise conditioning following Wan [22]: the scalar noise level σ is encoded through a Fourier feature embedding (512-dimensional) passed through a small MLP to produce a conditioning vector. This vector further passes through a CondHead module which generates three modulation parameters per sub-layer: scale s, bias b, and gate g; as used in adaptive layer normalization:

    AdaLN(x; s,b,g)=g⊙LN(x)·(1+s)+b,

    		(1)

    where LN denotes layer normalization. The CondHead weights are shared across all 24 transformer layers. This weight tying substantially reduces parameter count while maintaining effective noise conditioning throughout the network depth. The CondHead output projection is zero-initialized (AdaLN-Zero) to ensure identity-like behavior at the beginning of training. Additionally, a learnable per-layer bias is added to each conditioning layer’s output which provides layer-specific offsets alongside the shared head.

    2.5 Positional Encoding: OrthoRoPE

    Position is encoded via OrthoRoPE, an orthogonal variant of Rotary Position Embeddings [18] that applies independent rotations for spatial (x, y) and temporal (t) dimensions within a single per-head embedding. With a head dimension of 64, we allocate 8 dimensions per spatial axis and 16 dimensions to the temporal axis, providing distinct Nyquist-tuned frequency bands for spatial proximity and temporal ordering. Spatial frequencies are scaled to the video’s spatial Nyquist frequency. Temporal frequencies use a standard base of 10,000.

    2.6 Controller Conditioning

    At each transformer block, the model receives controller inputs: discretized button states (256-bucket encoding), continuous mouse displacement (Δx,Δy), and scroll sign. These are concatenated and projected to d_model via a learned MLP, then fused into the block’s intermediate representation through MLPFusion, a lightweight residual module:

    x ← x+SiLU (W₁x+W₂c)·W₃,

    		(2)

    where c is the projected controller embedding. During training, controller conditioning is randomly dropped with probability p_cfg to support classifier-free guidance (CFG) at inference time.

    2.7 Model Configuration

    A summary of the model configuration is provided in Table 1.

    3 Training

    3.1 Diffusion Forcing

    We pretrain using Diffusion Forcing[6][17], a training objective that supports causal autoregressive rollout without sacrificing the expressiveness of a full diffusion model. The key difference from standard video diffusion training is that rather than applying a uniform noise level across all frames in a clip, Diffusion Forcing assigns an independent noise level σᵢ to each frame i, sampled from a per-frame distribution over [0,1]:

    σᵢ=sigmoid(εᵢ), εᵢ∼ℕ(0,1), i=1,…,N.

    		(3)

    Given clean video latents x∈ℝ^B×N×C×H×W, the rectified-flow target velocity, noised input, and training objective are:

    v^*=ε-x, ε∼ℕ(0,I),(4)
    xₜ=x+v^*·σᵢ,(5)
    v̂=F_θ(xₜ, σ, c),(6)
    L=𝔼 [∥v^*-v̂∥²],(7)

    where c denotes all conditioning inputs (previous frames, controller). Training on frames with heterogeneous, independently sampled noise levels teaches the model to denoise each frame conditioned on all preceding frames at their respective noise levels. This mirrors the autoregressive inference regime, where past frames sit at a low noise level (σ_ctx≈0.15) as clean context while the current frame is denoised from σ=1 to σ=0, and naturally pushes the model to handle the partial corruption of prior states it will encounter at rollout time.

    3.2 NorMuon

    All 2D weight matrices (query, key, value, and output projections, and MLP weights) are optimized with NorMuon[11][13] at a learning rate of 1×10⁻³. All remaining parameters (embeddings, biases, normalization scalars) use AdamW at 1×10⁻⁴.

    3.3 Input Conditioning

    Waypoint-1.5 models the transition function p(zₜ|z_2. CFG dropout during training enables unconditional rollouts at inference. At deployment, user inputs are sanitized and mapped to the expected controller format before reaching the model, which also serves as an additional safety layer as described in Section 9.

    4 Post-Training

    Direct inference with the pretrained Waypoint-1.5 model runs into two problems. The first is compute: each frame requires solving a multi-step ODE (typically 60 solver steps), and classifier-free guidance doubles the effective step count by requiring independent forward passes for conditioned and unconditioned predictions, bringing the effective inference cost to ∼120 forward passes per frame. The second is exposure bias: the model is trained on ground-truth context frames corrupted with varying noise, but at inference it must condition on its own imperfect predictions from prior steps. This mismatch causes visual drift and incoherence over long rollouts.

    We address both with a custom Self-Forcing DMD post-training procedure, drawing on Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) [23], Self-Forcing [10], and Self-Forcing++ [7]. The procedure jointly optimizes a student model F_θ, a frozen teacher copy F_φ, and a trainable critic F_ψ. Self-forcing trains the student to generate video autoregressively, conditioning exclusively on its own previously generated clean frames:

    p_θ(z_1:T)=∏ₜ₌₁ᵀp_θ (zₜ \middle| ẑ_

    		(8)

    where ẑ_

    The teacher is evaluated under multi-condition CFG:

    v̂_teacher=v_∅+ω_ctrl (v_ctrl-v_∅)+ω_ctx (v_ctx-v_∅),

    		(9)

    with ω_ctrl=15.0, ω_ctx=2.0, and v_∅ the unconditioned prediction. The student learns to match this guided distribution directly, removing the need to compute v_∅ at inference. The DMD loss [23] minimizes an approximate KL divergence between the student and teacher denoising distributions, with the critic providing the score gradient signal. Training stability is further supported by two regularization terms from SenseFlow [8]: IDA (Implicit Distribution Alignment) keeps the critic parameters close to the student via an EMA update after each student step, preventing critic divergence; and ISG (Intra-Segment Guidance) enforces consistency between adjacent noise levels by matching student and teacher predictions at intermediate points along the denoising trajectory.

    Sequence-Packed Teacher Forcing.

    To compute gradients over autoregressive sequences without costly per-frame backward passes, we use sequence-packed teacher forcing: context and current frames are concatenated into a single forward pass, with a binary mask distinguishing context-only tokens (\textttcid=0, no gradient) from gradient-carrying tokens (\textttcid=1). A similar strategy was developed concurrently by [16]. A custom attention rule prevents leakage between the two copies of the same frame: context tokens attend only to context, current-frame tokens attend only to their own same-frame tokens, and current-frame tokens are blocked from attending to the context copy of the same frame.

    This distillation procedure yields an approximate 30× total inference speedup over the pretrained baseline. Baking in CFG eliminates the 2× per-step overhead, cutting the effective forward pass count from 120 to 60. Compressing the denoising trajectory from 60 steps down to 4 provides an additional ∼15× throughput improvement. The resulting 4-step model generates high-quality frames conditioned on a rolling window of clean, self-generated context, and remains stable over long rollout horizons.

    5 Inference

    5.1 Autoregressive Generation and KV Caching

    Waypoint-1.5 generates video autoregressively, producing one latent frame at a time. At each step, the model receives a single noisy frame and all controller inputs for that frame, and denoises it conditioned on the full history of past clean frames. Rather than re-encoding the entire history at every step, we use a static rolling KV cache that stores key-value representations of past frames and is updated incrementally.

    The cache is structured as a ring buffer per transformer layer. Each layer maintains a buffer of capacity (L+t_pf) token slots, where L is the layer’s context window in tokens and t_pf is the number of tokens per frame. The final t_pf slots form a dedicated tail that always holds the current frame under active denoising. During multi-step denoising, the cache is frozen: the tail is written on every denoising step (allowing the model to attend to the current noisy frame), but the ring buffer is not updated. Once the frame is fully denoised to σ=0, the cache is unfrozen and the clean frame is committed to the ring. This ensures the persistent context consists exclusively of fully denoised frames, avoiding error accumulation from noisy context frames.

    For layers with global dilated attention (every 4th layer), the ring buffer uses a pinned dilation factor of 8: new frames evict slots at spacing 8 within the 128-frame window, retaining an evenly-spaced snapshot of the long-range history. Local attention layers maintain a dense 16-frame ring.

    5.2 Seed Frames and Context Priming

    Generation begins with a set of seed frames: clean ground-truth latents provided as initial context. By default, a single seed image is used. The first generated latent is conditioned on this seed frame and subsequent latents are generated in groups of 4. The seed frame is not re-denoised. Instead, a zero-noise forward pass (σ=0) is run to populate the KV cache without modifying the latent. This primes the cache with the seed before the first generated frame is produced.

    During the pretrained (pre-distillation) inference regime, previously generated context frames are held at a small fixed noise level σ_ctx=0.15 when used as conditioning. This parameter introduces a slight corruption that bridges the gap between the clean seed frames and the partially noisy frames the model encountered during Diffusion Forcing training. After Self-Forcing distillation, the model conditions on fully clean self-generated history, so it is set to 0.0.

    5.3 Denoising Schedules

    Pre-distillation.

    The pretrained model uses 60 denoising steps per frame with a flow-matching Euler scheduler. A shift of 3.0 applied to the noise schedule compresses it toward lower noise levels, concentrating the sampling budget in the refinement regime. CFG is applied at each step by running a conditioned and unconditioned forward pass and combining them with a guidance weight, doubling the effective per-frame cost to 60×2=120 model evaluations per frame.

    Post-distillation.

    After Self-Forcing distillation, the denoising schedule collapses to 4 steps per frame with a fixed trajectory: σ∈{1.0,0.9,0.75,0.3,0.0}. CFG is no longer applied separately, as it is baked into the student during distillation, so each frame requires only 4 forward passes. The teacher CFG scales used are ω_ctrl=15.0 and ω_ctx=2.0. The distilled model conditions on clean self-generated context, removing the context corruption used during pretraining.

    5.4 Runtime Optimizations

    The frozen-cache denoising step and the unfrozen cache-writing step are compiled ahead of time with torch.compile, using max-autotune mode with full graph capture and static shapes. This enables kernel fusion, memory layout optimization, and CUDA graph capture, eliminating Python dispatch overhead on each forward pass. The full diffusion model is deployed in INT8 quantized precision for throughput-critical inference, as reflected in the benchmark results of Section 8. BF16 inference is also supported where VRAM permits.

    6 Autoencoders & Tokenization

    6.1 Latent Autoencoder

    Waypoint-1.5 encodes video into a compact latent representation using TAEHV 1.5[4], a tiny autoencoder designed to approximate the latent space of the Hunyuan VAE 1.5. TAEHV 1.5 applies spatial downsampling alongside a temporal compression factor of 4, mapping 60 raw FPS to 15 latent frames per second. The encoder produces 32-channel latent frames, significantly more compact than the original VAE latent. For a 512×1024 input clip the encoded latent has spatial dimensions 32×64, and for a 256×512 input clip it is 16×32. This compression reduces a 13-second video clip (768 raw frames) to 192 latent frames, making transformer-scale training over long sequences tractable.

    6.2 Distilled Autoencoder Decode

    Standard high-fidelity autoencoders are designed for quality rather than throughput, and naive inference can make the decode step a significant bottleneck in a real-time pipeline. TAEHV 1.5 sidesteps this by design: as a tiny distilled approximation of the full Hunyuan VAE 1.5, it trades a small amount of reconstruction fidelity for a dramatically reduced parameter count and arithmetic cost. Inference runs in FP16, achieving approximately 800 FPS decode throughput on an NVIDIA RTX 5090, fast enough to make decoder overhead negligible relative to the diffusion model.

    6.3 Patchification

    After encoding, each latent frame is further tokenized by a learned 2×2 patch embedding (Conv2d with kernel size and stride [2,2]). At 512×1024 this produces 16×32=512 tokens per latent frame, and at 256×512 it produces 8×16=128. The spatial layout of patches is arranged to align with the block boundaries used by FlexAttention’s sparse kernel, ensuring block-level parallelism maps to spatially contiguous regions.

    7 Data

    7.1 Owl-Control Dataset

    Waypoint-1.5 is trained on Owl-Control, a proprietary dataset of controller-synchronized video game footage comprising over 100,000 hours of gameplay across hundreds of distinct games. Each recording pairs high-fidelity visual observations with the full controller input stream that produced them, enabling the model to learn a grounded mapping from game state to player action.

    Raw video is captured at 720P and 60 FPS. Controller inputs (keyboard states, raw mouse displacement, and scroll events) are recorded at up to 10,000 Hz via a high-fidelity hardware logging layer, precisely synchronized to the video timeline to enable accurate alignment between visual frames and the controller actions that produced them.

    7.2 Preprocessing Pipeline

    The preprocessing pipeline is illustrated in Figure 4. Raw 60 FPS RGB video is processed offline through the TAEHV 1.5 encoder at a 4× temporal compression factor, producing latent sequences at 15 frames per second. In parallel, the high-frequency controller stream is aligned to the latent frame grid and bucketed into 15 snapshots per second. Each snapshot encodes the full button state vector (256-bucket discretization), the net mouse displacement (Δx,Δy) accumulated since the previous snapshot, and the scroll direction. The resulting paired clips (latent frames and controller sequences) are stored in a preprocessed format for efficient data loading.

    7.3 Sequence Packing

    To maximize GPU utilization and minimize padding waste during training, we apply cross-document sequence packing: latent sequences from multiple game clips are concatenated into a single training sequence with document IDs tracked per token. Attention masking prevents information from crossing clip boundaries, preserving the causal structure across packed sequences while allowing the model to train on long effective context windows without padding overhead.

    8 Evaluation

    The central design objective of Waypoint-1.5 is real-time interactive generation on consumer hardware. We therefore evaluate the system primarily on throughput, measured in latent frames per second (latent FPS) across a range of consumer NVIDIA GPUs. Latent FPS measures the rate at which the diffusion model generates latent frames; pixel-space video is subsequently decoded by the TAEHV 1.5 autoencoder at approximately 800 FPS, adding negligible overhead. Latent FPS is therefore responsible for governing the interactive responsiveness of the system.

    We benchmark the 720P and 360P variants under two precision regimes: INT8 quantization (enabled via custom kernels and torch.compile) and standard BF16. Results are reported in Table 2. We treat ≥30 latent FPS as a practical threshold for smooth real-time interactive generation.

    At 720P, INT8-quantized Waypoint-1.5 meets the 30 latent FPS threshold on all GPUs from the RTX 5060 Ti upward. The 360P variant reaches this threshold on all tested hardware, including the RTX 3060. INT8 quantization provides a consistent 1.5–2× throughput improvement over BF16 across all GPUs, and additionally resolves out-of-memory (OOM) conditions for the 720P BF16 model on the RTX 3070, whose 8 GB VRAM is insufficient to hold the full BF16 KV cache and model weights simultaneously. The RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell achieves the highest throughput at 132 latent FPS (720P INT8), more than 4× the real-time threshold.

    9 Safety & Ethics

    Safety in interactive world models presents challenges distinct from those in text, image, or even video generation systems. Unlike models that produce a single static output, world models generate persistent environments at high frame rates that respond continuously to user input. A single prompt can yield minutes of interactive content spanning diverse visual states, making post-hoc output review insufficient on its own. Safety must therefore be addressed across the full pipeline: in the training data, at prompt ingestion, during generation, at output delivery, and through ongoing monitoring.

    Safety has been part of the development process from the beginning. Rather than treating it as a post-deployment addition, we have built layered safeguards into each stage of the Waypoint pipeline. This section describes those layers, the tradeoffs involved, and our plans for continued improvement.

    We acknowledge that safety in generative systems involves inherent tensions between creative freedom and content restriction, between open research and controlled deployment, and between moving quickly as a startup and building robust safeguards. We do not claim to have resolved these tensions. Instead, we describe the systems we have built so far and the framework under which we continue to iterate.

    9.1 Safety Procedures Per Major Model Release

    Waypoint-1.5 underwent a structured safety review before release. We conducted internal testing to identify known failure modes, calibrate filtering thresholds, and evaluate the model’s behavior under adversarial prompting. A soft, controlled release was conducted via our self-hosted streaming service to evaluate how users attempt to circumvent safeguards or telegraph intended use.

    Safety review is not a single gate but a recurring cycle. Waypoint-1.5 incorporated lessons from prior deployment, including observed user behavior patterns, attempted jailbreaks, and content distribution analysis from real-world usage.

    9.2 Data Source Curation

    Training data and the decisions surrounding the data included in training is the first step towards ensuring safety. We apply source-level filtering before any data enter the training pipeline. This includes excluding sources known to contain disproportionate amounts of personally identifiable information (PII), adult content, or content that violates terms of service.

    Domain selection is guided by the model’s intended use case. We are primarily concerned with creating an interactive entertainment experience and enabling creative use. We prioritize sources whose content distribution aligns with that goal.

    9.3 Dataset Analysis & Filtering

    Beyond source-level curation, we perform clip-level and frame-level analysis of the pretraining corpus. We built a video scanning pipeline that processes the full dataset using a multi-stage classification approach. The pipeline runs two classifiers sequentially: a ResNet-50-based explicit content detector and a CLIP-based classifier (ViT-B/32) queried with prompts targeting potential depictions of minors across photorealistic, cartoon, and stylized formats.

    Each processed video produces structured metadata recording flagged frames by category and a determination of whether the clip should be excluded from training. This frame-level approach avoids the blunt removal of entire clips when only isolated frames are problematic, preserving useful training signal while removing unsafe content.

    Flagged content above confidence thresholds is downloaded and manually reviewed before final calibration, resulting in a dataset corpora with metadata which can be audited. This metadata also enables retrospective analysis: if filtering criteria change in future releases, previously processed data can be re-evaluated without full reprocessing.

    9.4 Prompt Filtering & Sanitation

    User prompts pass through an intermediate sanitation layer before reaching the world model. This layer serves a dual purpose: 1) safety enforcement and 2) structural alignment with the model’s training distribution.

    On the safety side, the sanitizer detects and transforms prompts containing references to explicit sexual content, depictions of minors, celebrity likeness, recognizable branded intellectual property, and other content categories. Rather than rejecting prompts outright, the system rewrites user intent into a safe environmental description suitable for generation. For example, a prompt referencing a specific copyrighted work is transformed into a description that captures the intended aesthetic without producing derivative content.

    On the structural side, as described in Section 3.3, the sanitizer enriches under-specified prompts into the structured signal format the world model expects: a) a seed image, b) a short synthetic video extension, and c) aligned control signals derived from the inverse dynamics model. This multi-feature approach means that the safety layer is not simply an optional filter but an integral component of the generation pipeline.

    Early versions of the sanitizer returned structured information about the elements removed alongside the sanitized prompt, which was useful for debugging but introduced unnecessary complexity. The current system returns only the sanitized prompt, reducing latency and surface area for failure.

    9.5 Mid-Generation Classification & Redirection

    Because world models generate content continuously and interactively, safety cannot rely solely on input filtering and output review. A prompt that passes all safety checks may nonetheless lead to unsafe visual states as the generated environment evolves in response to user actions.

    9.6 Output Classification & Transformation

    In addition to input and mid-generation safeguards, we apply post-generation analysis to completed outputs. Generated content passes through output classifiers before delivery to users.

    9.7 Prompt-Output Audit Dashboard

    Monitoring deployed systems requires visibility into what users are requesting and what the model is generating. We maintain moderation dashboards that track prompt distributions, flagged content rates, and generation outcomes over time.

    This monitoring serves multiple purposes: detecting emerging misuse patterns, identifying gaps in the filtering pipeline, and informing the prompt distribution analysis that guides future training data curation (see Section 7).

    9.8 Red-Teaming & Independent Audit

    Structured adversarial testing is a critical component of safety evaluation for generative systems. We conduct internal red-teaming before each major release, with team members attempting to elicit disallowed content through prompt manipulation, multi-step interaction sequences, and edge-case inputs.

    As a small team, we recognize that internal perspectives are limited. We actively seek external input from researchers, artists, and community members, and maintain public channels for reporting problematic generations.

    9.9 Model Cards, Model Licenses & Release Qualification

    Each release of the Waypoint model family includes documentation of capabilities, known limitations, and intended use cases in a published model card. We encourage downstream users and researchers building on Waypoint to publish model cards for their derivative work as well.

    Our release strategy reflects a commitment to open research alongside responsible deployment. Waypoint releases include:

  • •

    An Apache-licensed base model for broad research and commercial use.

  • •

    A larger non-commercial research model for academic experimentation.

  • •

    WorldEngine, our GPL-licensed inference library.

    • This tiered licensing structure supports open experimentation while discouraging closed, unattributed derivatives. The GPL license on WorldEngine ensures that modifications to the inference pipeline, including any safety-relevant changes, remain open.

    Terms of Service apply to hosted deployments and to partners hosting Waypoint models. These terms define prohibited content categories, usage restrictions, and reporting obligations. Licensing is treated as a safety mechanism in its own right: it shapes how the model is used in practice and establishes accountability for downstream deployment.

    10 Conclusion

    We have presented Waypoint-1.5, a 1.28B parameter single-stream causal Diffusion Transformer for real-time interactive video generation on consumer hardware. The system integrates frame-causal attention with a static rolling KV cache, Diffusion Forcing pretraining, Self-Forcing DMD post-training distillation, and the TAEHV 1.5 compact autoencoder, all trained on over 100,000 hours of controller-synchronized gameplay from the Owl-Control dataset. Together, these components enable stable long-horizon autoregressive rollout at 4 denoising steps per frame, with classifier-free guidance baked into the student during distillation rather than applied separately at inference.

    Benchmarked across ten consumer NVIDIA GPUs, the INT8-quantized 720P variant meets the 30 latent FPS real-time threshold on all GPUs from the RTX 5060 Ti upward, and the 360P variant achieves this on all tested hardware including the RTX 3060. These results show that interactive, controllable video generation at real-time frame rates is achievable on hardware end users already own, without enterprise-level infrastructure or streamed delivery. We hope Waypoint-1.5 serves as a practical foundation for future research in real-time world models and interactive video generation.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：用 10 万小时按键鼠标对齐的游戏录像训练，在消费级显卡上实时生成可玩画面。

要点：

  • 预训练数据是 10 万小时、与键盘鼠标输入逐帧对齐的多游戏视频
  • 提出区分 rendered FPS、latent FPS 与 control rate 三类指标，不拿画面帧率冒充交互性
  • 给出两个分辨率变体，覆盖从桌面独显到轻薄本的消费级硬件谱系

为什么值得看：评估 AI 原生引擎时，「画面帧率」和「控制响应率」是两件事，这套指标拆法可以直接拿来做验收口径。

中文摘要：Waypoint-1.5 把交互式世界模型（iWM）当成一个工程系统来写：它必须在严格延迟与吞吐约束下响应高密度用户输入。模型预训练于 10 万小时、与键盘鼠标控制对齐的多游戏视频，可按完整键鼠输入条件生成可玩画面，并提供两个分辨率变体以覆盖不同档位消费级显卡。论文给出一套评估语言：把渲染帧率、潜空间帧率与控制率分开度量，再以延迟和吞吐刻画交互性；同时完整交代了数据管线、网络结构、训练方法与运行时系统，最后讨论了这类模型特有的安全与伦理问题。对做生成式玩法的团队，这是一份难得的「全链路怎么搭」的公开说明。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

Waypoint-1.5: A Real-Time Video World Model for Consumer Hardware

Abstract

We present Waypoint-1.5, a real-time diffusion world model for interactive video generation on consumer-grade hardware. Unlike general video diffusion models, interactive world models (iWMs) must respond to dense user controls under strict latency and throughput constraints. Waypoint-1.5 is pre-trained on 100,000 hours of diverse, control-aligned video game data across hundreds of games, and generates playable video conditioned on full keyboard and mouse input. The model includes two resolution variants that run across a wide spectrum of consumer hardware. To characterize this unique setting, we distinguish rendered FPS, latent FPS, and control rate. We describe the data pipeline, architecture, training methodology, and runtime system behind Waypoint-1.5. We evaluate interactivity through latency and throughput. We conclude with a discussion of the safety and ethical considerations unique to iWMs.

1 Introduction

Neural networks are now capable of synthesizing coherent visual dynamics across space and time, as recent progress in generative video models has demonstrated. Impressive results in visual quality, temporal consistency, and prompt adherence have been achieved by systems including WAN ([22]), Hunyuan Video ([12]), LTX-Video ([9]), and comparable models. These models, however, are built mainly for offline text-guided video generation. Accordingly, prompt adherence, visual fidelity, and temporal coherence serve as the natural evaluation axes, measured by metrics such as VideoBench ([14]) and FVD ([21]). What this form of video generation does not offer is interactivity: users cannot actively steer the environment in real time through low-latency actions like keyboard and mouse inputs, but must instead rely on static text prompts.

Action-conditioned video world models on the other hand offer a solution to this problem. Systems at the frontier of this area: Sora ([5]), Genie ([3]), Hunyuan-GameCraft ([12]) among others, [24][15][19][20][16][1] have shown that coherent visual scenes and interactive worlds can be generated in direct response to user input. Such results suggest a future in which learned world models underpin interactive entertainment, simulation, and embodied AI.

However, there is a large hurdle to cross between research demonstrations and deployment in real-world systems. A large chunk of the existing video world models require enterprise level inference infrastructure (e.g H200s, B200s), yet cannot achieve high FPS or long-horizon rollouts with sufficient action adherence. In order for video world models to become a practical tool in domains such as game development, creative applications, immersive entertainment, and physical AI (e.g robotics, self-driving), it is critical that they must run on consumer grade hardware (e.g RTX 4090).

With this problem in mind, we present Waypoint-1.5, a video world model built from the ground up for real-time inference on consumer GPUs. Our model comprises a single-stream causal Diffusion Transformer (DiT) trained in the latent space of a distilled autoencoder, with design choices centered around the latency and throughput requirements for real-time interactive generation on consumer hardware. Our training methodology includes causal diffusion forcing pretraining, NorMuon optimization, and sequence packing to maximize GPU utilization. Together, these choices allow Waypoint-1.5 to excel and run in real time on a wide range of consumer GPUs (see Section 8).

In this technical report, we describe the model architecture (Section 2), pretraining methodology and input conditioning (Section 3), post-training distillation (Section 4), inference system (Section 5), autoencoder design (Section 6), data pipeline (Section 7), evaluation (Section 8), and safety considerations (Section 9).

2 Architecture

Waypoint-1.5 uses a a 1.28 billion parameter Diffusion Transformer model that processes all video latent frames in a clip as a unified sequence of tokens as a single-stream in contrast to dual-stream or cross-attention-based video DiTs that maintain separate pathways for conditioning and content. The training pipeline and overall architecture are illustrated in Figure 2.

2.1 Spatial Tokenization

We use TAEHV-1.5 to encode video frames into latents which compresses spatially by 16× and temporally by 4×. A 512×1024 frame, for example, yields a 32×64 latent, while a 256×512 frame yields a 16×32 latent. Each latent has 32 channels.

2.2 Frame-Causal Attention with KV Caching

We use factorized spatiotemporal attention wherein within each latent, tokens may attend bidirectionally to all other tokens. Across latents, a causal mask is applied using FlexAttention, which enables efficient and temporally autoregressive generation.

To balance short-term local context with long-range temporal coherence, we use a two-level attention hierarchy:

  • •

    Local window: each frame densely attends to the preceding 16 frames.

  • •

    Global dilated window: every 4th block also attends to a set of evenly-spaced frames within a 128-frame context window, using a pinned dilation factor of 8. This sparse global attention efficiently covers long-range context without quadratic memory growth.

    • Static Rolling KV Cache.

    During inference, a static ring-buffer KV-cache stores the key-value representations of past fully denoised frames. Noisy intermediate frames during multi-step denoising are not cached. The cache is pre-allocated to a fixed capacity to prevent unbounded VRAM growth: for local attention layers, a dense ring of 16 frames is maintained, with the oldest frame evicted when a new one is committed. Every 4th block uses global dilated attention with a 128-frame ring and a fixed dilation of 8, meaning new frames evict older ones at regular intervals rather than simply discarding the oldest.

    2.3 Grouped Query Attention

    In order to reduce the KV memory footprint and memory bandwidth, we use Grouped Query Attention (GQA) [2] with 32 query heads and 16 key-value heads (2:1 ratio). This halves the KV memory footprint relative to standard multi-head attention.

    2.4 WAN-Style AdaLN Noise Conditioning

    We perform noise conditioning following Wan [22]: the scalar noise level σ is encoded through a Fourier feature embedding (512-dimensional) passed through a small MLP to produce a conditioning vector. This vector further passes through a CondHead module which generates three modulation parameters per sub-layer: scale s, bias b, and gate g; as used in adaptive layer normalization:

    AdaLN(x; s,b,g)=g⊙LN(x)·(1+s)+b,

    		(1)

    where LN denotes layer normalization. The CondHead weights are shared across all 24 transformer layers. This weight tying substantially reduces parameter count while maintaining effective noise conditioning throughout the network depth. The CondHead output projection is zero-initialized (AdaLN-Zero) to ensure identity-like behavior at the beginning of training. Additionally, a learnable per-layer bias is added to each conditioning layer’s output which provides layer-specific offsets alongside the shared head.

    2.5 Positional Encoding: OrthoRoPE

    Position is encoded via OrthoRoPE, an orthogonal variant of Rotary Position Embeddings [18] that applies independent rotations for spatial (x, y) and temporal (t) dimensions within a single per-head embedding. With a head dimension of 64, we allocate 8 dimensions per spatial axis and 16 dimensions to the temporal axis, providing distinct Nyquist-tuned frequency bands for spatial proximity and temporal ordering. Spatial frequencies are scaled to the video’s spatial Nyquist frequency. Temporal frequencies use a standard base of 10,000.

    2.6 Controller Conditioning

    At each transformer block, the model receives controller inputs: discretized button states (256-bucket encoding), continuous mouse displacement (Δx,Δy), and scroll sign. These are concatenated and projected to d_model via a learned MLP, then fused into the block’s intermediate representation through MLPFusion, a lightweight residual module:

    x ← x+SiLU (W₁x+W₂c)·W₃,

    		(2)

    where c is the projected controller embedding. During training, controller conditioning is randomly dropped with probability p_cfg to support classifier-free guidance (CFG) at inference time.

    2.7 Model Configuration

    A summary of the model configuration is provided in Table 1.

    3 Training

    3.1 Diffusion Forcing

    We pretrain using Diffusion Forcing[6][17], a training objective that supports causal autoregressive rollout without sacrificing the expressiveness of a full diffusion model. The key difference from standard video diffusion training is that rather than applying a uniform noise level across all frames in a clip, Diffusion Forcing assigns an independent noise level σᵢ to each frame i, sampled from a per-frame distribution over [0,1]:

    σᵢ=sigmoid(εᵢ), εᵢ∼ℕ(0,1), i=1,…,N.

    		(3)

    Given clean video latents x∈ℝ^B×N×C×H×W, the rectified-flow target velocity, noised input, and training objective are:

    v^*=ε-x, ε∼ℕ(0,I),(4)
    xₜ=x+v^*·σᵢ,(5)
    v̂=F_θ(xₜ, σ, c),(6)
    L=𝔼 [∥v^*-v̂∥²],(7)

    where c denotes all conditioning inputs (previous frames, controller). Training on frames with heterogeneous, independently sampled noise levels teaches the model to denoise each frame conditioned on all preceding frames at their respective noise levels. This mirrors the autoregressive inference regime, where past frames sit at a low noise level (σ_ctx≈0.15) as clean context while the current frame is denoised from σ=1 to σ=0, and naturally pushes the model to handle the partial corruption of prior states it will encounter at rollout time.

    3.2 NorMuon

    All 2D weight matrices (query, key, value, and output projections, and MLP weights) are optimized with NorMuon[11][13] at a learning rate of 1×10⁻³. All remaining parameters (embeddings, biases, normalization scalars) use AdamW at 1×10⁻⁴.

    3.3 Input Conditioning

    Waypoint-1.5 models the transition function p(zₜ|z_2. CFG dropout during training enables unconditional rollouts at inference. At deployment, user inputs are sanitized and mapped to the expected controller format before reaching the model, which also serves as an additional safety layer as described in Section 9.

    4 Post-Training

    Direct inference with the pretrained Waypoint-1.5 model runs into two problems. The first is compute: each frame requires solving a multi-step ODE (typically 60 solver steps), and classifier-free guidance doubles the effective step count by requiring independent forward passes for conditioned and unconditioned predictions, bringing the effective inference cost to ∼120 forward passes per frame. The second is exposure bias: the model is trained on ground-truth context frames corrupted with varying noise, but at inference it must condition on its own imperfect predictions from prior steps. This mismatch causes visual drift and incoherence over long rollouts.

    We address both with a custom Self-Forcing DMD post-training procedure, drawing on Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) [23], Self-Forcing [10], and Self-Forcing++ [7]. The procedure jointly optimizes a student model F_θ, a frozen teacher copy F_φ, and a trainable critic F_ψ. Self-forcing trains the student to generate video autoregressively, conditioning exclusively on its own previously generated clean frames:

    p_θ(z_1:T)=∏ₜ₌₁ᵀp_θ (zₜ \middle| ẑ_

    		(8)

    where ẑ_

    The teacher is evaluated under multi-condition CFG:

    v̂_teacher=v_∅+ω_ctrl (v_ctrl-v_∅)+ω_ctx (v_ctx-v_∅),

    		(9)

    with ω_ctrl=15.0, ω_ctx=2.0, and v_∅ the unconditioned prediction. The student learns to match this guided distribution directly, removing the need to compute v_∅ at inference. The DMD loss [23] minimizes an approximate KL divergence between the student and teacher denoising distributions, with the critic providing the score gradient signal. Training stability is further supported by two regularization terms from SenseFlow [8]: IDA (Implicit Distribution Alignment) keeps the critic parameters close to the student via an EMA update after each student step, preventing critic divergence; and ISG (Intra-Segment Guidance) enforces consistency between adjacent noise levels by matching student and teacher predictions at intermediate points along the denoising trajectory.

    Sequence-Packed Teacher Forcing.

    To compute gradients over autoregressive sequences without costly per-frame backward passes, we use sequence-packed teacher forcing: context and current frames are concatenated into a single forward pass, with a binary mask distinguishing context-only tokens (\textttcid=0, no gradient) from gradient-carrying tokens (\textttcid=1). A similar strategy was developed concurrently by [16]. A custom attention rule prevents leakage between the two copies of the same frame: context tokens attend only to context, current-frame tokens attend only to their own same-frame tokens, and current-frame tokens are blocked from attending to the context copy of the same frame.

    This distillation procedure yields an approximate 30× total inference speedup over the pretrained baseline. Baking in CFG eliminates the 2× per-step overhead, cutting the effective forward pass count from 120 to 60. Compressing the denoising trajectory from 60 steps down to 4 provides an additional ∼15× throughput improvement. The resulting 4-step model generates high-quality frames conditioned on a rolling window of clean, self-generated context, and remains stable over long rollout horizons.

    5 Inference

    5.1 Autoregressive Generation and KV Caching

    Waypoint-1.5 generates video autoregressively, producing one latent frame at a time. At each step, the model receives a single noisy frame and all controller inputs for that frame, and denoises it conditioned on the full history of past clean frames. Rather than re-encoding the entire history at every step, we use a static rolling KV cache that stores key-value representations of past frames and is updated incrementally.

    The cache is structured as a ring buffer per transformer layer. Each layer maintains a buffer of capacity (L+t_pf) token slots, where L is the layer’s context window in tokens and t_pf is the number of tokens per frame. The final t_pf slots form a dedicated tail that always holds the current frame under active denoising. During multi-step denoising, the cache is frozen: the tail is written on every denoising step (allowing the model to attend to the current noisy frame), but the ring buffer is not updated. Once the frame is fully denoised to σ=0, the cache is unfrozen and the clean frame is committed to the ring. This ensures the persistent context consists exclusively of fully denoised frames, avoiding error accumulation from noisy context frames.

    For layers with global dilated attention (every 4th layer), the ring buffer uses a pinned dilation factor of 8: new frames evict slots at spacing 8 within the 128-frame window, retaining an evenly-spaced snapshot of the long-range history. Local attention layers maintain a dense 16-frame ring.

    5.2 Seed Frames and Context Priming

    Generation begins with a set of seed frames: clean ground-truth latents provided as initial context. By default, a single seed image is used. The first generated latent is conditioned on this seed frame and subsequent latents are generated in groups of 4. The seed frame is not re-denoised. Instead, a zero-noise forward pass (σ=0) is run to populate the KV cache without modifying the latent. This primes the cache with the seed before the first generated frame is produced.

    During the pretrained (pre-distillation) inference regime, previously generated context frames are held at a small fixed noise level σ_ctx=0.15 when used as conditioning. This parameter introduces a slight corruption that bridges the gap between the clean seed frames and the partially noisy frames the model encountered during Diffusion Forcing training. After Self-Forcing distillation, the model conditions on fully clean self-generated history, so it is set to 0.0.

    5.3 Denoising Schedules

    Pre-distillation.

    The pretrained model uses 60 denoising steps per frame with a flow-matching Euler scheduler. A shift of 3.0 applied to the noise schedule compresses it toward lower noise levels, concentrating the sampling budget in the refinement regime. CFG is applied at each step by running a conditioned and unconditioned forward pass and combining them with a guidance weight, doubling the effective per-frame cost to 60×2=120 model evaluations per frame.

    Post-distillation.

    After Self-Forcing distillation, the denoising schedule collapses to 4 steps per frame with a fixed trajectory: σ∈{1.0,0.9,0.75,0.3,0.0}. CFG is no longer applied separately, as it is baked into the student during distillation, so each frame requires only 4 forward passes. The teacher CFG scales used are ω_ctrl=15.0 and ω_ctx=2.0. The distilled model conditions on clean self-generated context, removing the context corruption used during pretraining.

    5.4 Runtime Optimizations

    The frozen-cache denoising step and the unfrozen cache-writing step are compiled ahead of time with torch.compile, using max-autotune mode with full graph capture and static shapes. This enables kernel fusion, memory layout optimization, and CUDA graph capture, eliminating Python dispatch overhead on each forward pass. The full diffusion model is deployed in INT8 quantized precision for throughput-critical inference, as reflected in the benchmark results of Section 8. BF16 inference is also supported where VRAM permits.

    6 Autoencoders & Tokenization

    6.1 Latent Autoencoder

    Waypoint-1.5 encodes video into a compact latent representation using TAEHV 1.5[4], a tiny autoencoder designed to approximate the latent space of the Hunyuan VAE 1.5. TAEHV 1.5 applies spatial downsampling alongside a temporal compression factor of 4, mapping 60 raw FPS to 15 latent frames per second. The encoder produces 32-channel latent frames, significantly more compact than the original VAE latent. For a 512×1024 input clip the encoded latent has spatial dimensions 32×64, and for a 256×512 input clip it is 16×32. This compression reduces a 13-second video clip (768 raw frames) to 192 latent frames, making transformer-scale training over long sequences tractable.

    6.2 Distilled Autoencoder Decode

    Standard high-fidelity autoencoders are designed for quality rather than throughput, and naive inference can make the decode step a significant bottleneck in a real-time pipeline. TAEHV 1.5 sidesteps this by design: as a tiny distilled approximation of the full Hunyuan VAE 1.5, it trades a small amount of reconstruction fidelity for a dramatically reduced parameter count and arithmetic cost. Inference runs in FP16, achieving approximately 800 FPS decode throughput on an NVIDIA RTX 5090, fast enough to make decoder overhead negligible relative to the diffusion model.

    6.3 Patchification

    After encoding, each latent frame is further tokenized by a learned 2×2 patch embedding (Conv2d with kernel size and stride [2,2]). At 512×1024 this produces 16×32=512 tokens per latent frame, and at 256×512 it produces 8×16=128. The spatial layout of patches is arranged to align with the block boundaries used by FlexAttention’s sparse kernel, ensuring block-level parallelism maps to spatially contiguous regions.

    7 Data

    7.1 Owl-Control Dataset

    Waypoint-1.5 is trained on Owl-Control, a proprietary dataset of controller-synchronized video game footage comprising over 100,000 hours of gameplay across hundreds of distinct games. Each recording pairs high-fidelity visual observations with the full controller input stream that produced them, enabling the model to learn a grounded mapping from game state to player action.

    Raw video is captured at 720P and 60 FPS. Controller inputs (keyboard states, raw mouse displacement, and scroll events) are recorded at up to 10,000 Hz via a high-fidelity hardware logging layer, precisely synchronized to the video timeline to enable accurate alignment between visual frames and the controller actions that produced them.

    7.2 Preprocessing Pipeline

    The preprocessing pipeline is illustrated in Figure 4. Raw 60 FPS RGB video is processed offline through the TAEHV 1.5 encoder at a 4× temporal compression factor, producing latent sequences at 15 frames per second. In parallel, the high-frequency controller stream is aligned to the latent frame grid and bucketed into 15 snapshots per second. Each snapshot encodes the full button state vector (256-bucket discretization), the net mouse displacement (Δx,Δy) accumulated since the previous snapshot, and the scroll direction. The resulting paired clips (latent frames and controller sequences) are stored in a preprocessed format for efficient data loading.

    7.3 Sequence Packing

    To maximize GPU utilization and minimize padding waste during training, we apply cross-document sequence packing: latent sequences from multiple game clips are concatenated into a single training sequence with document IDs tracked per token. Attention masking prevents information from crossing clip boundaries, preserving the causal structure across packed sequences while allowing the model to train on long effective context windows without padding overhead.

    8 Evaluation

    The central design objective of Waypoint-1.5 is real-time interactive generation on consumer hardware. We therefore evaluate the system primarily on throughput, measured in latent frames per second (latent FPS) across a range of consumer NVIDIA GPUs. Latent FPS measures the rate at which the diffusion model generates latent frames; pixel-space video is subsequently decoded by the TAEHV 1.5 autoencoder at approximately 800 FPS, adding negligible overhead. Latent FPS is therefore responsible for governing the interactive responsiveness of the system.

    We benchmark the 720P and 360P variants under two precision regimes: INT8 quantization (enabled via custom kernels and torch.compile) and standard BF16. Results are reported in Table 2. We treat ≥30 latent FPS as a practical threshold for smooth real-time interactive generation.

    At 720P, INT8-quantized Waypoint-1.5 meets the 30 latent FPS threshold on all GPUs from the RTX 5060 Ti upward. The 360P variant reaches this threshold on all tested hardware, including the RTX 3060. INT8 quantization provides a consistent 1.5–2× throughput improvement over BF16 across all GPUs, and additionally resolves out-of-memory (OOM) conditions for the 720P BF16 model on the RTX 3070, whose 8 GB VRAM is insufficient to hold the full BF16 KV cache and model weights simultaneously. The RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell achieves the highest throughput at 132 latent FPS (720P INT8), more than 4× the real-time threshold.

    9 Safety & Ethics

    Safety in interactive world models presents challenges distinct from those in text, image, or even video generation systems. Unlike models that produce a single static output, world models generate persistent environments at high frame rates that respond continuously to user input. A single prompt can yield minutes of interactive content spanning diverse visual states, making post-hoc output review insufficient on its own. Safety must therefore be addressed across the full pipeline: in the training data, at prompt ingestion, during generation, at output delivery, and through ongoing monitoring.

    Safety has been part of the development process from the beginning. Rather than treating it as a post-deployment addition, we have built layered safeguards into each stage of the Waypoint pipeline. This section describes those layers, the tradeoffs involved, and our plans for continued improvement.

    We acknowledge that safety in generative systems involves inherent tensions between creative freedom and content restriction, between open research and controlled deployment, and between moving quickly as a startup and building robust safeguards. We do not claim to have resolved these tensions. Instead, we describe the systems we have built so far and the framework under which we continue to iterate.

    9.1 Safety Procedures Per Major Model Release

    Waypoint-1.5 underwent a structured safety review before release. We conducted internal testing to identify known failure modes, calibrate filtering thresholds, and evaluate the model’s behavior under adversarial prompting. A soft, controlled release was conducted via our self-hosted streaming service to evaluate how users attempt to circumvent safeguards or telegraph intended use.

    Safety review is not a single gate but a recurring cycle. Waypoint-1.5 incorporated lessons from prior deployment, including observed user behavior patterns, attempted jailbreaks, and content distribution analysis from real-world usage.

    9.2 Data Source Curation

    Training data and the decisions surrounding the data included in training is the first step towards ensuring safety. We apply source-level filtering before any data enter the training pipeline. This includes excluding sources known to contain disproportionate amounts of personally identifiable information (PII), adult content, or content that violates terms of service.

    Domain selection is guided by the model’s intended use case. We are primarily concerned with creating an interactive entertainment experience and enabling creative use. We prioritize sources whose content distribution aligns with that goal.

    9.3 Dataset Analysis & Filtering

    Beyond source-level curation, we perform clip-level and frame-level analysis of the pretraining corpus. We built a video scanning pipeline that processes the full dataset using a multi-stage classification approach. The pipeline runs two classifiers sequentially: a ResNet-50-based explicit content detector and a CLIP-based classifier (ViT-B/32) queried with prompts targeting potential depictions of minors across photorealistic, cartoon, and stylized formats.

    Each processed video produces structured metadata recording flagged frames by category and a determination of whether the clip should be excluded from training. This frame-level approach avoids the blunt removal of entire clips when only isolated frames are problematic, preserving useful training signal while removing unsafe content.

    Flagged content above confidence thresholds is downloaded and manually reviewed before final calibration, resulting in a dataset corpora with metadata which can be audited. This metadata also enables retrospective analysis: if filtering criteria change in future releases, previously processed data can be re-evaluated without full reprocessing.

    9.4 Prompt Filtering & Sanitation

    User prompts pass through an intermediate sanitation layer before reaching the world model. This layer serves a dual purpose: 1) safety enforcement and 2) structural alignment with the model’s training distribution.

    On the safety side, the sanitizer detects and transforms prompts containing references to explicit sexual content, depictions of minors, celebrity likeness, recognizable branded intellectual property, and other content categories. Rather than rejecting prompts outright, the system rewrites user intent into a safe environmental description suitable for generation. For example, a prompt referencing a specific copyrighted work is transformed into a description that captures the intended aesthetic without producing derivative content.

    On the structural side, as described in Section 3.3, the sanitizer enriches under-specified prompts into the structured signal format the world model expects: a) a seed image, b) a short synthetic video extension, and c) aligned control signals derived from the inverse dynamics model. This multi-feature approach means that the safety layer is not simply an optional filter but an integral component of the generation pipeline.

    Early versions of the sanitizer returned structured information about the elements removed alongside the sanitized prompt, which was useful for debugging but introduced unnecessary complexity. The current system returns only the sanitized prompt, reducing latency and surface area for failure.

    9.5 Mid-Generation Classification & Redirection

    Because world models generate content continuously and interactively, safety cannot rely solely on input filtering and output review. A prompt that passes all safety checks may nonetheless lead to unsafe visual states as the generated environment evolves in response to user actions.

    9.6 Output Classification & Transformation

    In addition to input and mid-generation safeguards, we apply post-generation analysis to completed outputs. Generated content passes through output classifiers before delivery to users.

    9.7 Prompt-Output Audit Dashboard

    Monitoring deployed systems requires visibility into what users are requesting and what the model is generating. We maintain moderation dashboards that track prompt distributions, flagged content rates, and generation outcomes over time.

    This monitoring serves multiple purposes: detecting emerging misuse patterns, identifying gaps in the filtering pipeline, and informing the prompt distribution analysis that guides future training data curation (see Section 7).

    9.8 Red-Teaming & Independent Audit

    Structured adversarial testing is a critical component of safety evaluation for generative systems. We conduct internal red-teaming before each major release, with team members attempting to elicit disallowed content through prompt manipulation, multi-step interaction sequences, and edge-case inputs.

    As a small team, we recognize that internal perspectives are limited. We actively seek external input from researchers, artists, and community members, and maintain public channels for reporting problematic generations.

    9.9 Model Cards, Model Licenses & Release Qualification

    Each release of the Waypoint model family includes documentation of capabilities, known limitations, and intended use cases in a published model card. We encourage downstream users and researchers building on Waypoint to publish model cards for their derivative work as well.

    Our release strategy reflects a commitment to open research alongside responsible deployment. Waypoint releases include:

  • •

    An Apache-licensed base model for broad research and commercial use.

  • •

    A larger non-commercial research model for academic experimentation.

  • •

    WorldEngine, our GPL-licensed inference library.

    • This tiered licensing structure supports open experimentation while discouraging closed, unattributed derivatives. The GPL license on WorldEngine ensures that modifications to the inference pipeline, including any safety-relevant changes, remain open.

    Terms of Service apply to hosted deployments and to partners hosting Waypoint models. These terms define prohibited content categories, usage restrictions, and reporting obligations. Licensing is treated as a safety mechanism in its own right: it shapes how the model is used in practice and establishes accountability for downstream deployment.

    10 Conclusion

    We have presented Waypoint-1.5, a 1.28B parameter single-stream causal Diffusion Transformer for real-time interactive video generation on consumer hardware. The system integrates frame-causal attention with a static rolling KV cache, Diffusion Forcing pretraining, Self-Forcing DMD post-training distillation, and the TAEHV 1.5 compact autoencoder, all trained on over 100,000 hours of controller-synchronized gameplay from the Owl-Control dataset. Together, these components enable stable long-horizon autoregressive rollout at 4 denoising steps per frame, with classifier-free guidance baked into the student during distillation rather than applied separately at inference.

    Benchmarked across ten consumer NVIDIA GPUs, the INT8-quantized 720P variant meets the 30 latent FPS real-time threshold on all GPUs from the RTX 5060 Ti upward, and the 360P variant achieves this on all tested hardware including the RTX 3060. These results show that interactive, controllable video generation at real-time frame rates is achievable on hardware end users already own, without enterprise-level infrastructure or streamed delivery. We hope Waypoint-1.5 serves as a practical foundation for future research in real-time world models and interactive video generation.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 一张 5090 跑 60 帧游戏世界模型：拆解 Matrix-Game 4.0 的「引擎接地」架构 ｜ 一张5090跑60帧游戏世界模型
item.description:
一句话：把系统劈成两半——引擎管规则、模型只画画面，是它能在单卡上实时的根本原因。

要点：

  • 运行时是五层单向流水线：原生引擎出低模 RGB 与逐帧元数据，因果视频模型每块 4 帧流式生成，有界发布层 4 槽队列，WebRTC 传输，最后才是 HUD 与声音对齐
  • 渲染层主干是 Wan2.2 5B 潜空间：48 个潜变量通道、空间分辨率 30×54、时间压缩因子 4，首块 1 帧、之后每块 4 帧，预测结果以零噪声写回 KV 缓存
  • 所有权边界写得很硬：推理包不依赖游戏/HTTP/GStreamer，C++20 游戏不 import Python，服务端只持有一个会话；5080 达 67 FPS、5070 Ti 为 58 FPS

为什么值得看：它示范了「模型只是引擎里的一个可替换部件」这种分工方式，以及为了实时性必须在架构层做出的解耦。

中文摘要：文章按「问题—架构—数据流—推理优化—边界」五层拆解昆仑万维 2026 年 10 月 15 日开源的 Matrix-Game 4.0。核心决策是放弃纯生成路线，改走引擎接地：可执行的 low-poly 引擎持有玩法、物理与输入，模型只把干净的低模 RGB 逐帧翻译成电影质感画面，因此规则确定、世界不漂移、生成负担骤降。运行时是一条五层单向流水线，模型以因果分块方式流式生成（首块 1 帧、之后每块 4 帧），每块结果以零噪声写回 KV 缓存；发布层用 4 槽有界队列，拥塞时只丢显示帧、绝不阻塞推理。HUD 与声音被刻意排除在模型之外，在帧真正呈现时对齐。作者也点出代价：480×864 的分辨率与约七帧的延迟，仍与原生引擎不在一个量级。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：公众号·陈嗣俊（中文）

一张5090跑60帧的游戏世界模型2026 年 10 月 15 日，昆仑万维（Skywork AI）开源了 Matrix-Game 4.0，口号是"面向可玩游戏的流式神经渲染"（Streaming Neural Rendering for Playable Games）。第二天，项目仓库连续提交了 RTX 5090、RTX 5080、RTX 5070 Ti 的单卡推理优化：在 864×480 分辨率、固定提示词加 SageAttention 的稳态吞吐下，RTX 5080 跑到 67 FPS，RTX 5070 Ti 跑到 58 FPS。换句话说，你桌上一张消费级显卡，就能实时驱动一个画面由生成式模型逐帧"画"出来、但规则由真实游戏引擎严格执行的可玩 3D 游戏。

这不是一个"AI 生成视频游戏"的玩具 Demo。随 4.0 一起放出的是三个完整可玩的原生游戏——第三人称射击的《中世纪城堡》和《古埃及》，以及赛车游戏《城市竞速》；模型权重、游戏素材全部挂上 Hugging Face，代码仓库（Apache-2.0）里既有离线渲染管线，也有单用户 WebRTC 浏览器实机演示，还附带了刚发布的技术报告。从 2025 年 5 月的 1.0 到现在，Matrix-Game 已经迭代了四个大版本，是目前开源互动世界模型里路线最清晰的一个系列。

这篇文章要拆的是它最核心的一个架构决策，也是我认为最值得做生成式互动内容的工程师研究的地方：为什么它没有让大模型"生成整个游戏"，而是坚定地把系统劈成两半——引擎管规则，模型管画画。这个分工看似朴素，实则同时解决了世界模型落地游戏的两大死穴：物理一致性和实时性。下面按"问题—架构—数据流—推理优化—边界"五层拆开讲，所有数字都来自官方 README、架构文档和技术报告。

一、先厘清：世界模型做游戏，有两条根本不同的路用生成式模型做"可玩的互动内容"，业界目前有两条技术路线。

第一条是纯生成路线。模型直接吃玩家的键盘鼠标输入和历史帧，吐出下一帧画面。物理碰撞、物体持久性、因果关系全部隐式压缩在神经网络权重里。这条路最激进，想象空间最大——理论上不需要游戏引擎，任何画面都能生成。但它有两个至今没有根治的问题：一是一致性崩坏，转角再转回来房间布局可能变了，子弹打中没有打中全凭模型"记忆"，长时序下世界会漂移；二是延迟和算力，每帧都要完整扩散采样，480p 都很难在单卡上跑到可玩帧率，更别说给玩家一个"确定"的规则系统（竞赛、判定、联网都无从谈起）。

第二条就是 Matrix-Game 4.0 走的引擎接地路线（engine-grounded）。保留一个真正可执行的低多边形（low-poly）游戏引擎，游戏逻辑、物理状态、玩家输入全部留在引擎里，由它精确模拟；模型不做决策、不碰规则，只负责一件事——把引擎输出的干净低模 RGB 画面，逐帧"翻译"成高细节的电影质感画面。你可以把它理解成：游戏世界的"骨架和物理定律"是传统引擎，模型是一层实时神经后期滤镜，但这层滤镜强大到能把简陋方块变成有光影、材质和氛围的写实场景。

这个分工带来三个决定性好处。规则绝对确定：命中判定、碰撞、胜负由引擎代码保证，绝不会因为模型抽风而改变。世界绝不漂移：模型每一帧都以引擎的真实几何为条件，它没有机会"自由发挥"改房间布局。生成负担骤降：模型不需要无中生有地预测整个世界，只需要在给定几何、给定条件下做视觉细化，这使得单步去重、少步采样成为可能，实时帧率才有了工程基础。

二、整体架构：一条严格单向的运行时流水线官方架构文档里把运行时契约（runtime contract）写成一行流水线，我把它转成不会错位的分层结构，每一层的职责和数据都标清楚。

# Matrix-Game 4.0 运行时五层流水线

① 原生游戏引擎层

可执行 low-poly 游戏(射击 120Hz 物理), 处理玩法/物理/输入, 输出干净 RGB + 逐帧元数据

② 因果视频渲染层

causal video model, 以 low-poly RGB + 文本提示为条件, 流式分块(每块 4 帧)生成高细节画面

③ 有界显示发布层

bounded publisher, 仅解码后的显示帧可丢弃, 队列 4 槽, 网络拥塞绝不阻塞模型推理

④ WebRTC 传输层

视频流走 WebRTC 推到浏览器, 帧元数据绑定真实 RTP 时间戳

⑤ 表现层

HUD 和声音在画面呈现时才对齐, 不属于模型输出; 射击音为合成, 赛车音由遥测驱动

关键所有权边界: 推理包不 import 游戏/HTTP/GStreamer; 原生游戏不 import Python; 服务端只拥有一个会话并连接双方。

注意这套设计在工程上的洁癖。官方文档专门写了"Ownership"一节：模型推理包不依赖游戏、不依赖 HTTP、不依赖 GStreamer；原生游戏是 C++20 写的，完全不 import Python；由服务端独占一个会话把两侧接起来。离线渲染甚至不需要 aiohttp、GStreamer 或一个正在运行的游戏。这种强解耦让模型团队和游戏团队可以完全并行迭代，也是它能同时交付离线渲染和在线演示两套路径的原因。

HUD（血条、小地图、准星）和声音被刻意放在模型之外，作为帧对齐的表现层。这是个很聪明的决定：HUD 要求绝对清晰可读，交给生成模型反而会糊掉、会跳字；让 HUD 在最终画面上叠加，既省生成算力，又保证 UI 精确。声音同理，射击游戏的枪声是合成的，赛车的引擎声由车速遥测实时驱动音高和音量，在视频帧真正呈现的那一刻对齐——而不是消息到达时对齐，避免音画不同步。

三、模型内核：Wan2.2 5B 潜空间 + 因果分块流式生成渲染层的主干不是从零造的，而是基于 Wan2.2 的 5B 潜空间：48 个潜变量通道，空间分辨率 30×54，时间压缩因子 4。这里有几个对理解性能和画质至关重要的细节。

因果分块（causal chunk）。模型不是一次生成整段视频，而是一块一块流式生成。第一个 RGB 块是 1 帧，之后每块 4 帧。每生成一块，干净的预测结果以"零噪声"写回 KV 缓存（drop_control=True），下一块在这个确定的历史上继续。这正是"因果"二字的含义——严格按时间顺序，只依赖过去，天然适合边玩边生成的流式场景。

有界的 21 潜变量缓存。它没有无限增长的注意力窗口，而是用一个固定的 sink（汇聚帧）加 21 个潜变量的有界缓存，配固定的 sink RoPE 位置编码，CFG（分类器自由引导）设为 1，时间步映射用 shift-5。控制住上下文长度，就控制住了单帧延迟和显存——这是能跑到实时的前提。一个会话有有限的 RoPE 预算（默认 8192 个生成潜变量块），到了就开新会话，而不是偷偷让位置编码回绕，避免长局画面崩坏。

赛车与射击的 sink 用法不同。射击场景没有给"高质量首帧"，独立编码的 sink 图只是 KV 里的恒等前缀，本身不被渲染、不当作控制帧；而赛车场景用的是绝对 sink RoPE，给定的参考图会被解码成第 0 帧，直接种进解码器历史。这种差异来自两类游戏对开场画面的不同需求，文档里讲得很细。

# 因果流式渲染的核心参数

# 射击模型关键配置 (architecture.md)

输出分辨率      : 480 x 864 (竖屏第三人称)

引擎采集        : 1280 x 720 low-poly RGBA -> RGB

双线性缩放 + 中心裁剪到训练预处理

潜空间          : Wan2.2 5B, 48 通道, 30x54, 时间因子4

因果块          : 第 1 块 1 帧, 此后每块 4 帧

注意力缓存      : sink + 21 潜变量有界窗口, CFG=1

干净回写        : 每块后零噪声写回 KV, drop_control=True

单会话 RoPE 预算 : 8192 潜变量块, 到限开新会话

四、最难的工程题：物理 120Hz，生成只有几十帧，怎么同步游戏物理跑在 120Hz，而模型只能输出 20 到 60 FPS，两者节奏天然不匹配。这是所有"引擎+生成"方案最容易翻车的地方。Matrix-Game 4.0 的处理方式值得逐条看。

每帧推进整数个物理步。在线采集时，每一帧画面对应整数个物理步进，所以支持的目标帧率必须能整除 120：20、24、30、40、60 FPS 都是合法值。不会出现"半次物理更新"这种不确定状态。射击游戏本地录制还有一个独立的 48 FPS / 2 倍仿真时间模式；赛车则在线支持 1 到 60 FPS 任意档，由引擎选一个能被采集节奏整除的物理速率。

有界 IPC 与背压（backpressure）。游戏和模型之间走私有 socketpair，协议是"长度前缀 JSON + 原始像素"，只接受有界数据包和连续帧序号，防止一个慢消费者拖垮整个系统。预处理只允许一块前瞻，绝不允许跳过模型的条件帧、也不允许改变它们的仿真时间节奏。最关键的一条策略：当模型生产被阻塞时，游戏会相对于墙上时钟变慢，而不是事后猛追一段 burst。也就是说宁可让游戏整体慢下来，也不允许物理在模型卡顿后瞬间补跑一大段——因为补跑会破坏玩家输入和画面的因果对应。

只丢"解码后的显示帧"，绝不丢推理帧。显示帧队列只有 4 个槽，媒体子进程和浏览器即使在网络抖动时也不会反过来阻塞模型推理。帧元数据绑定真实的 RTP 时间戳，浏览器在某一帧视频真正呈现时才去匹配 HUD 和音频。输入侧同样有界：射击鼠标增量约 120Hz 发送、按物理速率消费，待处理旋转被限制在 50 毫秒以内，镜头每秒最多转 90 度，防止延迟堆积导致"转身瞬移"。

五、60 帧是怎么省出来的：把每一个部件都换成快路径很多人看到"5B 视频模型实时游戏"的第一反应是不可能。关键在于它在推理路径上做了一整套协同优化，而且区分了两个画质档位。

两个预设档位。quality 档用 Wan 官方 VAE 编解码、两次去噪（时间步 1000 和 500，含启动）、原生 DiT，画质优先；realtime 档用 TAEHV 近似编解码器、单步去噪、ring/fused 内核的 DiT 再加 CUDA Graph 回放。需要说明的是，TAEHV 是近似编码器，与 Wan VAE 并非数值等价，快路径还会改变浮点归约顺序——官方明确建议做基准对照时保留 native 档。实时可玩，靠的就是 realtime 这一档。

消费级显卡的针对性量化。RTX 5090 预设在加载时把 DiT 块的线性层权重转成 FP8、推理时对激活做量化，而嵌入层和输出头保留 BF16，用的是同一份场景检查点，不需要单独的量化模型。更有意思的是 RTX 5070 Ti：在这个模型的 GEMM 形状下，INT8（W8A8，免校准）比 FP8 更快，所以 16GB 卡反而用 INT8 块线性层，调参逻辑直接开放在配置文件里。SageAttention 则为完整历史窗口提供更快的自注意力后端（窗口预热期仍回退 SDPA），编译时还为 CUDA Graph 打了专门的补丁。

# 官方性能数据 (2026-10-16)

# 各显卡实测模型吞吐 (864x480, 稳态, 不含视频I/O)

显卡             预设              FPS     显存

A100 80GB        realtime/固定     38-39    -

A100 (赛车动态)   realtime/动态     28.9     -

RTX 5080 16GB    rtx5080           ~42     ~9.6 GB

RTX 5080 16GB    +SageAttention    ~67     ~12.8 GB

RTX 5070 Ti      rtx5070ti         ~41     ~9.2 GB

RTX 5070 Ti      +SageAttention    ~58     ~10.9 GB

# 注: 5080/5070Ti 仅支持固定提示词; 16GB 上 T5

# 编码完提示词后即释放, 再加载 DiT

有几个数字上的"水分"必须讲清楚，官方文档也没有藏着。第一，这些 FPS 是模型吞吐（model throughput），不是你在浏览器里看到的呈现帧率，更不是"动作到光子"（action-to-photon）延迟；视频编码、网络传输、缓冲、浏览器解码都要再加延迟。第二，命令行里的 --fps 40 是"游戏采集节奏目标"，不是吞吐保证。第三，赛车动态提示词模式下，T5 要常驻、文本变化时刷新交叉注意力 KV，吞吐会从约 38.5 掉到约 28.9 FPS，所以 5080 和 5070 Ti 干脆只开放固定提示词。把这些限定条件读全，才不会被标题党式的"60 帧"误导——但即便如此，5B 因果视频模型在单张消费卡上做到 40 到 67 FPS 的稳态生成，依然是实打实的工程突破。

# 快速上手

# 本地离线渲染一条 low-poly 录像

matrix-game render --scene ancient-egypt \

--input lowpoly.mp4 --resources resources \

--preset rtx5090 --prompt-mode fixed \

--output outputs/egypt

# 在线浏览器演示 (服务端, 客户端无需GPU)

mediamtx configs/mediamtx.yml

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 bash scripts/serve.sh \

--scene ancient-egypt --resources resources \

--preset rtx5090 --prompt-mode fixed --fps 40

# 浏览器打开 http://127.0.0.1:8025/

六、这套架构的启发：生成模型该当"大脑"还是当"感官皮肤"Matrix-Game 4.0 给整个生成式互动内容领域提供了一个可复用的范式：把确定性留给符号系统，把不确定性留给生成模型。引擎负责状态、规则、物理、输入这些"必须正确"的部分，模型负责视觉表现这种"需要丰富、但允许近似"的部分。两者通过一路严格的条件信号（干净 RGB + 文本 + 有界因果缓存）耦合，模型永远在事实的缰绳之内创作。

这和当下智能体系统的设计哲学其实是相通的：让大模型直接端到端决定一切，往往又慢又不可控；而把它放在一个有确定状态机、有工具、有约束的回路里，让它做它最擅长的感知与表达，系统反而又快又稳。引擎之于生成模型，正如工具调用之于语言模型——不是能力的妥协，而是工程上的最优分工。

也要客观看到边界。目前它是单用户、单场景模型、单会话的可信本地演示，HTTP/RTSP/WebRTC 默认只绑回环地址，官方安全文档明确说不要直接暴露到公网，它不是一个多租户云游戏服务。分辨率目前是 864×480，竖屏射击为主，横屏赛车是另一条管线。画质依赖每场景训练的专属检查点和固定提示词，换一个全新游戏仍需重新训练和准备素材。开源协议上代码是 Apache-2.0，但模型权重和素材携带各自的许可声明，商用前需要单独核对。

但方向已经很清楚了。从 1.0 的初次开源，到 3.0 的长时记忆实时流式，再到 4.0 把"可执行引擎 + 因果神经渲染"跑通到消费级单卡 60 帧，这条路线正在把"可玩的生成世界"从论文视频变成你我可以 clone 下来亲自试的东西。对游戏开发者，这意味着一种新的分工：先用极简几何快速验证玩法，再用神经渲染决定最终美术风格，同一套玩法可以换多张"视觉皮"。对做世界模型的研究者，4.0 的因果分块、有界 KV、背压同步、分档推理，都是能直接迁移的工程模板。也许下一代游戏引擎里，"渲染器"这三个字的含义，会被这批开源项目彻底重写。
