    Appendix B Analytical Formulation

    Let s be a game seed, p=f(s) its PRD, and q=c(p) the query delivered to the coding agent. The seed constrains the intended experience but generally admits multiple valid designs. The PRD describes one candidate design consistent with the seed. Its additional design choices resolve the implementation of that candidate design. We measure the subsequent compression through the remaining text length and the explicit coverage of a fixed set of gameplay relations.

    Let L(x) be the token length of text x, and let Eₛ be a fixed inventory of gameplay clauses in p, such as a failure triggering respawn or a timer triggering the results screen. Each clause states a dependency together with its specified conditions and parameters. With nₛ=|Eₛ|>0, let Kₛ(x) count the clauses completely expressed in x. By construction, Kₛ(p)=nₛ. Define retained length rₛ, relation retention Rₛ, and omission fraction Dₛ as

    rₛ=L(q)/L(p), Rₛ=Kₛ(q)/nₛ, Dₛ=1-Rₛ.

    		(1)

    Here Dₛ measures omissions from the reference inventory. For relation density ρₛ(x)=Kₛ(x)/L(x), the relation density formulation yields the density gain Gₛ=Rₛ/rₛ=(1-Dₛ)/rₛ. Length, retention, and density are reported together to describe the query representation.

    A conceptual construction objective is to minimize query length while passing the protected-dependency checks:

    \min_qL(q) subject to q∈ℚ_protected(s,p),

    		(2)

    where ℚ_protected(s,p) contains seed-compatible queries that pass the prompt-based checks for protected gameplay dependencies. Clause selection and revision implement this design objective with task-adaptive detail budgets. The separate text audit measures complete retention of sampled PRD clauses, including their exact parameters; Dₛ describes that audit rather than an admission threshold.

    We evaluate the resulting queries through the games they produce. For a fixed teacher, environment, and execution budget B, query q induces an artifact distribution π_B(a|q). If Vₛ is the set of playable implementations compatible with the seed, then

    U_B(q;s)=\Pr_a∼π_B(·|q)[a∈Vₛ].

    		(3)

    We compute rₛ, Rₛ, and Gₛ for all 124 GameGoBench tasks using a fixed inventory of 927 eligible PRD clauses. Complete, partial, and absent clause labels record the level of expression in each query. Human comparisons assess artifact preference on the same tasks under the shared execution budget. Appendix G details clause selection, annotation, and aggregation.

    Appendix C Data Construction Details

    C.1 Game Seed Sources and Screening

    The data are organized into the three source families described in the main text—Steam, browser-game portals, and WeChat mini-games—and four provenance collections. The eighteen source entries comprise one Steam entry, sixteen browser-game entries across two collections, and one WeChat entry. Within the browser-game family, the legacy web-game corpus comprises historical snapshots from Y8, Playgama, 4399, Poki, and CrazyGames. The separate multi-site pool covers eleven portals, with GameDistribution, CrazyGames, ArmorGames, TwoPlayerGames, Poki, Kongregate, AddictingGames, and Kizi as its largest sources. The browser-game entry count is collection-specific: a portal represented in both collections contributes an entry to each, so these entries are not a count of unique domains. The WeChat collection comes from the public 17yoo mini-game directory, and the Steam collection comes from public store pages and metadata endpoints.

    Records are mapped to a common schema while preserving field boundaries between title, description, instructions, categories, and tags. Text normalization removes HTML markup, control characters, invisible characters, and source-specific promotional templates. For the two web collections and WeChat mini games, a conservative two-stage screen checks whether a record contains concrete evidence about player actions, controlled objects, rules, objectives, feedback, or interactions. A record is removed only when both stages find no such evidence. Steam uses rules to route obvious cases and applies the same two-stage standard to boundary cases, followed by an audit of rule-based retention. Ambiguous cases and failed judgments are retained. Category and genre metadata are not used as game-type annotations.

    C.2 Gameplay-Level Deduplication

    Lexical deduplication alone cannot identify games that describe the same mechanic using different themes or wording. Following prior work on semantic dataset deduplication [Abbas et al. (2023); Tirumala et al. (2023)], we retrieve semantically related records, but define equivalence using a game-specific criterion: whether one core gameplay implementation and state machine can realize both records after changing only content, presentation, parameters, or optional rules.

    For each record, an LLM extracts a structured gameplay signature containing the primary mechanic, core loop, player actions, controlled entities, world state, objective, scoring, failure conditions, progression, resource economy, multiplayer structure, and camera view. The extractor must ground these fields in the source text and places thematic information in a separate field. Candidate generation combines exact matching, word and character TF-IDF, MinHash, and nearest-neighbor retrieval over 1,024-dimensional Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B signature embeddings. We retrieve the top 15 embedding neighbors per record, merge them with lexical candidates, and use Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B to retain the top five candidates per record.

    An LLM judge assigns each successfully judged candidate pair one of three relations. Relation A indicates a reusable gameplay template, relation B indicates insufficient or conflicting evidence, and relation C indicates a difference in core actions, state transitions, loops, objectives, or required failure rules. Unresolved pairs do not create duplicate edges. Only A relations create edges in the gameplay graph. Because pairwise similarity is not strictly transitive, we remove weak bridge edges that lack at least two shared A-neighbors and then apply weighted Leiden community detection. Exact matches and high-confidence edges with signature cosine similarity of at least 0.90 bypass the shared-neighbor rule.

    Selection is performed within each resulting cluster. Clusters of at most five records are retained in full. For a cluster of size n>5, we retain round(5+√n-5) records, prioritizing information sufficiency, rotation across source collections, source-text length, and finally a stable record identifier. This quota policy controls the frequency of repeated gameplay within the training pool while preserving small gameplay families and alternative source descriptions. Multiple examples of a gameplay pattern may be retained under the quota. The clustering and quota-based selection stage processes 70,000 records and retains 67,564 seeds. Training and benchmark data are strictly separated from the seed stage onward: benchmark seeds and their derived examples are excluded from all training sets.

    C.3 Specification Routes and Stage Validation

    The task-definition stage chooses the routes used by the remaining planning calls. The rendering route distinguishes layered two-dimensional interaction, true three-dimensional scenes observed from a fixed 2.5D camera, and three-dimensional worlds with a movable camera. The corresponding guidance specializes coordinate systems, input semantics, collision, camera behavior, spatial readability, and asset construction. A separate gameplay route retrieves guidance for the selected primary category and finer archetype. Small expert cards may additionally focus a planning call on applicable concerns such as combat, level flow, animation, audio, sprite production, asset sourcing, or shaders. The retrieved material is framed as attention guidance and is prohibited from adding an unsupported mechanic.

    Each planning call produces a structured JSON artifact. The next call is run only after the preceding artifact can be parsed and satisfies its stage checks. The asset stage additionally validates required asset definitions, executable file types, prompt references, rendering-branch consistency, and coverage of blueprint requirements. Invalid outputs enter a bounded revision step. Canonical compilation then selects fields from the stage that owns them and removes repeated descriptions before producing the full PRD.

    C.4 Task-Adaptive Query Construction Policy

    The large-scale converter first recovers the authoritative rendering dimension from affirmative declarations in the full PRD, ignoring mentions that only forbid an alternative dimension. The compressor then returns an agent-facing query together with its semantic-complexity estimate and five audit fields: preserved axes, protected risks, implementation freedom, complexity basis, and omitted details. Separate continuous output envelopes are used for two-dimensional and spatial games. Independent LLM validators check query fidelity to protected gameplay dependencies and the implementation freedom left to the coding agent. If a query falls outside its envelope, fails either semantic check, omits a protected-risk analysis, or leaves no implementation decision open, it is revised without changing the original complexity estimate.

    The production version also introduces sparse implementation diversity after the task has passed a semantic eligibility test. A stable hash of the task identifier selects at most one optional direction from four cases: reflections for water-dominant 3D scenes, richer geometry for an identity-critical 3D focal object, coherent sprite sheets for eligible 2D side-view action games, or portraits for character-driven card games. The suggestion is expressed as an option rather than a task requirement. When a selected technique is adopted, a short adoption contract prevents degenerate use, such as generating a sprite sheet while rendering a procedural fallback as the default character. The selection and retention decision are stored in the audit record.

    C.5 React trajectory quality checks

    The curation rules target React development trajectories. As described in the main text, admission requires executable projects with complete codebases, valid parsed structures, and verified runtime success. The trajectory-level checks below form part of this multi-stage filtering protocol. Structural checks reject malformed query or tool records, undefined tool names, session timeouts, unfinished final tool-call turns, and trajectories with fewer than eight messages. Non-grep tool calls are checked for missing required arguments and undeclared parameters. Retained trajectories must contain at least one create_file or edit_file operation. The checks also reject repeated or malformed tool-output patterns, including concatenated list_files responses and truncated JSON arguments.

    Execution checks reject trajectories with at least ten failed tool calls. They also reject nominally successful tool responses that contain transport failures, failed MCP calls, or broken-pipe errors. Calls to Supabase tools must follow initialization. To limit unsuccessful repair loops, trajectories are rejected when lint failures lead to more than three file-repair rounds or when at least fourteen consecutive assistant turns edit the same file.

    The build check inspects the final four assistant turns. If it finds a build_project call, the corresponding result must be present and report JSON status success. A trajectory is not rejected solely because no build call occurs in this window. After a successful terminal build, trailing turns are removed while retaining all parallel tool results associated with that build. These checks assess the recorded development process; they complement the project-level executability, integrity, and runtime-success requirements for admission.

    The retained records are serialized directly into MS-SWIFT messages JSONL for supervised training. Requirements and Quality scores belong to artifact evaluation and are not admission thresholds for these trajectory checks. Corpus accounting records query submission, trajectory collection and curation, and the model-specific training counts in Table 4.

    C.6 Corpus accounting

    To this end, from 67,564 submitted task-specific queries, 67,487 initial trajectories are recorded. Among these, 65,082 complete the primary execution phase successfully, achieving a 96.3% completion rate over submitted queries. Subsequent artifact integrity and formatting verification retain 55,060 examples, corresponding to an overall GameGoData yield of 81.5% over submitted queries. Table 4 summarizes the seed-selection, collection, curation, and training counts. The 55,060 curated examples constitute the final GameGoData corpus and are used as input to both dense-model training runs; model-specific length filtering removes no further examples.

    C.7 GameGoBench Task Selection

    GameGoBench seeds were selected and separated from the training seeds before development of the task-construction pipeline, using stratified selection to cover rendering formats and implementation difficulties. Training and test data are strictly isolated from the seed stage onward: none of the 124 benchmark seeds, their derived specifications, queries, or trajectories enters any training set. The benchmark contains 47 2D, 22 2.5D, and 55 3D tasks, stratified into Easy, Medium, and Hard within each rendering format. The training and test seeds subsequently pass through the same specification and query-construction pipeline, which was not designed around the test set. Details of gameplay clustering and training-pool quotas are provided in Appendix C.2.

    Appendix D Evaluation Design and Collection Cost

    The study evaluates task representations through fixed-teacher artifact comparisons and corpus utility through student fine-tuning. Direct queries are produced by DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp from source seeds, rewriting supported gameplay into self-contained browser-game requests without the multi-stage PRD. All 124 query identifiers match the PRD and task-specific conditions. Their median length is 227.5 tokens, close to 235 for task-specific queries; these are seed rewrites rather than PRD summaries. The held-out comparison evaluates the construction procedure without tuning it on GameGoBench.

    Collecting high-quality teacher trajectories is the main cost of representation-level training comparisons. Each alternative query changes implementation decisions, tool interactions, execution feedback, and repairs, requiring a fresh sandbox rollout and subsequent student training. Repeating this process for direct queries and full PRDs at corpus scale would multiply the teacher-collection cost. We therefore compare all three representations through controlled artifact evaluations on the 124 held-out seeds, while concentrating large-scale trajectory collection and SFT on the task-specific queries. This design allocates teacher compute to the final training corpus and evaluates the representation choices under a shared teacher, scaffold, and interaction budget. The same confidential teacher is used for trajectory collection and the task-representation comparisons. In each comparison condition, the task input is the corresponding direct query, full PRD, or task-specific query; the compact condition does not additionally supply the full PRD or the three planning-stage outputs. The Base/MoE study additionally examines learning from a pretrained initialization.

    The static analysis covers the same 124 GameGoBench tasks as the artifact comparisons. Paired text lengths measure compression, while an audit of 927 PRD clauses measures complete, partial, and absent expression in the task-specific queries. We report clause retention and density alongside artifact preferences on this shared task set. Downstream experiments evaluate the training utility of the collected corpus across model backbones.

    Appendix E Training and Public Evaluation Details

    E.1 Model and Inference Settings

    The principal dense models are Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.8-27B, initialized from their corresponding instruction-tuned checkpoints. A separate Qwen3.5-35B-A3B MoE run is retained as an additional training study. All three runs apply SFT to all language-model parameters rather than using LoRA, while visual towers and aligners remain frozen. The final GameGoData corpus contains 55,060 trajectories, all of which are retained for both dense-model training runs after length filtering. The dense-model configurations and training counts are reported below.

    The local training runs use NVIDIA H800 GPUs with approximately 80 GB per GPU, BF16 arithmetic, public random seed 42, and Linux. The dense runs use PyTorch 2.9.1+cu128, MS-SWIFT 4.4.0, Transformers 5.12.1, DeepSpeed 0.19.2, Megatron-Core 0.16.1, FlashAttention 2.8.3, and Transformer Engine 2.10.0. The training trajectories are converted directly into MS-SWIFT messages JSONL records with template=qwen3_5, agent_template=qwen3_5, and padding_free=true. With truncation_strategy=delete, an over-length trajectory is removed as a whole rather than left- or right-truncated.

    Within each benchmark, all compared models use the same Code Arena scaffold, sandbox environment, and inference budget, as specified in the main text. For GameGoCoder and its matched base checkpoints, the inference settings are temperature 0.6, top-p=0.95, at most 100 interaction steps, and a maximum of 65,536 generated tokens per model call. The dense models are served with vLLM in BF16 using tensor parallelism 8 and a 262,144-token context limit. Each model makes one generation attempt per query. The accompanying configurations specify training and inference settings.

    E.2 Dense-model training configuration

    Each dense model is trained for one epoch over its retained GameGo training subset. After length filtering, both the Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.8-27B runs contain 55,060 training trajectories. Both use fused AdamW, peak learning rate 1×10⁻⁵, cosine decay to zero, 3% warm-up, (β₁,β₂)=(0.9,0.95), ε=10⁻⁸, weight decay 0.1, gradient clipping at 1.0, gradient checkpointing, and DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 with CPU-pinned optimizer offload. The effective global batch size is 8 and the maximum supported sequence length is 262,144 tokens.

    The Qwen3.5 dense runs use 8 or 16 H800 GPUs across launches, reflecting resource allocation. Activation CPU offload supports long-context training. Checkpoints contain model, optimizer, scheduler, and RNG state. The final reported model is the last checkpoint of its corresponding SFT run.

    E.3 MoE training study

    The Qwen3.5-35B-A3B Base experiment uses 64 H800 GPUs with MS-SWIFT Megatron/Megatron-Core rather than DeepSpeed. Training runs for six epochs at sequence length 262,144 with 19,148 packed sequences. Tensor, pipeline, data, and expert parallelism are TP=8, PP=1, DP=8, and EP=8, with expert tensor parallelism ETP=1, context parallelism CP=1, and sequence parallelism enabled. The microbatch size is 1 and the global batch size is 128, corresponding to 16 microbatches per optimizer update on each data-parallel replica. The model has 256 routed experts and activates the top 8 experts per token.

    The MoE run uses Adam with a linear learning-rate decay from 5×10⁻⁵ to 5×10⁻⁶, no warm-up, (β₁,β₂)=(0.9,0.95), ε=10⁻⁸, weight decay 0.1, and gradient clipping at 1.0. Router computation uses FP32 with load-balancing coefficient 10⁻³; grouped GEMM, all-to-all dispatch, FlashAttention, fused cross entropy, and full uniform activation recomputation are enabled. Epoch checkpoints are checkpoint-149, -298, -447, -596, -745, and -894, with checkpoint-897 as the training endpoint. This run resumed from weights without restoring optimizer moments or RNG state. Restarted jobs preserve model weights and scheduler position and initialize fresh optimizer state.

    E.4 Loss masking and serialization

    The response-masked objective in the main text is implemented at message level. system, user, and tool_response tokens receive label -100 and contribute context only. Assistant thinking, assistant natural-language responses, and tool calls are supervised with their original token IDs. Tool calls are first serialized as assistant-side messages, whereas tool responses are serialized as tool messages. Consequently, the objective supervises the agent’s decisions and actions while preserving execution feedback as conditioning context.

    E.5 Public Benchmark Evaluation

    We evaluate 413 ArtifactsBench-G tasks and 156 Cookie-Bench-G tasks using their official queries and evaluation pipelines, with Claude Sonnet 4.6 powering both verifier pipelines as in the main text. Each model generates one artifact for every query. Failed builds receive the score prescribed by the corresponding official evaluator. Table 1 reports task-level mean scores; comparisons with the corresponding base checkpoint use the same benchmark tasks. The reported values are task-level mean point estimates.

    Appendix G GameGoBench Task-Representation Analysis

    G.1 Task matching and length measurement

    We analyze the stored PRDs and task-specific queries of all 124 GameGoBench tasks used in the artifact comparisons. Records are aligned by their original task identifiers across the PRD file and the query exports containing 40, 13, and 71 tasks. Three empty query fields in the exports are recovered from their archived gallery inputs and checked against the corresponding original query records. The analysis retains the fixed evaluation queries and records source hashes and recovery provenance.

    Token lengths are measured with the Qwen3.5-27B tokenizer, with special tokens disabled and no chat template. We count the stored Markdown and serialized specifications. The first complete Deterministic Asset Execution Contract heading separates each PRD into its body and asset appendix. We compute retained length and compression for each matched task before aggregating. Table 6 reports medians of these per-task ratios alongside median text lengths.

    G.2 Clause selection and annotation

    Reference clauses are selected from PRD text before examining query coverage. A deterministic script extracts spans of 45 to 230 characters containing a condition or transition cue, prioritizing core mechanics and rule sections and using controls, progression, and other gameplay sections as a fallback. Asset, execution, feedback, color, shader, performance, and acceptance sections are excluded. Candidates are ordered by the SHA-256 hash of the task identifier and clause text, and up to eight are selected per task. The inventory is frozen before semantic annotation, with exact source paragraphs and clause hashes retained.

    A single AI-assisted text audit reviews the 977 candidates and excludes 50 attribute lists, presentation or implementation requirements, and uninterpretable fragments, leaving 927 gameplay clauses across all 124 tasks. Each eligible clause is labeled complete when the query expresses the full dependency, including its stated conditions and parameters; partial when the mechanism is expressed with some conditions, values, or consequences unspecified; or absent when the dependency is unexpressed or contradicted. Complete and partial labels include exact query quotations. The scoring script checks source and query quotations, task alignment, and arithmetic. These semantic annotations are AI-assisted; the six independent expert evaluators separately judge the generated games.

    For task s, the reference inventory Eₛ contains its nₛ eligible clauses, and Kₛ(q) counts the clauses labeled complete. We compute Rₛ=Kₛ(q)/nₛ, Dₛ=1-Rₛ, and Gₛ=Rₛ/rₛ using the definitions in Appendix B. Partial clauses are reported as a separate category, so Dₛ includes both partial and absent clauses. Each reference clause is weighted equally. We report pooled clause percentages and medians of per-task coverage and density separately; all 124 tasks contribute to the medians, including tasks with zero complete coverage.

    G.3 Compression, coverage, and density

    Median PRD and query lengths are 9,136 and 235 tokens. The median retained-length fraction is 2.26%, and median paired compression is 44.2×; compression relative to the PRD body is 21.6×. Every query contains less than 5% of its full PRD’s tokens. Across the 927 eligible clauses, 112 are complete, 577 are partial, and 238 are absent. Median complete-clause coverage is 12.5%, and the median density gain is 3.79× against full PRDs and 1.78× against PRD bodies.

    The clause labels distinguish preserved mechanisms from complete specification detail. For example, the workshop-brawler query names an airborne dive strike, while the sampled PRD clause additionally specifies its velocity, damage, impact radius, and target-height restriction; this clause is labeled partial. The 56 tasks with no complete sampled clause contribute zero density gain. These text measurements characterize the same tasks whose generated games are compared in Table 2, connecting the analysis of execution requirements with artifact-level evaluation.

    Appendix H Task-Construction Compilers and Prompt Specifications

    This appendix describes the implementation of the two pipelines used to construct tasks. The complete prompt specifications and routing policy will be released with the accompanying implementation upon acceptance, subject to applicable software licenses, as stated in the reproducibility statement. This release does not include GameGoData trajectories or their associated artifacts. The listings below record the canonical stage interfaces and the decisions that affect downstream execution. Both pipelines use three planning stages followed by canonical PRD compilation and task-adaptive query construction; downstream implementation executes the resulting query. They differ in the source envelope and the visual-asset contract.

    H.1 End-to-end pipeline

    The Image-Grounded Game Task Compiler accepts either an ordinary query or a record containing minimal text fields and at most five screenshots. The Text-Grounded Web-Game Task Compiler accepts an ordinary query or a web-game catalog record containing title, description, instructions, categories, and tags; it does not read screenshots or source URLs. In both cases, the execution order is:

    In unattended batch production, both pipelines stop after Canonical + Compact and write one task-identifier/query record per input; execution is then run by the downstream trajectory-collection process. The three planning-stage outputs and the full PRD are internal construction representations; the task-specific query is the task description supplied for GameGoData collection. Each stage must emit its declared output before the next stage starts. The default revision budget is one revision per stage. Invalid JSON, failed schema checks, or failed asset-contract checks trigger this bounded revision; unresolved failures are retained as failed items rather than silently exported.

    H.2 Stage 1: seed distillation and routing

    Stage 1 is the only stage that interprets the source record. It emits a self-contained, de-identified specification and does not prescribe the implementation architecture. The routing decisions are authoritative for all later stages:

  • •

    Gameplay route: exactly one primary category from the 20-category taxonomy, one finer-grained gameplay_archetype, and only implementation-relevant secondary tags. The output also lists archetype-specific required phases and a complete gameplay_flow_contract from entry to restart.

  • •

    Rendering route:2d for layered Canvas/SVG/Sprite interaction, 2.5d for real 3D geometry under a fixed camera, and 3d when play requires camera motion or free spatial observation. camera_mobility and concrete dimension_evidence must agree with this choice.

  • •

    Scope route:compact_loop for a short fixed round and multi_phase_journey for non-interchangeable setup, progression, exploration, or multi-scene phases. The route is based on the required player journey, not on asset count or visual style.

  • •

    Asset route:procedural_pixel is selected only when the source contains explicit pixel-art evidence; otherwise the default is generated_hybrid. The evidence is copied into asset_production_evidence.

    • For Steam inputs, screenshots are used only to record reliable image_only_facts; uncertain visual inferences are separated and the source title, characters, locations, trademarks, and text are removed from the downstream request. For WebGame inputs, the visual plan is text-derived. The text-grounded pipeline therefore additionally emits visual_evidence_level, semantic visual anchors, and separate environment/entity/UI/typography color roles. These fields constrain later visual choices rather than adding unsupported style identity.

    H.3 Stages 2 and 3: conditional planning and asset grounding

    Stage 2 consumes only the approved Stage-1 output and the de-identified source context. The pipeline loads a rendering overlay corresponding to the selected rendering branch and a gameplay profile selected by the primary category and archetype. The gameplay router always provides a core gameplay lens; it may additionally provide combat, level-flow, game-feel, or audio guidance when the approved seed contains the corresponding evidence. These lenses focus attention on failure-prone implementation relations and are explicitly forbidden from introducing new product requirements.

    The deterministic skill policy is shared by the two pipelines. Stage 1 receives the routing-observer lens. Stage 2 starts with gameplay_core; it adds action_combat for combat-oriented evidence, level_flow for spatial categories, 3D tasks, or multi-phase journeys, animation_game_feel for action/arcade/rhythm-like categories, and audio_web when audio or mood is supported by the seed. Stage 2 is capped at four lenses. Stage 3 starts with art_bible_compact and asset_source_gate; it may add sprite_pipeline for eligible 2D generated-hybrid tasks and audio_web when needed. The text-grounded pipeline additionally adds shader_fx only when Stage 2 emits a concrete shader opportunity, and injects at most three technique metadata references. Skill selection is recorded per run and can be disabled for ablations.

    Stage 2 owns the canonical gameplay representation: gameplay_flow_contract, rules, controls, entities, progression, scene/state flow, camera and viewport contracts, feedback, implementation technology, and observable acceptance criteria. Stage 3 reads the approved seed and blueprint, loads the same rendering and gameplay routes, and owns only the executable asset plan. It maps each required scene, entity, UI element, transition, and feedback to a stable asset ID, source, dimensions, generation prompt or procedural construction, integration location, and scene coverage record. The text-grounded asset contract additionally supports project-owned inline shaders. Shader guidance is injected only when the blueprint contains an approved shader opportunity; at most three compact technique references are supplied, and the generated module must define its own uniforms, render state, performance bound, gameplay variation, and fallback.

    H.4 Canonical Compilation and Task-Adaptive Query Construction

    Canonical compilation prevents later stages from redefining earlier decisions. Stage 1 owns product identity, source-derived constraints, routing, scope, and originality rules; Stage 2 owns gameplay and implementation; Stage 3 owns visual and audio realization. The compiler selects only these authoritative fields, replaces repeated prose with stable IDs and references, and removes the Stage-1 draft request once the blueprint has resolved it. For image-grounded assets, reference identity is redacted before downstream stages and graphic planning context is neutralized; for the text-grounded pipeline, shader contracts are reduced to executable project-owned modules rather than copied reference compositions.

    Task-adaptive query construction recovers the authoritative rendering dimension, estimates semantic complexity from dependencies among player actions, states, and camera behavior, and checks the effect of removing each candidate clause. It retains a clause when removing it would change task identity, break the playable loop, make controls or space ambiguous, or remove a critical visual dependency. It deliberately leaves routine architecture, exhaustive counts, ordinary layout, and nonessential tuning open to the coding agent. The output is an English query plus an audit of preserved axes, protected risks, implementation freedom, complexity basis, and omitted detail.

    H.5 Validation and implementation handoff

    The pipeline materializes structured outputs only after successful parsing and object-level checks. Required top-level fields are checked per stage; rendering branch consistency and cross-stage field ownership are enforced; Stage 3 additionally checks executable extensions, asset-source contracts, required asset IDs, prompt references, and complete scene coverage. A failed stage receives at most one bounded revision under the default configuration. For the text-grounded pipeline, inline shaders are rejected if they embed reference source code, leave unresolved Shadertoy interfaces, omit a fallback, or exceed their declared contract. After compaction and independent validation of query fidelity and execution freedom, the implementation handoff supplies the task-specific query to the coding agent. The three approved planning outputs are used to construct that query rather than concatenated into its execution request. The downstream process records the development trajectory and final game artifact, which are admitted under the checks in Appendix C.5.

item.title: Player-1：用合成经验把电脑操作智能体练成游戏玩家 ｜ Player-1: Learning to Play from Synthetic Experience
item.description:
一句话：扩展动作空间 + 6044 条对局轨迹初始化 + 16 个合成环境做 RL，产出 9B 与 35B-A3B 两档。

要点：

  • 把电脑操作的动作空间扩到相对指针移动、持续按压与组合动作，贴近真实游戏手柄/键鼠操作
  • 用 6044 条精挑对局轨迹（动作、任务指令与视觉推理配对）做监督初始化
  • 自建 16 个合成 2D/3D 环境，具备程序化可验证奖励与随机化观测/控制动态，支持 PPO 多环境 RL

为什么值得看：要给 NPC 或自动化测试机器人做通用控制，这套「动作空间扩展 + 环境合成 + 可验证奖励」是可复用的最小闭环。

中文摘要：电脑操作智能体已经能看懂屏幕并执行键鼠动作，但游戏世界视觉丰富、机制多样，是迈向通用数字控制更难的下一级台阶。现有游戏智能体训练管线依赖大规模示范，覆盖的动态状态有限，可扩展的交互训练环境也不易获得。Player-1 提出一个后训练框架：先把动作空间扩展为相对指针移动、持续按压与组合动作；用 6044 条精挑的对局轨迹（录制动作、任务指令与视觉推理三件套）做监督初始化；再构建 16 个合成 2D/3D 环境，围绕跨游戏共享的控制需求设计，配备程序化可验证奖励与随机化观测和控制动态，从而支持多环境 PPO 强化学习。最终得到 Player-1-9B 与 Player-1-35B-A3B 两档模型，把「超越示范」作为训练目标。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.AI（English）

Player-1: Learning to Play from Synthetic Experience

Abstract

Computer-use agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in interpreting screens and executing keyboard and mouse actions. However, games, with their visually rich worlds and diverse mechanics, remain challenging and offer a demanding next step toward general digital control. Current game-agent learning pipelines often rely on large-scale demonstrations with limited coverage of dynamic game states, while scalable environments for interactive training remain difficult to obtain. We introduce Player-1, a post-training framework for learning game control beyond demonstrations through synthetic experience. We extend the computer-use action space with relative pointer motion, sustained inputs, and composite actions. For supervised initialization, we fine-tune computer-use models on 6,044 curated gameplay trajectories that pair recorded actions with task instructions and visual reasoning. We construct Player-1-Gym, sixteen synthetic 2D and 3D environments designed around control demands shared across games. Programmatically verifiable rewards and randomized observations and control dynamics support multi-environment reinforcement learning with PPO. The resulting Player-1-9B and Player-1-35B-A3B improve MineDojo-300 success over their SFT policies by 27.8 and 17.7 percentage points, respectively. Player-1-9B reaches 38.33% success compared with 12.63% for the strongest evaluated baseline, with further gains over SFT on ViZDoom-10 and GameWorld. Further analyses show that broader synthetic environment coverage improves transfer, while the use of composite actions that combine multiple keyboard and mouse inputs increases during RL. We demonstrate that learning from synthetic experience substantially improves game control beyond supervised initialization, with gains that generalize beyond the RL training suite.

11footnotetext: Work done during internship at ARC Lab, Tencent IEG. † Project Lead. ‡ Co-corresponding Authors.

Project:player-1-project.github.io/Code:github.com/TencentARC/Player-1

1 Introduction

Foundation models have developed broad capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, and instruction following [(OpenAI, 2024; Anthropic, 2025; Gemini Team, 2025)]. Computer-use agents bring these capabilities to digital interfaces, interpreting screens and executing keyboard and mouse actions [(Wang et al., 2025a; Bai et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026)]. Games offer a demanding next step toward general digital control: their visually complex environments and diverse mechanics require precise, sustained, and concurrent control under dynamic and rapidly changing visual feedback [(Luo et al., 2026a)].

Recent game agents learn from large-scale gameplay demonstrations and interactive experience [(Wang et al., 2025b; Magne et al., 2026; SIMA Team, 2025; Shi et al., 2026)]. Yet demonstrations cover only a limited portion of the states an agent may encounter in open-ended tasks, while scalable environments for interactive training remain difficult to obtain. Despite differences in appearance and rules, we find that many games share recurring control demands such as precise aiming, sustained movement, and coordinated inputs. This motivates our central question: Can synthetic experience advance game-control capabilities beyond supervised initialization, with gains that generalize to games outside the RL training suite?

Three challenges shape this approach. First, gameplay demonstrations recorded with heterogeneous input conventions and temporal resolutions must be converted into a shared action space, and paired with task instructions and visual reasoning that reflect the player’s intent. Second, learning beyond demonstrations requires feedback on states reached by the policy’s own actions, but implementing programmatic rewards across diverse commercial games is difficult to scale. Third, experience from environments with different control demands, dynamics, and reward scales must be incorporated into a shared policy that generalizes beyond the training suite. These challenges motivate our supervised initialization from curated demonstrations, followed by learning in controllable synthetic environments with verifiable rewards.

We present Player-1, a post-training framework for learning game control beyond demonstrations through synthetic experience, as illustrated in Figure 1. We extend the computer-use action space with relative pointer motion, sustained inputs, and composite actions. Curated gameplay demonstrations pair recorded actions with task instructions and visual reasoning to initialize game control. Player-1-Gym then provides sixteen synthetic 2D and 3D environments designed around recurring control demands across aiming, combat, driving, navigation, and UI interaction. Programmatic game-state rewards and randomization of observations and control dynamics support multi-environment reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), yielding Player-1-9B and Player-1-35B-A3B. Table 1 summarizes the differences and focuses of representative game-agent learning pipelines.

Our results demonstrate that learning from synthetic experience improves game-control capabilities, with gains extending beyond the RL training suite. On MineDojo-300, Player-1-9B improves from 10.54% success after SFT to 38.33%, exceeding the strongest evaluated external baseline at 12.63% under our evaluation protocol. The same policy also improves on ViZDoom-10 and GameWorld, both outside the RL training suite. We summarize our main contributions as follows:

  • •

    We present Player-1, a post-training framework that builds on supervised initialization to learn transferable game-control capabilities from synthetic experience. A shared action space supports relative pointer motion, sustained inputs, and composite actions, while 6,044 curated gameplay trajectories provide supervised initialization for subsequent interactive learning.

  • •

    We introduce Player-1-Gym, sixteen synthetic 2D and 3D environments designed around recurring control demands across games. Programmatically verifiable rewards, together with randomized observations and control dynamics, provide diverse experience for multi-environment reinforcement learning beyond demonstrations.

  • •

    We demonstrate that learning from synthetic experience advances game-control capabilities beyond supervised demonstrations: Player-1-9B and Player-1-35B-A3B gain 27.8 and 17.7 pp in MineDojo-300 success, respectively, with further gains on ViZDoom and GameWorld outside the RL training suite. Further analyses show improved transfer with broader environment coverage and increased composite-action use during RL.

    • 2 Related Work

    Generalist and Computer-Use Agents.

    Foundation models provide broad language, reasoning, and multimodal capabilities that underpin general-purpose agents [(OpenAI, 2024; Anthropic, 2025; Gemini Team, 2025; Yang et al., 2025)]. Vision-language models (VLMs) connect visual perception with language, supporting scene understanding and spatial grounding [(Bai et al., 2025)]. Computer-use agents (CUAs) specialize these capabilities for screenshot-conditioned interaction, using keyboard and mouse actions to complete multi-step tasks [(Hu et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; Lu et al., 2026)].

    Game Agents, Development, and Environments.

    Game-agent research spans planning-based systems [(Tan et al., 2025b)], learned visual policies and vision–language–action (VLA) models [(SIMA Team, 2024; Tan et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Magne et al., 2026; Yue et al., 2026)], and joint video–action models [(Guo et al., 2026)]. Reinforcement learning further supports self-improvement and long-horizon control [(SIMA Team, 2025; Shi et al., 2026)]. Most recently, Jev demonstrates low-latency game control through a text-only interface, relying on structured game-state representations rather than screenshot observations [(Almeida, 2026)]. Complementary benchmarks evaluate gameplay [(Ouyang et al., 2026)] and agentic game development [(Chi et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026b)]. Code world models synthesized from rules and trajectories support planning [(Lehrach et al., 2026)], while game engine development provides trajectory data for world-model training [(Zhou et al., 2026)], connecting game creation to learning [(Luo et al., 2026a)].

    Agent Post-Training with Verifiable Rewards.

    Post-training with verifiable rewards enables agents to learn from the outcomes of their own actions. Environment-synthesis approaches expand training coverage by constructing interactive tasks with verifiable rewards [(Dong et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a)]. Adaptive approaches learn which environments to generate or jointly improve the policy, environment, and reward model [(Liu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b)]. In games, SIMA 2 combines supervised initialization with online RLVR and further demonstrates self-improvement transfer across Genie 3 environments [(SIMA Team, 2025)]. Player-1 combines supervised initialization with learning from synthetic experience in environments organized around shared control demands, demonstrating game-control gains that generalize beyond the RL training suite.

    3 Method

    Player-1 connects supervised initialization with learning from synthetic experience through a shared game-control action space. We first extend computer-use actions to support dynamic game control, and initialize the policy using curated gameplay demonstrations. We then optimize the policy across Player-1-Gym’s synthetic environments using PPO with verifiable rewards.

    3.1 Extending the Computer-Use Action Space

    We extend the computer-use action space for dynamic game control while retaining screenshot-conditioned decision making. At turn t, the policy receives task instruction q, screenshot Iₜ, and interaction history C_H(h_Section 3.2):

    (zₜ,âₜ)∼π_θ(·|q,Iₜ,C_H(h_

    Here zₜ is reasoning and âₜ the proposed action. The game-control action space extends the base model’s computer-use actions with relative pointer motion, sustained inputs, and composite actions.

    Relative pointer motion.

    For the mouse actions, CUAs typically use normalized absolute coordinates to select visible targets by specifying their on-screen positions. In game-play scenarios, to control the camera without a visible pointer, we extend this action space with relative displacements:

    Aₚₒᵢₙₜₑᵣ=\underbrace{absolute(x,y)}_Retained CUA coordinates ∪ \underbrace{relative(Δx,Δy)}_Relative-motion extension.

    Absolute coordinates satisfy x,y∈[0,1000], while relative displacements Δx,Δy∈[-1000,1000] are normalized by screen width and height. Positive Δx denotes rightward motion, and positive Δy denotes downward motion. The resulting view rotation depends on the game’s camera gain.

    Sustained inputs.

    We extend taps and clicks with holds lasting one full control step of duration Δt. For a key or mouse button b, the press or long-hold action space is

    Aₚᵣₑₛₛ(b)=\underbrace{tap/click(b)}_Retained CUA taps/clicks ∪ \underbrace{hold(b;Δt)}_Sustained extension.

    Repeating holds across consecutive control steps sustains movement and interaction.

    Composite actions.

    We define a composite action as two or more compatible keyboard or mouse inputs executed concurrently within one control step. The step action space is

    Aₛₜₑₚ=\underbrace{wait}∪A_keyboard∪Aₘₒᵤₛₑ_Individual CUA inputs ∪ \underbrace{input₁∥⋯∥inputₘ}_Composite-action extension.

    Each inputᵢ∈A_keyboard∪Aₘₒᵤₛₑ; ∥ denotes concurrent execution and m≥2. These combinations support coordinated movement and combat that is crucial for game control. For example, holding ‘W’ while tapping ‘Space’ enables running jumps, and pointer motion with a right-button hold and left-button click enables concurrent aiming and firing.

    3.2 Supervised Initialization for Game Control

    The extended action space in Section 3.1 defines the available controls, but the policy must learn when and how to use them. In this section, we describe how we use SFT on a compact collection of curated gameplay demonstrations to initialize computer-use models for subsequent learning from synthetic experience.

    Demonstration trajectory curation.

    We curate 6,044 gameplay trajectories comprising 295,097 interaction turns from public datasets [(Choi et al., 2026; Markov AI, 2026; Yue et al., 2026; Baker et al., 2022)] and in-house recordings, mapping recorded controls to the shared game-control action space defined in Section 3.1. Controls are aligned to shared action intervals, and source-specific mouse calibration expresses relative inputs in normalized, pixel-equivalent coordinates. After filtering incomplete or redundant recordings, we use a VLM [(Google DeepMind, 2026)] to annotate the recorded actions with task instructions and per-turn visual reasoning. For reasoning annotation, the VLM conditions on the task instruction, current and past observations, and the action target. Figure 2 illustrates input coverage and an annotated demonstration. Appendix B details the sources, alignment, calibration, and annotation procedures.

    Supervised fine-tuning.

    We construct each SFT example as (q,Iₜ,C_H(h_D.1 to increase exposure to less frequent controls and composite actions.

    3.3 Player-1-Gym: Learning from Synthetic Experience

    We construct Player-1-Gym, a suite of synthetic environments organized around control demands shared across games. Programmatically verifiable rewards, together with randomized observations and control dynamics, support our multi-environment PPO training of the SFT-initialized policy.

    Verifiable environment construction.

    We identify recurring control demands across games and organize training tasks into five families: aiming, combat, driving, navigation, and UI interaction. For example, aiming tasks require pointer-based or camera-relative target tracking, while combat tasks combine movement with attack timing. Building upon our own shared 2D and 3D engines, reusable assets, and scene templates, we implement sixteen environments that require these forms of control through different game mechanics, viewpoints, and spatial layouts, as shown in Figure 3(a–b). A unified runtime provides screenshot observations and executes the shared game-control action space. This shared foundation facilitates extending the suite with new environments while maintaining consistent observation and action interfaces.

    To provide verifiable training feedback, each environment defines game- and task-specific scoring rules over changing game states. Score increments supply step-level rewards, providing dense and verifiable feedback without a learned judge, while privileged state is not exposed to the policy.

    Environment randomization.

    To further broaden training experience within each environment, we randomize four complementary dimensions in Player-1-Gym: (1) Appearance: colors, lighting, and assets; (2) Camera: projection, placement, and initial orientation; (3) Scene: layouts, spawns, and task-specific configurations; and (4) Control: input-response gains for camera rotation, movement, driving, and steering where applicable. All four dimensions are jointly randomized during training where supported. Examples are provided in Figure 3(c). Appendix C further specifies the distributions and per-environment settings.

    Multi-environment reinforcement learning.

    We jointly optimize the SFT-initialized policy with PPO across randomized environments with different control demands, dynamics, and reward scales. To limit the effect of reward-scale differences on policy-update magnitudes, we apply per-environment advantage normalization to generalized advantage estimates (GAE):

    Ã_i,j=(A_i,j-μₑ)/(√σₑ²+ε), μₑ=(∑_(i,j)∈SₑA_i,j)/(Nₑ), σₑ²=(∑_(i,j)∈Sₑ(A_i,j-μₑ)²)/(Nₑ-1).

    		(1)

    Here i indexes turns and j response tokens. For each environment e, Sₑ contains its response-token indices in the rollout batch, with Nₑ=|Sₑ|. We normalize each A_i,j for (i,j)∈Sₑ using the corresponding advantage mean μₑ and sample variance σₑ². Return-to-go targets accumulate rewards from subsequent turns, allowing later outcomes to inform earlier control decisions. Appendix D.2 further details reward construction, cross-turn credit, loss aggregation, and optimization.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Training setup.

    We initialize Player-1-9B and Player-1-35B-A3B from their respective Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B backbones. Both undergo two epochs of SFT on the full demonstration dataset with action-balanced sampling. We then apply proximal policy optimization (PPO) in the sixteen-environment Player-1-Gym suite. Both model sizes train on the full sixteen-environment suite with a budget of 200 RL steps. Each training step collects 256 episodes allocated equally across environments, with at most 50 interaction turns per episode. More training details and hyperparameters are provided in Appendix D.

    Evaluation.

    Besides in-domain evaluation of sixteen Player-1-Gym environments, we construct two evaluation suites: MineDojo-300, comprising 300 tasks from the MineDojo [(Fan et al., 2022)] task collection in Minecraft, and ViZDoom-10, comprising ten maps from the twelve available maps in ViZDoom [(Kempka et al., 2016)]. We also evaluate browser-game interaction on GameWorld [(Ouyang et al., 2026)], covering 170 tasks across 34 games. Our standardized evaluation protocols use 8 trials per MineDojo task, 50 per ViZDoom map, and 3 per GameWorld task. Appendix E details benchmark composition, metrics, and budgets.

    We compare against game-specific models, including JARVIS-VLA [(Li et al., 2025)], NitroGen [(Magne et al., 2026)], Open-P2P [(Yue et al., 2026)], and GameWAM [(Guo et al., 2026)], as well as computer-use models, including UI-TARS-1.5-7B [(ByteDance Seed, 2025)] and our Qwen3.5 base models. We keep their native preprocessing and inference procedures across the benchmarks. We also compare the base models, our SFT-initialized models, and the final Player-1 models to separate the gains from SFT and those from synthetic experience.

    4.2 Main Results

    Task-directed control in Minecraft.

    On MineDojo-300, SFT raises success from 9.21% to 10.54% for 9B and from 7.79% to 23.38% for 35B-A3B. Interactive learning raises 9B success to 38.33%, a large gain of 27.79 percentage points over SFT. The number of tasks completed in at least four of eight trials increases from 20 to 136, showing gains in both task coverage and repeatability.

    Generalization beyond the RL training suite.

    The same policy improves performance on external games. On ViZDoom-10, Player-1-9B increases scaled return from 0.4361 after SFT to 0.6922. Player-1-35B-A3B achieves an overall scaled return of 0.7236, surpassing GameWAM, the strongest external baseline at 0.3938, by 83.7%. On GameWorld’s 3×170 episodes, progress rises from 31.43% to 34.45%. Together, these results show that control experience acquired in Player-1-Gym transfers to first-person shooting and distinct browser games, beyond the synthesized environments for RL. These gains support using synthetic experience to develop transferable control capabilities without reinforcement learning in each target game.

    Case Example: Control in an Unseen Commercial Game.

    We integrate Player-1 into commercial games using an observation–action loop with visual inputs and keyboard–mouse controls. Figure 4 shows an example sequence in Watch Dogs 2, a game unseen during both SFT and RL. Experience acquired during training enables the agent to reason and act across on-foot navigation, target approach, vehicle interaction, and driving scenarios.

    5 Analysis

    5.1 Learning Dynamics

    In this section, we illustrate the learning dynamics of the SFT-initialized policies over RL steps. Figure 5(a,b) separates penalized episode returns from unpenalized game scores, with each metric averaged across sixteen environments.

    Learning beyond SFT.

    As shown in Figure 5(a,b), both mean episode return and mean game score rise across the RL training steps. Gains are largest early in training and become more gradual later. The 35B-A3B curve finishes slightly above the 9B curve on both measures. These trends indicate that learning from synthetic experience improves game control beyond SFT.

    Effect of supervised initialization.

    Figure 5(c) contrasts the displayed Base→RL and SFT→RL trajectories for 9B over 100 RL steps. SFT→RL rises from 17.67% to 51.67% Minecraft success, while Base→RL rises from 12.67% to 16.67%, leaving a 35.00-percentage-point gap at step 100.

    Learning across environments.

    Figure 6 breaks down episode returns across all sixteen training environments. Both models show broad net gains, but their learning trajectories vary across environments. For example, performance on simpler tasks such as 2D aiming improves rapidly and then levels off, whereas gains in 2D circuit driving emerge much later.

    5.2 Environment Scaling

    Expanding the training suite.

    The scaling comparison allocates a fixed budget of 25,600 episodes over 100 RL steps across 2, 4, 8, or 16 environments, starting from the same Player-1-9B-SFT checkpoint. Each configuration uses 256 episodes per step, allocated equally across the environments. Appendix D.4 specifies the subsets and protocol.

    5.3 Evolution of Action Composition

    Figure 8 shows increased use of composite actions during RL. Across Player-1-9B’s in-suite validation trajectories, the share of turns with composite actions rises from 64.7% at the start of RL to 85.4% and 93.2% after 50 and 100 RL steps, respectively. This progressive increase occurs without an explicit reward for action composition, suggesting that task-driven RL reinforces coordinated inputs common to game control, such as aiming while firing or moving while adjusting the camera.

    6 Conclusion

    We presented Player-1, a post-training framework for learning game control beyond demonstrations through synthetic experience. Curated gameplay demonstrations initialize computer-use models in a shared game-control action space. Player-1-Gym then provides sixteen synthetic environments organized around shared control demands, with verifiable rewards and randomized observations and control dynamics for multi-environment RL. Evaluations on MineDojo-300, ViZDoom-10, and GameWorld demonstrate that learning from synthetic experience advances game-control capabilities beyond SFT, with gains that generalize beyond the RL training suite. Further analyses show improved transfer with larger training suites. Together, these findings establish synthetic experience as an effective resource for learning transferable game control without online training in each target game.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Game-Control Interface

    A.1 Coordinates and Composite Actions

    Table 5 specifies the execution semantics of the actions introduced in Section 3.1. For an observation of width W and height H, normalized absolute positions and relative displacements map to pixels as

    (x,y)↦(xW/1000,yH/1000), (Δx,Δy)↦(ΔxW/1000,ΔyH/1000).

    The origin is the upper-left corner, and positive displacement points right and down. One movement uses either absolute or relative coordinates. A key cannot be both held and tapped in the same step, nor can one mouse button be both held and clicked.

    A.2 Execution and Visual Feedback

    Relative motion requests input displacement, not a universal camera angle. For per-pixel camera gain g, requested yaw and pitch increments δψ and δφ have magnitudes

    |δψ|=gW|Δx|/1000, |δφ|=gH|Δy|/1000,

    before native camera limits; mouse displacement is not multiplied by action duration. The seven mouse-controlled 3D Player-1-Gym environments use a nominal gain g₀=0.00196 radians per observation pixel by default. With Control randomization, the effective gain is g=g₀L, where L is defined in Appendix C.2. Observation geometry and camera constraints remain fixed within a checkpoint comparison. Benchmark-specific settings are given in Appendix E.

    A.3 Observation and Interaction History

    SFT, RL, and evaluation all use two recent visual–action turns and two earlier action-only turns. In the earlier action-only turns, screenshots are replaced by ; reasoning in all retained historical turns is replaced by . The current screenshot and executed historical actions are retained.

    Appendix B Gameplay Demonstrations: Construction and Annotation

    B.1 Sources and Statistics

    Both model sizes are trained with the collection in Figure 9: 6,044 trajectories and 295,097 turns from 2,544 source-qualified recording sessions and 172 games. We approximate the sampled control hours, which equal the turn count × 200 ms, or 16.4 hours in total for the full annotated dataset.

    Quality selection.

    We automated validity, activity, and repetition checks that complement source-level and manual review of recording completeness, observation–action alignment, and sequence diversity. The collection contains 5,360 gameplay trajectories with a total of 268,000 turns and 684 in-game UI trajectories with a total of 27,097 turns.

    Action statistics.

    Figure 2(a) counts the distribution of each action across all samples in the dataset. Keyboard–mouse composites take precedence. Mouse-only turns are assigned by movement, click, hold, then scroll. Inputs per step count each key tap/hold and mouse operation separately, with wait as one no-op. Pointer-mode shares use all turns containing mouse_move, including keyboard–mouse composites.

    B.2 Action Standardization

    Temporal alignment.

    For continuous gameplay, source timestamps define contiguous intervals of 150–250 ms, projected onto a 200-ms target grid using cumulative boundaries. Relative input is summed within each source interval. Keyboard presses shorter than 100 ms become taps, and longer presses become holds on overlapping target steps. Mouse presses lasting at most 300 ms become clicks. Each target summarizes compatible recorded inputs for concurrent execution within one control step.

    UI trajectories also follow recorded operation boundaries. Clicks retain their recorded targets, key sequences expand into individual presses, drags use start and endpoint controls with an explicit release, and scroll gestures become directional steps. Execution uses the shared 200-ms action space. Sampled control hours use target execution duration, while UI trajectories retain their recorded, operation-dependent timing.

    Spatial alignment.

    Native relative-mouse input scales vary across data sources and recording setups. We therefore calibrate these inputs to pixel-equivalent displacements using freely moving GUI pointers from the same recording session. The mapping also applies to pointer-locked recordings. Camera response is defined in Appendix A.2. For native-input sums (rₓ,r_y), coefficients (kₓ,k_y), and logical recording size (Wₘ,Hₘ), the normalized target is

    Δx=round(1000kₓrₓ/Wₘ), Δy=round(1000k_yr_y/Hₘ).

    Mouse-move Calibration.

    In-house and D2E calibration uses GUI windows with stable focus and geometry, aligned timestamps, and no pointer clipping or recentering. For paired native input rᵢ and pointer displacement pᵢ, window and pooled session estimates are

    kᵢ=(rᵢ^⊤pᵢ)/(rᵢ^⊤rᵢ), k̂=(∑ᵢrᵢ^⊤pᵢ)/(∑ᵢrᵢ^⊤rᵢ).

    D2E uses window-equal estimates for a source-level coefficient; in-house coefficients are recording-specific. Pixel2Play uses per-axis Huber regression over at least two stable, non-overlapping two-second GUI blocks. Out-of-range projections are rejected rather than clipped to ensure the action quality. Table 6 lists the source mappings.

    B.3 Goal and Reasoning Annotation

    We use Gemini 3.8 Flash to build reusable profiles of rules, roles, inputs, and examples for each game in the trajectory, and check them for recorded-control coverage and action validity. It assigns goals from each profile, full-trajectory storyboard, and action timeline. The same game from different data sources should share the same assembled profile. For per-turn reasoning annotation, it re-uses the goal, fixed action target, and current and past frames.

    Appendix C Player-1-Gym: Tasks, Rewards, and Randomization

    C.1 Tasks and Verifiable Rewards

    By primary task, the sixteen environments comprise aiming (2), combat (5), driving (4), navigation (4), and UI interaction (1). Tables 7 and 8 specify their tasks, score components, and API state fields. Interaction tests, score checks, and human review verify controls, observable transitions, and reward events against human-defined rules.

    We designed the shared Three.js browser runtime to provide controllable resets, keyboard–mouse execution, screenshots, and rewards, with fixed-step simulation independent of inference latency. Each environment defines a cumulative score Sₑ(s) and supplies the increment r_e,t=Sₑ(sₜ₊₁)-Sₑ(sₜ) as reward. Reward computation and evaluation use privileged state, while the policy receives only screenshots and task/control text. Episodes only end on native completion or failure, or at the turn cap when the task is not completed under the limits.

    C.2 Randomization and Sampling

    Figure 10 shows individual and joint Appearance, Camera, and Scene variation. The parameters, distributions, and applicable environments for Appearance, Camera, Scene, and Control are specified in Table 9. Specifically, appearance preserves collision geometry and functional roles; Scene varies layouts, spawns, and subsequent entity generation, potentially changing task difficulty. Appearance and Camera are sampled at reset and fixed within each episode, with triangular modes at native values. Background lightness and saturation, ambient intensity, and key-light intensity share one sampled quantile, and linked asset components receive compatible color changes. Orthographic zoom is relative to the native view, including 2D platforming. Initial first-person point-of-view yaw/pitch is distinct from camera-rig pitch.

    Control-response sampling.

    Control varies input response independently of camera projection and scene configuration. For each supported response parameter k, we independently sample

    c_e,k∼Tri(a_e,k,1,b_e,k), c_e,k(t)=c_e,k(0) throughout the episode.

    		(2)

    The control seed is independent of domain randomization. Separate parameter substreams set values at reset, unchanged through respawns. The narrower chasing, platforming, and jump ranges preserve pursuit-speed and traversal constraints. Collision rules, gravity, attack timing, control bindings, and reward definitions remain fixed. Table 10 specifies the training mixture.

    Appendix D Post-Training Details

    D.1 Supervised Fine-Tuning

    For supervised fine-tuning, both model sizes use token-level cross-entropy on the current turn’s reasoning and action, with the history in Appendix A.3.

    Action-balanced sampling.

    In human gameplay recordings, some actions occupy only a small fraction of playing time but are critical for game progress. For example, left mouse button inputs account for less than 1% of valid inputs in the original recordings, which are dominated by keyboard inputs and mouse movement. In addition to selecting and filtering demonstrations for action coverage during data curation, we use action-balanced sampling to strengthen supervision for these infrequent but important actions. We classify each turn by its current recorded action into overlapping pools: keyboard, mouse movement, click, hold, any mouse button, keyboard–mouse, movement–click, keyboard–click, and keyboard–movement–click. Keyboard includes held and tapped keys; keyboard–mouse includes any mouse input, including scrolling. Other contains the remaining turns, including wait and scroll-only actions. Each draw selects a pool proportionally to its weight (1 for each control pool; 0.1 for Other), then samples a turn uniformly with replacement.

    D.2 Multi-Environment Reinforcement Learning

    During RL, we use synchronous PPO with a dense critic initialized from Qwen3.5-9B for both actor sizes. Before actor updates begin, the critic undergoes five warmup iterations under the same environment configuration. Rollouts retain the observations, prompts, responses, masks, and behavior log probabilities used at generation, preserving the same conditioning during optimization.

    Reward and cross-turn credit.

    For turn t in environment e, we define the penalized step reward and undiscounted return-to-go as

    r̃_e,t=r_e,t-pⁱⁿᵛᵃˡⁱᵈ_e,t-pˡᵉⁿᵍᵗʰ_e,t, G_e,t=∑ᵤ₌ₜᵀr̃_e,u,

    		(3)

    where r_e,t is the game-score increment (Appendix C.1) and T the terminal turn. Training curves average episode returns G_e,1. The penalties are

    pⁱⁿᵛᵃˡⁱᵈ_e,t=1[invalid action], pˡᵉⁿᵍᵗʰ_e,t=\min{1, 0.005\max(0,nₜʳᵉᵃˢᵒⁿ-64)},

    where nₜʳᵉᵃˢᵒⁿ counts generated reasoning/prose tokens. An invalid action executes the runtime’s wait fallback. We apply no additional terminal-failure penalty or task-wise reward rescaling. With γ=λ=1, return targets are computed over complete trajectories, preserving cross-turn credit.

    Advantage normalization and loss reduction.

    We normalize advantages globally in GAE, then within environments using Equation (1), with Nₑ≥2 and ε=10⁻⁸; critic return targets are unchanged. For minibatch B, let Tᵢ be turn i’s nonempty response-token set selected by the loss mask. The clipped PPO loss averages within turns, then across turns:

    L_policy(θ)=(1)/(|B|)∑_i∈B(1)/(|Tᵢ|)∑_j∈Tᵢℓ^PPO_i,j(θ;Ã_i,j).

    		(4)

    The critic uses the same reduction. Normalization is token-weighted within environments, whereas losses weight turns equally. Each environment therefore contributes in proportion to its included turns.

    D.3 Training Implementation

    Table 10 summarizes the shared recipe for both model sizes. For each model size, the SFT stage uses 32 NVIDIA H200 GPUs and takes approximately 24 hours, while a 200-step RL run uses 64 H200 GPUs and takes approximately 36 hours. Both durations include validation. Browser rollouts use a cluster-wide pool of 32 workers, each managing up to 16 isolated Playwright browser contexts, for a total capacity of 512 concurrent environments. Browser processes and contexts are reused across episodes to amortize startup costs.

    D.4 Environment-Scaling Protocol

    For Section 5.2, 9B policies start independently from the same SFT checkpoint, sharing the PPO, history, reward, and randomization settings in Table 10. Table 11 gives the suites and matched episode budgets, while interaction lengths and compute may vary within different episodes. Comparisons share Minecraft development tasks and trial seeds, with SFT as the zero-environment reference.

    Appendix E Evaluation and Results

    Table 12 lists the full panels and budgets. Methods share each panel’s tasks, trial seeds, and decision budgets while retaining model-specific preprocessing and inference schedules. Periodic evaluation during RL steps uses 100 Minecraft tasks with three trials each, ten ViZDoom maps with ten episodes each, and 170 GameWorld tasks with one trial each. Qwen3.5, Player-1-SFT, and final Player-1-9B are deployed with the history in Appendix A.3.

    Evaluation cost.

    Our full MineDojo-300, ViZDoom-10, and GameWorld protocols allocate up to 3.14 million agent decision turns per model. Our in-suite validation records average roughly 3,000 input tokens and 100 output tokens per turn, including visual context and generated reasoning. Using these observed lengths as a workload proxy, a full-budget evaluation would cost approximately USD$110,000 at GPT-6 Astra’s standard API rates of USD$10 and USD$50 per million input and output tokens, respectively, before caching discounts.111https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6-astra, accessed Sep 24, 2026. Actual costs depend on model-specific tokenization, reasoning, and episode lengths. Considering the estimated cost, our focus is mainly on representative released game-control and computer-use policies rather than proprietary API models.

    E.1 Baseline Inference and Action Adapters

    We deploy JARVIS-VLA with its action-token decoder and two history entries to predict one action per decision. UI-TARS-1.5-7B uses three previous screenshots, deterministic decoding, and a 400-token output limit. Its adapter maps pixel-coordinate actions to one benchmark interval, with drag and double-click unsupported. NitroGen aggregates an 18-action chunk into six benchmark decisions (three native actions per decision), refreshing the image after each chunk. GameWAM predicts 16 actions and executes eight before replanning, using its Minecraft checkpoint outside Doom and its ViZDoom checkpoint for Doom. Open-P2P uses visual-only conditioning and session-specific recurrent state. All temporal inference state is isolated between episodes.

    Model inputs retain the released preprocessing for the best practice of each baseline: Minecraft is rendered at 864×480. We resize the screenshots to 640×360 for JARVIS-VLA and UI-TARS, 256×256 for NitroGen, 224×224 for GameWAM, and 192×192 for Open-P2P. JARVIS-VLA and GameWAM retain their native degree-based Minecraft camera actions, while Open-P2P uses an adapter gain of 0.15 degrees per raw mouse pixel. Browser-game adapters project native actions onto per-game and per-role bindings. Benchmark action intervals remain fixed, so a native action chunk can span different simulated durations across benchmarks.

    E.2 Player-1-Gym In-Suite Validation

    In-suite validation uses the seeded panel in Table 12 with the training randomization settings. For an episode of T turns in environment e, the return is

    G_e,1=∑ₜ₌₁ᵀ(r_e,t-pⁱⁿᵛᵃˡⁱᵈ_e,t-pˡᵉⁿᵍᵗʰ_e,t).

    Here r_e,t=Sₑ(sₜ₊₁)-Sₑ(sₜ) is the native game-score increment (Appendix C.1), and the invalid-action and length penalties are defined in Appendix D.2. We report mean episode return, averaging trials within each environment and then equally across the sixteen environments.

    E.3 MineDojo-300

    MineDojo-300 contains 200 Combat and 100 Harvest tasks from MineDojo, ported to MineStudio on Minecraft 1.16.5. World and task seeds are deterministically derived from each task and trial. Success is verified after initialization from inventory acquisition for Harvest tasks or target kills for Combat tasks. We average success over trials within each task, then equally over tasks. One decision advances a 50-ms simulator tick. Player-1’s camera adapter uses a nominal gain of 0.00196 radians per observation pixel, subject to native constraints.

    We also report Task coverage in Cₘ=∑ᵢ₌₁^N1[sᵢ≥m] for m∈{1,2,4}, where sᵢ counts successes among eight trials for task i. Entries Cₘ/N, with N=300, count tasks meeting each threshold. Overall success intervals use 100,000 percentile task-cluster bootstrap replicates, stratified by Combat and Harvest while retaining all eight trials per task and the panel’s category weights. The 95% intervals quantify within-panel task-sampling uncertainty. For all-zero outcomes, we report [-].
