Direct illumination from non-trivial emitters with occluding housing, high-polygon emissive meshes, spatially varying emission, or deformable assemblies is a persistent bottleneck in real-time rendering. Current real-time solutions either rely on simplified analytical representations or fall back to runtime sampling. Analytical methods are restricted to simple emitter geometry, pure sampling-based estimators need high sampling budgets to be noise-free, and proxy representations still require runtime integration over outgoing radiance around the emitter. We present Neural Emission Fields (NEF), a representation that eliminates runtime integration by precomputing the illumination in the volume around the emitter. This neural field is parameterized by position, normal, view direction, and material parameters. Using a two-headed diffuse/glossy architecture, it yields noise-free unoccluded direct illumination from a single network evaluation per shading point. Because training is performed in the emitter’s local frame, a trained NEF acts as a portable lighting asset reusable across scenes under rigid transforms. Internal interreflections, self-occlusion, spatially varying emission, and deformations are absorbed into the learned representation at zero additional runtime cost.

1 Introduction

Direct illumination is a major cost in real-time rendering pipelines, especially when emitters are non-trivial—luminaires with housing geometry that occludes the internal filament, emissive meshes with thousands of polygons, light sources with spatially varying or textured emission profiles, or deformable emitters that change shape over time. While path tracing [17] handles all of these correctly, converging to noise-free direct illumination from non-trivial emitters is incompatible with real-time rendering budgets. Existing alternatives that do meet those rendering budgets typically compromise on generality, accuracy, or noise-free output.

Analytical methods like Linearly Transformed Cosines (LTC) [15] are extremely fast but assume 2D polygonal emitters and scale linearly with the emitter’s vertex count. For more general emitters, Monte Carlo estimators of direct illumination, including reservoir methods [6], support arbitrary emitters but produce noise that must be removed by a denoiser, which often introduces unwanted temporal and spatial artifacts. Proxy-based representations [14, 35], including recent neural variants [43], sidestep both limitations by precomputing the outgoing radiance into a 4D near-field proxy, factoring out the cost of sampling paths within the emitter assembly. However, receiver points must still integrate over this proxy at runtime.

Our key insight is that this remaining runtime integration is avoidable. Rather than precomputing only the radiance leaving an emitter (which still needs to be integrated), we precompute the pre-integrated outgoing direct illumination with respect to a receiver point (any shaded surface point in the volume around the emitter). We represent this as a neural field parameterized by the receiver’s position, normal, view direction, and material parameters, learned by a neural network conditioned on a material model. By shifting the integration to a one-time precomputation phase, a single network evaluation replaces the entire integral over the (proxy) emitter.

Because the network is trained in the emitter’s local coordinate frame, the resulting model functions as a portable lighting asset. World-space queries are mapped into the emitter’s frame at shading time rather than baked into the network weights, so a trained NEF can be translated, rotated, and uniformly scaled at runtime without retraining. A single training run therefore amortizes across every scene and every instance in which the emitter is placed—much like a baked texture or precomputed BRDF.

This design facilitates several critical performance advantages over traditional methods. Inference cost is fundamentally decoupled from the geometric complexity of the emitter; the computational cost is determined by the network’s size rather than the polygon count of the emitter. Furthermore, because the receiver’s BRDF is incorporated into the learning objective, complex emissive effects are absorbed into the representation at no additional runtime cost. Finally, since the training phase relies solely on path-traced radiance estimates for training data, the same training procedure is used for simple planar polygons, complex emissive meshes, and deformable emitter assemblies.

We summarize our contributions as follows:

  • •

    A reformulation of direct illumination as a pre-integrated, receiver-aware quantity, eliminating the runtime integration retained by prior analytical, sampling-based, and proxy-based methods.

  • •

    A neural emission field employing a two-headed diffuse/glossy architecture and reflected-direction encoding, yielding noise-free direct illumination and accurate specular highlights from a single network evaluation per shading point.

  • •

    Scene-independent training in the emitter’s local coordinate frame, so a single pre-trained NEF can be translated, rotated and scaled across different scenes without retraining.

  • •

    Extensions to complex emissive assemblies with internal interreflections, spatially varying emission, and deformable emitters which are non-trivial or unsupported in state-of-the-art real-time methods.

    • 2 Related Work

    We categorize previous work into three primary categories: analytical solutions, Monte Carlo estimators, and proxy-based representations. Finally, we discuss the broader context of using neural networks in the context of rendering.

    Analytical Solutions. Analytical closed-form solutions for simple emitter geometries (e.g., planar polygons) exist for various receiver types, including diffuse [5] or glossy receivers like the Phong distribution [3], and more general glossy reflections [15, 19, 20]. Analytical methods are extremely efficient for low-polygon emitters, but their cost scales linearly with the number of emitter vertices [3], making them prohibitively expensive for high-polygon emitters in real-time applications. Furthermore, even on supported geometry they diverge from a path-traced reference when receivers are glossy or emission is non-uniform [15]. Our neural approach achieves more accurate shading with respect to a ground truth solution, natively supports non-convex and non-planar emitters, and decouples cost from the emitter geometry, drastically reducing shading time for complex emissive meshes.

    Many-Light Sampling. Monte Carlo integration supports estimating direct illumination from any emitter but requires specialized sampling strategies to manage runtime noise. Early techniques addressed the many-lights problem by ranking lights according to their potential contribution [40] or by classifying them as important or unimportant to guide sampling [31]. In complex scenes, hierarchical representations [37, 23, 42] can be used to enable emitter sampling at sublinear cost. More recently, ReSTIR [6] introduced spatiotemporal reservoir resampling, achieving high-quality direct illumination under tight sampling budgets. Despite these advancements, the residual variance inherent to all Monte Carlo approaches typically necessitates a denoiser. In contrast, NEF avoids runtime sampling entirely, shifting the computational burden to a (one-time) per-emitter offline training phase.

    Classical Pre-integration. Precomputation in rendering [28] trades offline computations for runtime cost by tabulating light transport over a discretised parameter domain. Precomputed radiance transfer (PRT) [33] projects the transfer function at each surface point onto a low-order spherical harmonics basis, reducing shading under distant lighting to a dot product. All-frequency variants require non-linear wavelet approximations to keep storage tractable [26]. More fundamentally, PRT relies on the distant-lighting assumption, which breaks down for near-field emitters whose incident lighting varies with receiver position.

    A complementary line of work stores lighting in a volume rather than on surfaces. Irradiance volumes [12] and their dynamic, ray-traced successors [21] cache irradiance at probes on a grid and interpolate between them at runtime. For strongly spatially varying signals, such as the near field of a complex emitter, these caches require careful probe placement [32, 39] and fine discretisation to avoid interpolation and light-leaking artifacts.

    These approaches share a common limitation: the storage of a tabulated representation grows exponentially with the dimensionality of the signal. Pre-integrated direct illumination around a near-field emitter depends on receiver position (3D), normal (2D), and reflected direction (2D), which is already seven dimensions for a single glossy material. Conditioning on roughness to cover a continuous family of materials, as done in this paper, adds an eighth parameter. A regular grid with only 32 samples per dimension would already require 32⁸≈10¹² entries. Adding a time parameter for dynamic emitters worsens this further: a naive per-keyframe cache scales linearly with the number of keyframes, and complex temporal variation demands many of them. Like prior neural precomputation methods [27, 9], NEF sidesteps this curse of dimensionality by fitting a compact, global representation that efficiently captures correlations in the high-dimensional signal.

    Pre-integrated Emitters. Estimating the radiance emitted by complex light sources is non-trivial, particularly when light paths are obstructed by housing geometry or undergo multiple internal reflections. Early research tackled this by replacing the emitter with a 4D proxy geometry. Canned light sources represent the radiance leaving the emitter’s bounding surface as a 4D light field slab so that scene points can be illuminated by ray-tracing against the proxy rather than the intricate original geometry [14]. Later work decoupled a luminaire’s dual roles in rendering: a radiance volume captures its appearance when viewed directly, while virtual point lights approximate how it illuminates the surrounding scene [35]. Neural variants [43] reduced the storage requirements of these tabulated representations and combined it with a learned importance sampling distribution. Subsequent work learned radiance-field representations of the luminaire for faster evaluation [7], or relied on wavelet-compressed light fields for fast per-ray reconstruction and hierarchical importance sampling [4].

    Despite these advances, these methods still treat the proxy as an emitter that must be integrated at runtime. Each shading point integrates the product of the radiance sampled from the proxy’s 4D near-field and the material evaluation. In contrast, NEF pre-integrates this contribution offline, storing the full outgoing pre-integrated direct illumination to be queried at runtime.

    Rendering with Neural Networks. A common use of neural networks in rendering is capturing the radiance distribution during a training phase which amortizes over subsequent viewings of the scene. Early work anchored a learned radiance representation to scene geometry for interactive viewing from arbitrary directions [30]. Modern variants extend this idea to high-quality static scenes [13], rotatable environment lighting [27], scene animations [8], variable scene configurations [10, 34], and volumetric irradiance caching [9]. These methods all rely on offline, scene-specific training. Alternatively, a small neural representation can be trained online as a radiance cache [25] with the additional runtime cost of ray tracing and denoising. NEF differs in that it is an offline method whose representation is anchored in the emitter’s local 3D extent rather than on the 2D scene manifold, making it a portable, reusable asset across scenes.

    3 Neural Pre-integrated Emitters

    Prior proxy methods reduce the runtime cost of internal emitter transport but still leave the receiver-side integral to be evaluated per shading point. We close this remaining gap by learning the full pre-integrated direct illumination as a neural field around the emitter. Section 3.1 derives this formulation; Section 3.2 defines the emitter-local frame that makes the representation portable; Section 3.3 introduces the diffuse/glossy decomposition; Section 3.4 describes training; and Section 3.5 outlines rendering.

    3.1 Pre-integrated Emitter

    Computing the direct illumination Lₒ with respect to a complex emitter involves two layers of integration: the recursive internal light transport inside the emitter, and the receiver’s shading integral over the hemisphere. Proxy-emitter methods [14, 35, 43] already peel away the inner layer by precomputing internal transport into a function ℙ defined on a bounding surface. The receiver, however, must still integrate against ℙ at runtime. We take this idea one step further by absorbing the receiver’s direct illumination integral into the learned field D_θ itself:

    Lₒ(x,ωₒ)=∫_Ω[∫_Ω⋯ dωᵢ^′] (internal transport)fᵣ(x,ωᵢ,ωₒ) (ωᵢ·n) dωᵢ(reference)
    =∫_Ωℙ(t(x,ωᵢ),-ωᵢ) (baked offline)fᵣ(x,ωᵢ,ωₒ) (ωᵢ·n) dωᵢ(proxy)
    ≈D_θ(x̃,ñ,ω̃ₒ,α) (baked offline)(ours)

    where (x,n,ωₒ) defines the world-space position, normal and outgoing direction at an intersection point, (x̃,ñ,ω̃ₒ) are their counterparts expressed in the emitter’s local frame (Section 3.2), ωᵢ is the incident direction, t(x,ωᵢ) returns the point where the ray from x in direction ωᵢ intersects the proxy surface, α are the material parameters for the BRDF fᵣ, (ωᵢ·n) is the cosine foreshortening term, and Ω denotes the hemispherical integration domain.

    Crucially, a pre-integrated quantity is not a property of the emitter alone. Since the BRDF fᵣ appears inside the direct illumination integral, different receivers will observe different values of D_θ at the same (x,n). The receiver’s shading model is therefore part of what is being learned. We instantiate this using the GGX microfacet model [38] over a roughness range of α∈[0.1,1]. By exposing α as input to the network, a single trained NEF represents the full roughness range for that material. While we restrict our scope to GGX in this work, our approach is generic and can be extended to other materials, such as Disney or layered BRDFs, by extending the conditioning inputs and the training distribution.

    At runtime, evaluating D_θ requires only a single network inference at the shading point. This eliminates the need for any sampling of the proxy ℙ, importance sampling, and denoising.

    Because D_θ is agnostic to the source of the radiance field, all the complexity that would otherwise have to be handled at runtime is shifted to the offline solver and baked into the network weights. This includes complex effects such as self-occlusion, multi-bounce transport and non-uniform emission (Section 4.2)—effects that often violate the assumptions made by analytical methods such as LTC [15]. As a result, D_θ can stand in for a path-traced estimate of direct illumination from an emitter, provided the field can be trained to faithfully represent it.

    3.2 Emitter-space

    Our neural field is defined in the emitter’s local frame (see Figure 1). Given a rigid world transform M, we map a world-space shading configuration (x,n,ωₒ) to its local counterpart (x̃,ñ,ω̃ₒ) by applying M⁻¹ to the position and the rotational part of M⁻¹ to the normal and outgoing directions.

    Pre-integrated direct illumination is only physically meaningful within a bounded region around the emitter. Emitted radiance falls off with distance, and beyond a certain range an emitter’s contribution becomes negligible. We therefore define the emitter-space as an axis-aligned bounding region in the local frame, sized to extend 20× the emitter’s largest extent on each axis—well beyond the 5× threshold at which the inverse-square law becomes an acceptable approximation for emitters [29]. Shading points inside this region are evaluated by a direct query of D_θ, which is sufficient for all emitters in this work.

    Analytical Fall-off. A simple heuristic to deal with points outside of the emitter-space, consists of clamping outside queries to the nearest boundary point and scaling the resulting shading value by (d_boundary/d_actual)², where d_boundary is the distance from the emitter center to the clamped boundary point and d_actual is the true distance from the emitter center to the shading point. As shown in Figure 2, this fall-off approach generates a result that is hard to visually distinguish from the ground truth reference. Alternatively, the emitter-space can be enlarged at training time to avoid the heuristic, potentially requiring a larger representation to get the desired level of accuracy everywhere in the emitter-space.

    Scene-independent placement. Anchoring the representation to the emitter’s local frame yields two practical benefits: scene-independence and free rigid placement at runtime. The trained NEF does not store scene-specific information, so the same parameters θ are reusable across scenes. At runtime, world-space shading configurations are mapped through M⁻¹ before being evaluated by D_θ. Since M is applied at shading time rather than baked into the network weights, translating or rotating the emitter is essentially free: it only changes the transformation applied to each query, not the representation itself. Uniform scaling is handled by folding the scale factor into M and scaling the emitter-space extent accordingly; non-uniform scaling and shears are not supported, as they would distort the learned angular distribution. A single NEF therefore defines a family of emitters related by similarity transformations, amortizing the training cost across all scenes and instances in which the emitter is placed (Figure 3).

    3.3 Diffuse–Glossy Separation

    Similarly to related work [27], we decompose our neural representation into separate diffuse f^θ_d(x̃,ñ) and glossy f_g^θ(x̃,ñ,r(ω̃ₒ,ñ),α) components. We compute the total pre-integrated direct illumination D_θ at a given shading point (x̃,ñ,ω̃ₒ,α) as their sum:

    D_θ(x̃,ñ,ω̃ₒ,α)=ρ_d(x)·f^θ_d(x̃,ñ) (diffuse)+ρ_g(x)·f_g^θ(x̃,ñ,r(ω̃ₒ,ñ),α) (glossy).

    Here, tilde denotes properties in the local emitter-space defined in Section 3.2, ρ_d and ρ_g are factored-out diffuse and specular textures of the shading point x which retain high-frequency texture details [25], θ are the trainable parameters of the neural representation, r(ω̃ₒ,ñ) is the reflected outgoing direction vector ω̃ₒ around the normal ñ, and α is the GGX roughness parameter. For emitters that are only expected to see diffuse surfaces at runtime, the glossy head f_g^θ can be omitted during training (and during shading).

    All network inputs are normalized to [0,1]³, and a learned multi-resolution hash encoding  [24] is applied to both the position x̃ and the reflected direction r(ω̃ₒ,ñ). Encoding the reflected direction is critical for capturing the sharp highlights and complex reflections characteristic of low-roughness receiver geometry (see supplemental material), consistent with findings in the field of novel view synthesis [36]. Both the glossy and diffuse head use a 4-layer MLP of width 128 with ReLU activations. More details on the network architecture can be found in the supplemental material.

    3.4 Training

    A schematic of the training procedure is shown in Figure 1. Training a NEF only requires a reliable estimate of the outgoing radiance Lₒ for any query within the network’s input domain, making the procedure agnostic to the underlying emitter geometry.

    Sample generation. For each training batch, we draw queries uniformly from the emitter-space (Section 3.2). For the glossy head f_g^θ, we sample a position x̃ uniformly in the local bounding box, and a normal ñ such that the emitter is visible in its hemisphere avoiding queries with zero radiance, an outgoing direction ω̃ₒ uniformly on the upper hemisphere defined by ñ, and a roughness α uniformly in [0.1,1]. The diffuse head f_d^θ uses the same procedure restricted to (x̃,ñ). For deformable or animated emitters, we additionally sample a time parameter t∈[0,1] corresponding to the emitter’s state, encoded with an 8-band Fourier encoding [22] and provided as an extra conditioning input.

    Radiance targets. Target radiance is obtained via offline path tracing against the (possibly time-varying) emitter geometry. Bare emissive surfaces are handled with standard next-event estimation; emitters with non-emissive housing geometry that causes self-occlusion or internal interreflections (Figure 5) are handled with full path tracing inside the emitter assembly, so that higher-order transport is naturally absorbed into the training signal. We use 64 samples per radiance estimate as default across all emitters in this paper as we saw diminishing returns beyond this (see supplemental material for an ablation). Targets are generated on-the-fly rather than cached, so all reported training timings include the cost of path tracing.

    Optimization. We minimize a relative L₂ loss [25] between the network prediction and the path-traced target averaged over the batch, L(θ)=((D_θ-⟨Lₒ⟩)²)/(sg(D_θ)²+ε), where ε=0.01 and sg denotes a stop gradient operation. The relative loss prevents bright regions of the emitter-space from dominating the gradient and helps the multi-resolution hash encoding to allocate capacity uniformly across the field. We use Adam [18] with a learning rate of 10⁻³, a batch size of 2¹⁶, and use cosine annealing learning rate decay. The number of training iterations for each of our emitter types can be found in the supplemental material. Total wall-clock time on an RTX 4090 ranges from one minute for diffuse receiver with planar emitters to three hours for emitters with complex emissive effects, dominated by the cost of generating path-traced target values.

    3.5 Rendering

    Because NEF stores a pre-integrated estimate of the outgoing radiance reflected by the receiver, no integration is required at runtime. Unlike methods that integrate with respect to the emitter geometry or to a proxy representation of the emitter [14, 35, 43], our approach reduces the shading process to a single network evaluation per pixel. At render time, we first perform a G-buffer pass to obtain the (x,n,ωₒ,α) channels at each shading point. These are transformed into the emitter’s local frame via its current world transform M (Section 3.2), encoded, and fed to D_θ to obtain the outgoing radiance contribution pre-integrated with respect to the emitter.

    Visibility. As with existing analytical methods [15, 5], NEF does not inherently capture occlusions of the emissive field caused by the surrounding scene. For simple emitters, a single shadow ray toward the emitter center is often sufficient (Figure 4); for soft shadows, established techniques such as shadow mapping [41] or a small ray-tracing budget combined with a denoiser [16] apply directly, which we implemented in the supplemental material. Crucially, shadow rays are only required against non-emitter scene geometry: the NEF itself bakes in self-occlusion and internal interreflections within the emitter assembly (Figure 5).

    4 Results

    We show that NEF matches the quality of analytical solutions (Section 4.1) and extends beyond what they handle, supporting emissive meshes and deformable emitters (Section 4.2). We then compare against two sampling-based techniques, where NEF’s sampling-free formulation yields a runtime advantage (Section 4.3).

    4.1 Planar Emitters

    We compare against analytical integration for diffuse receivers [5] and Linearly Transformed Cosines (LTC) for glossy receivers [15]. As shown in Figure 4, our method matches the analytical reference for diffuse receivers under uniform emission, confirming its accuracy.

    For glossy receivers (Figure 10), the larger capacity of NEF allows it to achieve lower rendering error across various roughness values α compared to LTC, highlighting LTC’s remaining approximation error. The near-mirror regime (α→0) remains challenging for a finite neural representation; we show an example of the increase in error at lower roughness in the supplemental material.

    While analytical methods have lower per-frame shading costs for simple polygons, their runtime scales linearly O(V) with the number of emitter vertices V. This linear cost is especially noticeable for large emissive emitters, as highlighted in Table 1. We show the crossover point between the analytical methods and our GlossyNEF—267 emitter vertices—in the supplemental material. The generality and computational efficiency of our approach become especially relevant when extending beyond planar geometry.

    4.2 Complex Emitters

    A key advantage of our approach is that inference cost is determined by the complexity of the emissive field, not by the complexity of the underlying geometry. While NEF inference cost does scale with emissive field complexity—a highly spatially varying emitter benefits from a larger or more expressive network—this complexity is typically much lower than that of the geometry itself. Naively subdividing an emissive mesh increases its vertex count but leaves its emissive field largely unchanged, so the same NEF capacity suffices regardless of tessellation. All results in this paper share a single network configuration sized for the most demanding case (the Pierced Sphere, whose housing interreflections produce a high-frequency emissive field); for simpler emitters such as the planar quad, a smaller architecture would suffice with no perceptible loss in quality (see supplemental material).

    Higher-order Emissive Effects. Our NEF formulation can also capture higher-order emissive effects arising from multi-bounce light transport within the emitter, such as internal reflections toward a filament. By replacing direct light-source sampling with path tracing during training, multi-bounce contributions are integrated into the training signal. Figure 5 shows three assemblies in which internal interreflections meaningfully shape the emissive field: a Dragon mesh acting as a bare emitter, a Pierced Sphere whose shell partially occludes and reflects an internal filament, and a Lattice Box which houses a spherical emitter. Obtaining a noise-free reference for these assemblies is expensive—on the order of 1M samples per pixel—because the interior light paths are not captured by simple next-event estimation against the bare emissive geometry. The effect varies by assembly: interreflections produce only a mild overall brightening on the Dragon, whereas the Pierced Sphere and Lattice Box show light diffusing through the apertures, softening cast shadows and noticeably brightening regions that the bare-emitter leaves dark. NEF reproduces all three references faithfully.

    Non-uniform emission. Since our NEF representation is agnostic to the emissive profile of the light source, it naturally accommodates spatially varying emission without modification. Figure  (center) shows an emitter with a non-uniform radiance distribution. While some prior methods support textured emitters, they rely on approximations that introduce error [15].

    Dynamic and Deformable Emitters. To support dynamic or deformable emitters, we extend NEF with a time-varying parameter t. As with the higher-order emissive effects in the previous section, this only requires that training data collection account for the time-varying state of the emitter. Figure 6 shows a textured fireball whose time parameter indexes into frames of a source video. See Figure 11 for an emitter with deformable geometry. We encourage the reader to consult the supplemental video for a detailed demonstration of the results.

    4.3 Comparison to Sampling-based Methods

    Both online many-light sampling methods and proxy-based emitters [14, 35, 43] require an integration step at runtime. We compare against a representative of each category: ReSTIR [6] and an oracle proxy formulation.

    Many-light Sampling. Unlike ReSTIR, which operates entirely at runtime with no precomputation, NEF amortizes work into a one-time training phase in exchange for a constant-time per-pixel inference cost. To make this trade-off concrete, we construct a Cornell Box scene with 1,000 point lights treated as a single composite emitter: the lights support global rigid transformations, but are fixed relative to each other. A single NEF is trained on this composite.

    We evaluate equal-quality convergence against three baselines: path-traced direct illumination, ReSTIR DI (M=32, K=5), and ReSTIR DI paired with an OptiX denoiser. To reach NEF’s error level, ReSTIR requires ∼256 SPP without denoising, or ∼32 SPP with denoising (Figure 8). While both unbiased sampling baselines eventually surpass NEF at high sample counts, even the 32 SPP denoised case exceeds the typical per-frame budget of real-time pipelines. However, ReSTIR remains more general: it handles arbitrary per-light motion at runtime, whereas NEF requires the emitter configuration to be fixed at training time. Rigid transforms of the entire emitter group and pre-arranged relative motion of the emitters in the composition (via a time parameter, Section 4.2) are supported, but arbitrary independent light motion requires retraining.

    Proxy Emitters.

    Proxy representations—whether using 4D light-field slabs [14], a radiance volume with virtual point lights [35], or neural fields [43]—gather radiance by sampling and integrating a proxy representation. We compare NEF against an oracle proxy: an idealized proxy whose near-field queries return a noise-free reference and whose evaluation cost is treated as zero. Any sampling-based proxy method is bounded from below by this oracle, so the comparison reveals the minimum number of proxy evaluations required to match NEF’s pre-integrated estimate, regardless of how the proxy itself is represented.

    As shown in Figure 7, for the Pierced Sphere scene (Figure 5), the oracle proxy requires approximately 734 samples per pixel to match the accuracy of a single NEF query when combined with a learned importance sampling routine from [43]. Each of those samples still requires a BSDF evaluation at the shading point: at 1920×1080 resolution, the 734 GGX evaluations alone cost 2.9 ms per frame in an optimized CUDA kernel. This already exceeds NEF’s total inference cost of 2.5 ms, before any of the proxy queries or importance sampling are accounted for. Moreover, the cost of those proxy queries is not negligible in practice. As a data point, a half-precision torch.compile’d forward pass of the evaluation network from [43] takes 103 ms per emitter sample per full-HD frame, and 49 ms to output the importance sampling distributions on the same hardware as our NEF timings.

    5 Discussion

    Visibility and soft shadows. Similarly to analytical methods and proxy emitters, NEF only captures the unoccluded emission field. In practice, this is well-addressed by combining NEF shading with a small budget of path-traced visibility samples and a denoiser that are used as a ratio estimator [16]. This approach yields plausible soft shadows while preserving the noise-free direct illumination produced by the NEF. Even 1 shadow ray per pixel yields perceptually accurate soft shadows (see Figure 9), with further samples producing diminishing returns. This makes NEF compatible with standard real-time visibility pipelines at minimal additional cost.

    Storage and training. All results in this paper were generated using a single NEF architecture totaling 15 MB (or 30 MB for the glossy variant) per emitter. For simpler emitters, this is often excessive and can be reduced (see supplemental). Training is a one-time offline cost, ranging from approximately one minute for simple planar emitters to three hours for emitters with internal interreflections, depending primarily on the cost of generating path-traced training samples. Crucially, this cost is incurred once per emitter and can be amortized across multiple scenes.

    Multiple emitters in a scene. Currently, a scene with N emitters requires evaluating N independent NEFs and summing their contributions (unless emitters are close enough to be represented jointly by a single NEF), scaling linearly with N. We see two avenues to mitigate this. First, a shared decoding MLP could learn to disentangle latents from multiple emitters; however a naive sum-then-decode scheme retains a linear cost for the latent fetching. Second, future work could combine NEF with lighting hierarchies [37, 23] to achieve sub-linear scaling.

    Sampling training data. We generate training targets by path tracing the emitter assembly with next-event estimation. For emitters with housing geometry more intricate than those presented in this work—heavily enclosing the emissive surface or admitting light only through narrow apertures—this strategy can produce a sparse training signal: most paths fail to reach the emitter and contribute zero, leaving the network to learn from a small fraction of informative samples. As shown in recent work [11], light tracing [2] can reduce the number of zero-radiance contributions. Orthogonally, when the emissive field around the emitter exhibits high-frequency variation, adaptive sampling the training loss [10] could training data on the regions that need it most.

    6 Conclusion

    We presented Neural Emission Fields, a pre-integrated neural representation of direct illumination from non-trivial emitters. By moving the receiver-side integral into an offline training phase, NEF reduces shading to a single network evaluation per pixel, at a cost independent of the emitter’s geometric complexity. The same formulation handles a wide range of lighting scenarios—including spatially varying emission, internal interreflections, and deformable emitters—within a single, unified training procedure; trained models then act as portable lighting assets that can be placed in any scene under rigid transforms and uniform scaling. We hope NEF proves a useful step toward treating expensive direct illumination as a bakeable, reusable component of real-time rendering pipelines.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Linear Scaling of Analytical Methods

    As shown in Figure 12, the computational cost of analytical methods like LTC [15] scales linearly with the number of emitter vertices. In contrast, NEF inference time remains constant for a given emitter geometry, regardless of the density of its tessellation. For glossy receivers, our method reaches a performance crossover at 267 emitter vertices. Notably, NEF maintains a constant 2.5ms shading time even for highly complex emitters like the Stanford Dragon (436k vertices), where analytical methods would be computationally prohibitive.

    Appendix B Representation Parameters

    We use a single set of hash grid parameters for all encoded inputs. The GlossyNEF architecture shares the positional encoding between the diffuse and glossy head. The multiresolution hash table has eight levels, each level increases in size with a rate of √2 per level, the corresponding latent vector consists of four floats, and the hash table uses 2¹⁹ entries. The additional inputs to the neural network, and the overall memory budget in half-precision, are summarized in Table 2.

    Appendix C Architecture Ablation

    We ablate several architecture choices (see Table 3) of our NEF by training a GlossyNEF on the same Quad emitter with the same number of training iterations.

    Applying the multiresolution hash encoding on the outgoing direction as opposed to the reflected direction, which is a common encoding choice for neural representations, reduces quality across all roughness values α.

    Splitting the network into a diffuse and glossy head similarly performs better than unifying into a single head.

    The original NEF architecture shares the positional encoding between the diffuse and glossy head. Decoupling this multiresolution hash table (i.e. diffuse and glossy each use a different one) yields no quality improvement, although it adds more capacity and extra runtime.

    Appendix D Training Budget

    Table 4 reports the training cost for each NEF in the paper, measured on a single RTX 4090 GPU. All timings include the cost of generating path-traced radiance targets on-the-fly, which dominates iteration time for the more complex emitters. Iterations and per-emitter training time scale with the difficulty of the underlying radiance field: planar emitters with uniform emission converge in minutes, bare emissive meshes and spatially varying emitters in under fifteen minutes, while configurations involving internal interreflections or temporal variation require several hours, both because the radiance field itself is more complex and because each path-traced target costs more to generate.

    Appendix E Overspent Capacity

    The default NEF architecture is sized for the most demanding emitter in our set (the Pierced Sphere) and is excessive for simpler emissive fields. We ablate two capacity axes—the MLP and the multiresolution hash encoding—on a simple Quad emitter (Figure 13). The two axes have different effects: reducing the MLP size quickly degrades quality, as the network loses the capacity to decode the encoded latents. Shrinking the hash encoding, in contrast, yields the largest reduction in memory footprint at negligible cost in error, since most of the parameter budget lives in the hash tables and the Quad’s emissive field does not need the default spatial resolution. In practice, simple emitters can therefore be deployed with a substantially smaller hash table while keeping the MLP near its default size.

    Appendix F Low-roughness Materials

    While there are no theoretical constraints preventing NEF from being trained on low-roughness receivers, practical results indicate a bottleneck as α→0, as illustrated in Figure 14. This degradation occurs because the specular highlight sharpens into a high-frequency signal that exceeds the network’s representational capacity. Consequently, while training is technically feasible across the entire roughness spectrum, the model struggles to resolve the near-singular gradients of mirror-like reflections, leading to the observed increase in approximation error in the highlight regions.

    Appendix G Impact of Training Data Noise

    The training targets used throughout this paper are generated via path tracing with Monte Carlo integration, leaving residual variance in the supervision signal. The magnitude of this variance depends on the emitter: emitters that are hard to sample yield noisier targets. The Pierced Sphere is a particularly challenging case, as its internal interreflections must also be captured during training, making it one of the noisiest emitters in our set. In Figure 15 we ablate the number of Monte Carlo samples used per training estimate and observe diminishing returns beyond 64 samples. We therefore adopt S=64 for all emitters throughout the paper, noting that this budget could safely be reduced for simpler emitters.

item.title: Mobile-4DGS：手机上的静态与动态高斯泼溅统一框架 ｜ Mobile-4DGS: Unified Static-Dynamic Real-time Mobile Gaussian Splatting
item.description:
一句话：把球谐系数解耦、按重要性增减基元，让 3DGS/4DGS 在移动端跑起来。

要点：

  • 用蒙特卡洛高光能量聚合，把球谐系数拆成基色与视角无关分量，存储分别减少 61% 与 26%
  • 按基元重要性做提升与剔除，单步最多调整 1% 的基元，避免表示不稳定地跳变
  • 用离屏基准协议评估渲染性能，绕开屏幕 120FPS 上限与 UI 开销，才能测到真实吞吐

为什么值得看：移动端上 3DGS 的瓶颈是存储与每帧计算，这里的球谐解耦与基元调度是可以直接借鉴的两条路。

中文摘要：3DGS 在新视角合成上表现很好，但把静态与动态高斯表示同时部署到资源受限的移动设备上依然困难：存储开销大、基元冗余、每帧计算昂贵。Mobile-4DGS 提出一个统一的轻量框架，同时支持高保真的静态与动态高斯渲染。外观建模上用蒙特卡洛高光能量聚合，把球谐系数解耦成基础与视角无关两部分，带来 61% 与 26% 的存储下降；表示管理上按基元重要性做提升与剔除，且每步最多只调整 1%，以免表示在训练中出现不稳定跳变。评测采用离屏基准协议，绕开屏幕显示 120 FPS 上限与 UI 开销，测得的是真实渲染吞吐。整体目标是在手机功耗与带宽预算内，让静态与动态高斯场景都能实时播放。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

Mobile-4DGS: Unified Static-Dynamic Real-time Mobile Gaussian Splatting

Abstract

Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have achieved remarkable performance in novel view synthesis, yet deploying both static and dynamic Gaussian representations on resource-constrained mobile devices remains challenging due to heavy storage, redundant primitives, and costly per-frame computation. We present Mobile-4DGS, a unified lightweight framework for high-fidelity real-time static and dynamic Gaussian rendering on mobile platforms. For compact appearance modeling, we introduce a Monte Carlo Specular Energy Aggregator that compresses high-order radiance residuals into the first-order Spherical Harmonics (SH), together with an Attribute-Conditioned SH Enhancement module whose predicted offsets are pre-baked before inference. We further propose a Multi-View Alpha-Based Densification and Pruning strategy to suppress redundant primitives while maintaining multi-view consistency. For dynamic scenes, we develop a compact explicit 4D representation by constructing second-order Gaussian motion, learnable temporal support, and a binary static-dynamic partition, enabling continuous-time modeling without runtime deformation networks. Based on this partition, a Depth-Order Certificate selectively reuses previously committed depth orders to reduce re-projection, sorting, merging, and index-buffer updates during playback. Extensive experiments on static and dynamic scenes demonstrate that Mobile-4DGS substantially reduces storage and rendering overhead while maintaining competitive visual quality, enabling real-time 3D and 4D Gaussian Splatting on mobile devices. Code has been released: https://xiaobiaodu.github.io/mobile-4dgs-project/.

I Introduction

Recent advancements in 3D scene reconstruction [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8] and novel view synthesis [9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14] have been driven by 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [1]. By representing scenes as millions of explicit and differentiable 3D Gaussians, 3DGS delivers high-fidelity, real-time rendering on desktop hardware. This capability has enabled diverse applications across autonomous driving [15, 16, 17], navigation [18, 19, 20], and virtual reality [21, 22, 23, 24]. Despite these successes, efficiently deploying static and dynamic Gaussian Splatting on resource-constrained mobile devices remains a critical bottleneck.

Mobile-GS [2] is the first to deploy 3DGS on mobile devices and achieves real-time rendering. It identifies the sorting process in the original volume rendering as causing slow rendering for mobiles. Therefore, it proposes an order-independent rendering pipeline to replace the traditional volume rendering so as to achieve fast rendering on mobiles. However, removing the sorting process causes Gaussian rendering in an arbitrary order, causing transparency artifacts in regions with overlapping geometry. Although Flux-GS [25] maintains the original sorting process and achieves faster rendering, it cannot support dynamic rendering [26] in our daily 4D space. The two lines of work therefore leave the same tension unresolved: giving up the sort buys throughput at the price of correct compositing, whereas keeping it means paying for a depth order that a 4D scene has to rebuild at every playback frame, together with the upload of the resulting index buffer.

In our experiments, we identified four primary bottlenecks that hinder the efficient deployment of Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) on mobile devices: (1) Third-Order Spherical Harmonics Overhead: Prior methods [27, 28, 29, 30, 31] commonly rely on third-order Spherical Harmonics (SH) to model complex, view-dependent radiance. However, third-order SH requires 48 floating-point parameters per Gaussian primitive. Scaled across millions of Gaussians, this creates prohibitive storage overhead and heavy memory bandwidth consumption during rasterization. (2) Redundant Primitive Densification: Lightweight 3DGS variants, such as Mobile-GS [2] and MEGS2 [32], typically adopt standard single-view gradient-based densification [1]. This approach aggressively spawns excess primitives, leading to overfitting and inflated point counts. The resulting primitive redundancy severely impacts training efficiency, storage footprint, and inference latency on the resource-constrained edge devices. (3) MLP-based Dynamic Representation: Previous works [26, 33, 34] leverage neural networks to model temporal variation, introducing non-trivial per-frame deformation inference and limiting rendering efficiency on resource-constrained devices. (4) Per-Frame Depth Ordering under Motion: Primitive motion continuously changes the relative depth of Gaussians, invalidating previously cached depth orders. As a result, the renderer must repeatedly re-project primitives, recompute their ordering, and update the draw list during playback, introducing additional runtime and data-transfer overhead.

In this work, we present Mobile-4DGS, a mobile real-time Gaussian Splatting method designed to deliver high-fidelity rendering with significantly fewer parameters. As illustrated in Fig. 1, our proposed Mobile-4DGS achieves rendering quality comparable to existing baselines while utilizing fewer Gaussian primitives, thereby outperforming Mobile-GS [2] in inference speed. Our framework is built upon four technical innovations: (1) Unified Mobile Static-Dynamic Representation: We extend the static Mobile-GS/Flux-GS foundations to a compact continuous-time representation in which each dynamic Gaussian requires only eight additional temporal scalars. Static scenes are represented as the zero-motion special case, allowing both modes to share the same appearance, compression, density-control, and rendering pipeline. (2) Monte Carlo Specular Energy Aggregator: As shown in Fig. 2, our approach is motivated by the observation that substantial radiance information can be compressed into a lower-order subspace without compromising view-dependent specular features. We propose a Monte Carlo Specular Energy Aggregator that aggregates high-order specular energy into a compact representation, effectively preserving the complex lighting characteristics. Furthermore, we decouple the SH representation into a view-independent base component and directional view-dependent components, allowing for a substantial reduction in SH memory overhead compared to traditional third-order baselines without the need for expensive offline distillation or pre-training. To recover the fine detail lost during this compression, we introduce an Attribute-Conditioned SH Enhancement module. This module utilizes a lightweight Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to model contextual offsets based on intrinsic Gaussian properties. More importantly, these offsets are statically baked into the explicit Gaussian parameters prior to inference, ensuring that this enhanced view-dependent modeling does not introduce additional computational overhead during inference. (3) Multi-view Alpha-based Densification and Pruning strategy: We further address the inefficiency inherent in the standard single-view gradient-based densification strategy, which often lacks multi-view structure consistency. We propose a Multi-view Alpha-based Densification and Pruning strategy that employs stratified camera sampling and alpha-weighted error accumulation across multiple viewpoints. With multi-view guidance, this strategy ensures a more compact representation by accurately pruning redundant primitives while focusing densification on regions with high multi-view reconstruction error. (4) Depth-Order Certificate for 4D Playback: The learned partition is exactly binary, so the depth order of the static subset depends on the camera alone and is cached for the whole clip, while a closed-form bound on the travel of the animated subset yields a per-frame depth-order certificate (DOC) that decides whether the committed draw list is still the sorted one. A frame that passes the certificate skips re-projection, sorting, merging and the index upload.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that Mobile-4DGS offers a robust and scalable solution for mobile real-time rendering. By achieving powerful first-order SH representation while maintaining competitive visual quality, our framework paves the way for the deployment of high-fidelity 3DGS on mobile devices. The same framework also keeps 4D playback affordable on the device: the exact certificate leaves the rendered image untouched on every frame it reuses, and the budget branch confines the reordering it admits to primitives whose footprints already overlap.

Relationship to Prior Conference Versions. This paper substantially extends our previous Mobile-GS [2] and Flux-GS [25] papers. Mobile-GS established a mobile-oriented Gaussian rendering pipeline together with a distillation-based appearance representation, whereas Flux-GS investigated Monte Carlo aggregation for compact static Gaussian Splatting. The present journal version unifies these foundations under a single deployment-oriented framework and extends them to dynamic scenes through explicit second-order motion, learnable temporal support, temporally stratified optimization, and quantized temporal attributes. It further incorporates a shared cross-platform rendering pipeline for both static and dynamic scenes. Importantly, static rendering is treated as a zero-motion special case of the same explicit representation. We extend the sorting pipeline of Flux-GS [25]: because the learned gate is exactly the partition the renderer consumes, the per-camera cache of the static depth order and the depth-order certificate that licenses reuse of the committed draw list follow from the representation itself rather than from a separate engineering effort. We summarize our contributions as follows:

  • •

    We extend the framework to 4D by incorporating non-linear temporal modeling and dynamic opacity lifespans, enabling real-time, high-quality 4D scene rendering on mobile platforms.

  • •

    We propose a Monte Carlo aggregation strategy that decouples SH components to compress high-order view-dependent energy into a lower-order subspace, paired with an Attribute-Conditioned SH Enhancement module whose offsets are statically baked in before deployment to eliminate runtime inference overhead.

  • •

    We propose a multi-view densification and pruning strategy using stratified camera sampling and alpha-weighted error accumulation, ensuring structural consistency across views while reducing redundant Gaussians.

  • •

    We propose a depth-order certificate (DOC) for mobile 4D playback, which caches the depth order of the static subset per camera and decides with a closed-form travel bound whether a committed draw list is still valid, so that certified frames skip re-projection, sorting, merging, and the index upload.

    • II Related work

    Neural Radiance Fields. Recent advances in novel view synthesis have been heavily driven by 3D neural representations. Initial approaches associated neural features with underlying geometric structures such as volumes [35], textures [36], or point clouds [37]. A major paradigm shift occurred with Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [10], which utilize multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) to directly query 3D density and color, enabling photorealistic rendering from 2D images without explicit proxy geometry. Subsequent research has focused on enhancing the rendering quality and computational efficiency of NeRF through optimized sampling [38], tensor decomposition [39], compact representations [40], and mobile-friendly pipelines [11]. Despite these improvements, the heavy computational and memory footprints of NeRF-based models remain prohibitive for real-time deployment on resource-constrained edge devices.

    3D Gaussian Splatting. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [1] has emerged as a powerful alternative, representing scenes via anisotropic 3D Gaussians and utilizing a tile-based rasterizer for real-time rendering. To scale this approach, recent works focus on accelerating training and managing memory. Scaffold-GS [41] introduces a hierarchical scaffold structure to reduce the number of Gaussians for high-quality rendering, while maintaining visual fidelity. Octree-GS [42] proposes a Level-of-Detail (LOD) structure for 3D Gaussian supporting level-of-detail decomposition. 3D-HGS [43] introduces a 3D-Half Gaussian as a novel reconstruction kernel to better learn the surface normal in 3D scenes. 3DGS-MCMC [44] formulates the training dynamics as a Markov Chain Monte Carlo process, while Revisiting Densification [45] proposes a loss-driven densification scheme. 3DGS-LM [46] utilizes a tailored Levenberg–Marquardt method [47] to replace the traditional Adam optimizer [48], while Taming 3DGS [49] enforces a strict user-defined Gaussian budget during optimization. MVGS [50] is the first to propose multi-view learning to enhance the multi-view constraint of 3DGS in the optimization stage, which significantly improves the holistic rendering performance. Furthermore, techniques like StopThePop [51] and FlashGS [52] tackle tile-intersection bottlenecks and depth-sorting challenges to mitigate popping artifacts and reduce computation complexity.

    Gaussian Pruning. Due to the inherent redundancy in dense 3D Gaussian representations [53, 54, 55], pruning has become a key strategy to boost rendering efficiency [56, 57, 58, 59]. Common pruning strategies rely on importance scores derived from accumulated transmittance [60, 61], Hessian-based sensitivity [62], or gradient-opacity combinations [63, 64]. While Mobile-GS [2] compresses the scene using opacity- and scale-based pruning, it struggles to preserve fine-grained details. Furthermore, standard single-view gradient-based densification tends to produce an excessive number of Gaussians. To address this, our proposed Mobile-4DGS introduces a multi-view alpha-based densification and pruning strategy, significantly minimizing the primitive budget while maintaining high rendering quality.

    Gaussian Compression. Early compression methods utilized vector quantization (VQ) [28, 65, 66, 67] and entropy coding [68, 69] to lower storage requirements. While highly effective, large codebooks in VQ-based methods lead to long training times. Although residual vector quantization (R-VQ) [63] mitigates this overhead, it incurs additional index storage costs. Recent work has shifted toward structured representations, combining anchor-based structures [41, 70, 63] or tensor factorization [71] with grid hierarchies [68, 42]. Contextual modeling [68, 69, 70, 72] has also been introduced to maximize rate-distortion performance, though at the cost of high rendering latency due to multiple MLP passes. Alternatively, neural field representations capture local continuity among neighboring Gaussians [28, 73]. For instance, Mobile-GS [2] distills spherical harmonics (SH) from a high-order teacher, but this process is computationally expensive. In contrast, our Mobile-4DGS introduces a Monte Carlo Specular Energy Aggregator that directly compresses third-order SH energy into a compact, low-order representation, bypassing costly distillation while preserving high-fidelity view-dependent details.

    4D Gaussian Splatting. To reconstruct dynamic scenes, recent methods extend static representations into the temporal domain by modeling time-dependent geometry and appearance [26]. Early attempts directly integrated time as a fourth coordinate or used dynamic multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) to deform standard 3D Gaussians over time [74]. However, relying heavily on neural networks for deformation often introduces a significant computational bottleneck, hindering real-time rendering speeds during inference. To address this, subsequent architectures have introduced explicit temporal structures, such as hexplane [75] or 4D grid decompositions [74], to separate spatial and temporal features efficiently. Other approaches leverage physical constraints or motion trajectories to track individual Gaussian primitives across frames, preserving fine-grained temporal consistency [76]. Despite these innovations, existing 4D architectures typically suffer from slow rendering speed on mobiles due to the volume of temporal tracking coefficients [77, 78]. In contrast, our approach optimizes temporal feature aggregation to maintain high-fidelity dynamic rendering without compromising efficiency on mobile devices.

    III Preliminary

    Gaussian Splatting: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [1] is an explicit Gaussian-based rendering method that represents a scene using a collection of anisotropic 3D Gaussians, enabling high-quality novel view synthesis. Each 3D Gaussian Gᵢ contains 3D geometry and appearance parameters, as (μᵢ,Σᵢ,oᵢ,cᵢ). For the geometry representation, μᵢ∈ℝ³ defines the 3D position of the 3D Gaussian in its world coordinates, while the covariance matrix Σᵢ∈ℝ^3×3, which is always positive semi-definite and symmetric, characterizes the spatial extent and orientation of the anisotropic Gaussian ellipsoid. In terms of geometric modeling, Σᵢ is decomposed into a scale component sᵢ and a rotation component rᵢ, where sᵢ controls the size of the Gaussian and rᵢ specifies its orientation. As for appearance, each Gaussian leverages a color cᵢ(ω) and an opacity value oᵢ∈[0,1], where Gaussian color cᵢ is represented using the spherical harmonic coefficients cᵢ.

    To render an image, all 3D Gaussians are projected onto the image space using a standard perspective camera model. After that, a depth-sorting procedure is then applied to ensure that ℕ Gaussians are rendered in a near-to-far order. Following this ordering, the final color of a pixel is computed via the alpha blending:

    C=∑ᵢ₌₁^ℕcᵢ(ω)αᵢTᵢ,

    		(1)

    Tᵢ=∏ⱼ₌₁ⁱ⁻¹(1-αⱼ),

    		(2)

    αᵢ(x)=oᵢ\exp(-1/2(x-μ^2Dᵢ)^⊤(Σ^2Dᵢ)⁻¹(x-μ^2Dᵢ)).

    		(3)

    where Tᵢ denotes the accumulated transmittance before the i-th Gaussian. ℕ is the total number of Gaussians contributing to the pixel. Overall, Gaussian Splatting provides a differentiable, efficient, and compact representation for complex scenes, making it well suited for real-time rendering.

    Spherical Harmonics: Spherical harmonics provide an orthonormal basis for square-integrable functions defined on the unit sphere S². Any sufficiently smooth directional function c(ω):S²→ℝ³ can be expanded as

    c(ω)=∑_ℓ=0^L∑_m=-ℓ^ℓc_ℓmY_ℓm(ω),

    		(4)

    where Y_ℓm denotes the real spherical harmonics basis functions, and c_ℓm are the corresponding SH coefficients. In practice, the expansion is truncated to a finite maximum degree L, yielding (L+1)² coefficients. In modern neural rendering systems, low-order SH (e.g., L≤2) are often preferred due to their compactness and numerical stability, while higher-order SH are sometimes used during training to capture high-frequency view-dependent effects.

    IV Methodology

    Vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) leverages explicit 3D Gaussians with volume rendering to represent a whole scene or object. Each 3D Gaussian Gᵢ is defined by a set of geometry and appearance parameters: (μᵢ,sᵢ,rᵢ,oᵢ,cᵢ). Specifically, μᵢ, sᵢ, and rᵢ represent spatial position, scale, and rotation, while oᵢ and cᵢ denote opacity and spherical harmonic coefficients for appearance modeling. To capture complex and view-dependent effects, standard 3DGS methods typically utilize third-order spherical harmonics (SH). While effective for modeling specular and intricate lighting, this approach incurs significant storage costs, as each Gaussian primitive requires 48 SH coefficients (16coefficients×3channels). As scene complexity grows into the millions of primitives, the resulting storage footprint and memory bandwidth requirements become prohibitive for mobiles.

    In this work, we propose Mobile-4DGS, which constrains the Gaussian appearance modeling to first-order spherical harmonics (requiring only 4 coefficients per channel). To ensure rendering fidelity, we propose a Monte Carlo Specular Energy Aggregator method to compress high-order radiance energy into a compact and lower-order subspace without pretraining or distillation. By bridging the gap between high-fidelity radiance modeling and hardware-efficient representation, Mobile-4DGS enables high-quality and efficient novel view synthesis performance on edge devices.

    IV-AMonte Carlo Specular Energy Aggregator

    \blacktriangleright“Insight 1”: Extracting Monte Carlo directional moments of specular residuals into pre-baked first-order parameters preserves complex lighting with zero runtime inference overhead.

    High-order SH polynomials in 3DGS are inherently inefficient for representing sharp, highly localized specular lobes due to their dense and global nature. Fitting a sparse specular peak requires numerous high-order SH merely to cancel out non-specular ringing artifacts. We observe that view-dependent energy is highly sparse in the angular domain, yet its directional phase is critical for accurate reconstruction. Rather than aggregating absolute photometric residuals, which destroys this vital angular gradient, we propose to extract the first-order directional moments of the specular residual via Monte Carlo projection. It projects the extracted directional energy into the 1st-order SH space. Consequently, this insight allows us to discard the redundant high-order SH while explicitly preserving both the magnitude and spatial direction of the view-dependent signal.

    Consider an RGB-valued directional function cᵢ(ω)=∑_ℓ=0^Lₒ∑_m=-ℓ^ℓc_ℓmY_ℓm(ω) defined over the sphere S². This function is initially represented by spherical harmonics of an original degree Lₒ, with a coefficient tensor: c∈ℝ^N×(Lₒ+1)²×3 where N represents the number of Gaussian primitives. Our objective is to compress this high-fidelity representation into a lower-order SH space of degree Lₜ (where Lₜ≤Lₒ), resulting in a reduced coefficient set: c^′∈ℝ^N×(Lₜ+1)²×3. For each primitive i, we formulate this as a least-squares optimization problem:

    c^′*=\arg\min_c^′∫_S²|| cᵢ(ω)-∑_ℓ=0^Lₜ∑_m=-ℓ^ℓc^′_ℓmY_ℓm(ω)||₂²dω,

    		(5)

    where Y_ℓm(ω) denotes a spherical harmonic basis function. To obtain a low-order representation, the optimal projection coefficients c^′_n,k that minimize the reconstruction error are given analytically by the inner product:

    c^′_i,ℓm=⟨cᵢ(ω),Y_ℓm⟩=∫_S²cᵢ(ω)Y_ℓm(ω)dω,

    		(6)

    where it defines the optimal orthogonal projection within the strict low-order SH subspace. However, this projection cannot retain information that lies exclusively in the discarded higher-order bands. Our Monte Carlo module is therefore not introduced to approximate the same projection. Instead, it estimates compact directional statistics from the discarded residual and uses them to reparameterize the first-order coefficients before deployment. To retain these high-frequency characteristics without incurring the prohibitive high-order SH, we aim to compress the discarded specular information into a compact latent representation. The perceptual impact of specular is fundamentally characterized by its photometric energy magnitude and dominant direction. We instead propose to sample the high-frequency residual on a uniform sphere then extract its first-order directional moments.

    Uniform Spherical Sampling: To generate a set of directional vectors D={dₖ}ₖ₌₁^K, we uniformly sample K points on the unit sphere S² using spherical coordinates. For each sample k, we draw two independent random variables θₖ and φₖ respectively representing the colatitude and longitude:

    φₖ∼U(0,2π), θₖ=\arccos(1 - 2ξₖ), ξₖ∼U(0,1),

    		(7)

    where U denotes the uniform sampling. These spherical coordinates are subsequently transformed into the Cartesian domain to obtain the unit direction vectors dₖ=\beginbmatrix\sinθₖ\cosφₖ,~\sinθₖ\sinφₖ,~\cosθₖ\endbmatrix where each dₖ represents a unit vector such that ∥dₖ∥₂=1. This collection of vectors D∈ℝ^K×3 serves as the set of incident directions for subsequent spherical harmonic compression.

    Energy Aggregation: Subsequently, we evaluate the photometric residual between the third-order SH radiance cᵢ(dₖ) and the second-order SH radiance cᵢ²(dₖ) via cᵣₑₛ(dₖ)=cᵢ(dₖ)-cᵢ²(dₖ). By aggregating these residuals, we formulate a compact, high-frequency dynamic energy and direction representation:

    E_mag=\max(0,cᵣₑₛ(dₖ)),

    		(8)

    E_dir=1/K∑ₖ₌₁^Kdₖ⊗E_mag,

    		(9)

    where E_mag and E_dir effectively encapsulate the overall energy and direction of the view-dependent specular for each Gaussian primitive, compressing the bulky high-order parameters into a highly lightweight low-dimensional descriptor. To strictly minimize memory overhead, we only store these compact latents E_dir and cᵈᶜ, where cᵈᶜ represents the base color SH, as the 0-th SH. We then employ a neural network to learn a non-linear mapping from this aggregated high-frequency latent space to the first-order SH parameters, conditioned on the normalized Gaussian position:

    c^′=Ψ(cᵈᶜ,E_dir,f(μ̂)),

    		(10)

    f(μ̂)=\begincasesμ̂&if∥μ̂∥₂≤1, (2-(1)/(∥μ̂∥₂))(μ̂)/(∥μ̂∥₂)&if∥μ̂∥₂>1,\endcases

    		(11)

    where Ψ is a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), and the result c^′∈ℝ^N×(Lₜ+1)²×3 represents the first-order SH coefficient (Lₜ=1). We normalize the Gaussian position μ to reduce the impact of spatial outliers for better convergence. By performing this mapping, Mobile-4DGS can dynamically adjust the Gaussian geometry and low-order appearance simultaneously, ensuring that the restricted SH capacity is allocated to the most visually salient scene features. In particular, our approach eliminates the need for expensive distillation while achieving significant compression in SH storage memory overhead compared to third-order baselines. More importantly, the first-order SH coefficients are decoded only once before inference, introducing no per-frame decoding overhead.

    Gaussian Attribute Awareness: Although the above process preserves the majority of radiance energy in an L² sense, projecting higher-order bands inevitably degrades overall color fidelity and scene structure. We observe that this discarded residual energy is highly correlated with intrinsic Gaussian attributes, such as spatial position and anisotropic scale. This motivates us to design a lightweight geometry-conditioned residual module to contextually refine the base representation and preserve the efficiency of first-order SH. Specifically, we introduce an Attribute-Conditioned SH Enhancement module parameterized by a lightweight MLP, denoted as Φ, to predict a residual offset Δc for the first-order SH coefficients c^′. The network aggregates the geometric and photometric properties by concatenating the normalized first-order SH ĉ^′, opacity α, normalized scales ŝ, spatial position μ, and rotation quaternion r. The enhanced SH coefficients cᵒᵘᵗ are formulated as:

    Δcᵢ=Φ([μᵢ,ŝᵢ,rᵢ,oᵢ,ĉ^′ᵢ]), cᵒᵘᵗᵢ=c^′ᵢ+Δcᵢ,

    		(12)

    where the final linear layer of Φ is strictly zero-initialized to ensure optimization stability, allowing the model to naturally fall back to the standard 3DGS representation at the beginning of training and smoothly learn the residuals. Crucially, because Φ relies strictly on intrinsic Gaussian attributes and is entirely independent of the camera viewing direction, the residual Δc only needs to be decoded once for subsequent inference. Prior to rendering, the SH offset is pre-computed and statically baked into the explicit Gaussian parameters. This design guarantees that our contextual modeling facilitates higher performance while introducing absolutely zero computational overhead during inference.

    Training Curriculum: Initially, we optimize 3D Gaussians utilizing full third-order SH coefficients for the first 3k iterations to establish a high-frequency representation. Subsequently, we aggregate these third-order coefficients down to a first-order SH representation via our proposed Monte Carlo Specular Energy Aggregator. After this mapping step, we initialize the Attribute-Conditioned SH Enhancement module to continually refine the low-order representation. Note that the compression from third-order to first-order is executed only once. After that, we only maintain and update the lightweight first-order parameters.

    IV-BMulti-view Alpha-based Densification and Pruning

    \blacktriangleright“Insight 2”: Stratified multi-view alpha-error accumulation maintains global structural consistency while pruning redundant primitives to prevent excessive Gaussian point inflation.

    To achieve a compact 3D Gaussian structure, we found that an accurate densification and pruning strategy is crucial. We observed previous methods [1, 57] using gradient-based or importance-based strategies in the single-view criterion to determine Gaussians’ densification and pruning. However, the single-view criteria lack a holistic understanding of the scene, as they account for geometry and appearance from only a single view. Therefore, we propose a multi-view alpha-based densification and pruning strategy in Fig. 4 to constrain the number of Gaussians based on multi-view evaluation so that ensure multi-view consistency.

    Stratified Camera Sampling: To ensure comprehensive geometric coverage and alleviate view redundancy within the training camera set, we adopt a Stratified Camera Sampling strategy. We partition the 3D scene into angular bins defined with respect to a focal point, enabling the selection of representative views that maximize view variation and angular dispersion. Prior to binning, we estimate the center of the scene, denoted as x^*. Given N_cam cameras with the centers {tᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N_cam and viewing directions {vᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N, we compute the point that minimizes the total squared distance to all camera rays. Let Pᵢ=I-vᵢvᵢ^⊤ be the projection matrix onto the subspace orthogonal to the i-th ray, where I is an identity matrix. The scene center x^* is obtained by solving the linear least-squares system via: (∑ᵢ₌₁^N_camPᵢ)x^*=∑ᵢ₌₁^N_camPᵢtᵢ, where each camera position is transformed into spherical coordinates (θ,φ,ρ). θ=arctan2(r_y,rₓ), φ=\arcsin(r_z / ∥rᵢ∥), and ρ=∥rᵢ∥, with rᵢ=tᵢ-x^*. The angular space is discretized into M_θ azimuth and M_φ elevation bins. Cameras are grouped according to their bin indices, and one representative is uniformly sampled from each non-empty bin. Finally, to satisfy a computational budget K, the selected candidates are randomly shuffled and truncated, yielding a camera subset ℂ with broad and uniform angular coverage.

    Photometric Loss Guidance: To effectively optimize the Gaussian Splatting representation, we employ a multi-view consistency-driven strategy. This strategy identifies regions of high and low reconstruction error across multiple viewpoints and uses the accumulated contribution of each Gaussian to guide geometry and appearance refinement. For each viewpoint in a curated camera set ℂ, we render the current Gaussian primitives and compute a pixel-wise photometric loss. Following standard 3DGS, we utilize the loss with a hybrid objective combining L₁ distance and Structural Similarity (SSIM) through:

    L=(1-λ)L₁(C,C_gt)+λL_DSSIM(C,C_gt),

    		(13)

    where C and C_gt represent the rendered image and Ground Truth. λ controls the weight for L₁ and L_DSSIM. Therefore, we can derive a binary Metric Map M∈{0,1}^H×W to identify areas of poor and high-quality reconstruction through:

    M_u,v⁺=I(L_u,v>τ⁺), M_u,v⁻=I(L_u,v<τ⁻),

    		(14)

    where I(·) is the indicator function and τ is the error threshold. A pixel (u,v) is flagged (M_u,v⁺=1) if its error exceeds a predefined threshold τ⁺, marking it as a region of poor reconstruction. On the contrary, M_u,v⁻=1 means that the region is well reconstructed, needed to prune redundant Gaussians.

    Multi-view Alpha-Weighted Error Accumulation: To map 2D image-space errors back to 3D Gaussian primitives, we customize the CUDA kernel for the rendering pipeline. For each Gaussian i, we compute the importance score Sᵢ⁺ and pruning score Sᵢ⁻ by summing its alpha contributions αᵢ across all flagged pixels in the metric map by:

    Sᵢ⁺=∑_c=0^ℂ∑_(u,v)∈Ωαᵢ·Mᵤᵥ^c,+, Sᵢ⁻=∑_c=0^ℂ∑_(u,v)∈ΩLᵤᵥ·αᵢ·Mᵤᵥ^c,-,

    		(15)

    where αᵢ=oᵢ\exp(-1/2ΔxᵢᵀΣᵢ⁻¹Δxᵢ) represents Gaussian alpha, indicating the Gaussian contribution to the pixel color. Ω⊂ℤ² denote the discrete image pixel domain. We aggregate these local metrics across the sampled views to compute these two primary scores. This multi-view aggregation effectively differentiates Gaussians that are important or redundant, allowing for more accurate geometry modification. By averaging across the sampling views, our Mobile-4DGS avoids over-fitting to single-view occlusions or transient artifacts. By using the alpha-based metric rather than the conventional gradient metric [1], we ensure that only the Gaussians with high visibility and contributing to the error are modified.

    Accurate Densification: The vanilla 3DGS employs a gradient-based strategy to identify underfitting Gaussians. We define the vanilla clone mask M_cloneᵇᵃˢᵉ and split mask Mₛₚₗᵢₜᵇᵃˢᵉ based on standard positional gradient threshold ∥∇_μᵢL∥₂>τ. However, relying solely on single-view positional gradients frequently results in excessive and redundant Gaussian densification. To mitigate this issue, we integrate our computed importance score into the traditional 3DGS gradient-based densification strategy. Our multi-view consistency-guided masks are formed by intersecting these base criteria with an importance quantile filter:

    M_clone=M_cloneᵇᵃˢᵉ∧(S⁺>Q_τ⁺(S⁺)),

    		(16)

    Mₛₚₗᵢₜ=Mₛₚₗᵢₜᵇᵃˢᵉ∧(S⁺>Q_τ⁺(S⁺)),

    		(17)

    where Q_τ⁺ denotes the quantile of the importance score distribution. This ensures that Gaussians are only cloned or split if they consistently contribute to high-error regions across multiple views. Consequently, these refined masks strictly govern the cloning and splitting operations, boosting Gaussians’ fitting capability while tightly controlling the primitive count.

    Moderate Pruning: Standard 3DGS defines a threshold oₘᵢₙ to eliminate Gaussian points with low opacity, leading to aggressive pruning and performance slump. To achieve moderate pruning, we introduce the pruning score S⁻ based on multi-view and loss-driven strategy. A larger S⁻ indicates the Gaussian that impacts more to low-error pixel regions, effectively flagging it as an artifact or redundant point. Our final pruning mask Mₚᵣᵤₙₑ identifies Gaussians that fall below the opacity threshold oₘᵢₙ and exceed the pruning score quantile Q_τ⁻ via:

    Mₚᵣᵤₙₑ=(oᵢQ_τ⁻(S⁻)),

    		(18)

    where we utilize Mₚᵣᵤₙₑ to cull non-contributing or artifact-inducing Gaussians while preserving essential scene geometry. In this way, we achieve moderate pruning while maintaining overall reconstruction fidelity.

    IV-CDynamic Modeling

    \blacktriangleright“Insight 3”: A learned binary static–dynamic partition allows each Gaussian to model continuous-time motion with simple vector operations, while the static subset remains exactly unchanged over time and can therefore be cached for mobile rendering.

    As illustrated in Fig. 5, we extend each static Gaussian with a compact set of temporal parameters. We normalize the timestamp of each input frame to t∈[0,1]. In addition to its canonical center μᵢ∈ℝ³, covariance Σᵢ, base opacity oᵢ, and appearance coefficients cᵢ, each Gaussian Gᵢ stores a velocity vᵢ∈ℝ³, an acceleration aᵢ∈ℝ³, a canonical time t^′ᵢ∈[0,1], and a log-duration ρᵢ∈ℝ. This adds only eight scalars per Gaussian. More importantly, all temporal states are explicit, so no deformation network needs to be evaluated during rendering. This avoids the per-frame neural inference required by implicit deformation-based methods.

    Gated Second-Order Trajectory: We model the position of each Gaussian at time t using a second-order motion model around its canonical time:

    μᵢ(t)=μᵢ+gᵢ(vᵢ Δtᵢ+1/2aᵢ Δtᵢ²), Δtᵢ=t-t^′ᵢ,

    		(19)

    where the velocity term models approximately constant motion, while the acceleration term captures changes in speed or direction. The binary gate gᵢ∈{0,1} determines whether the Gaussian is static or dynamic. When gᵢ=0, the entire displacement is exactly zero, and the Gaussian remains at its canonical position for all timestamps. When gᵢ=1, its position follows the learned trajectory. This gives a continuous trajectory over the whole sequence instead of predicting a separate state for every frame. We keep Σᵢ and cᵢ constant over time to further reduce temporal storage and computation.

    Soft Temporal Support: A dynamic Gaussian does not necessarily need to contribute to every frame. We therefore assign each Gaussian a positive temporal duration

    σᵢ=clip(\exp(ρᵢ), σ_\min, σ_\max),

    		(20)

    and define its temporal weight as

    wᵢ(t)=\exp[-1/2((t-t^′ᵢ)/(σᵢ+ε))²],

    		(21)

    where ε prevents division by zero. We then define the effective opacity as

    oᵢ(t)=[(1-gᵢ)+gᵢ wᵢ(t)] oᵢ,

    		(22)

    so that static Gaussians always keep their original opacity, while dynamic Gaussians smoothly appear and disappear around their canonical time t^′ᵢ. During rendering, we simply replace oᵢ with oᵢ(t) in the standard alpha compositing process. This temporal window helps model visibility changes, occlusions, and topology changes while remaining differentiable with respect to vᵢ, aᵢ, t^′ᵢ, and ρᵢ.

    Learned Static–Dynamic Partition: Most Gaussians in a dynamic scene usually belong to static regions such as the background, floor, and stationary objects. Modeling temporal variation for these Gaussians is unnecessary. On the other hand, incorrectly treating a moving Gaussian as static can leave a frozen copy of the moving object in the scene. We therefore learn whether each Gaussian is static or dynamic instead of assigning all Gaussians to the same category.

    Specifically, we jointly optimize a binary gate gᵢ and the motion parameters. We use a hard-concrete relaxation with a straight-through estimator, which gives a binary value in the forward pass while still allowing gradients to propagate during training. Given uᵢ∼U(0,1), we compute

    sᵢ=sigmoid ((ℓᵢ+\loguᵢ/1-uᵢ)/(T)),(23)
    s̃ᵢ=clamp (sᵢ(ζ-γ)+γ, 0, 1),

    followed by

    gᵢ=I [s̃ᵢ≥0.5], ĝᵢ=sg(gᵢ)-sg(s̃ᵢ)+s̃ᵢ,

    		(24)

    where ℓᵢ is the learnable gate logit, T is the temperature, (γ,ζ) define the relaxed range [-0.1,1.1], I[·] is the indicator function, and sg(·) denotes stop-gradient. Thus, ĝᵢ is exactly equal to the binary gate gᵢ in the forward pass, while its relaxed value provides gradients in the backward pass. During training, ĝᵢ is used in Eqs. (19) and (22).

    We gradually anneal the temperature from Tᵢₙᵢₜ=2.0 to T_final=0.1, allowing the gates to start with a smooth relaxation and gradually become binary. The partition is also preserved during densification. When a Gaussian is cloned or split, its new copies inherit the gate logit, forced-dynamic flag, committed label, and promotion evidence from the parent. Logistic noise is used only during the first 5k iterations. The gates are then evaluated deterministically, and the static–dynamic partition is committed and frozen at iteration 25k. The renderer and compression stage therefore operate on a fixed binary partition.

    Motion Evidence and Promotion: The static–dynamic assignment is not determined by the sparsity prior alone. We additionally use motion evidence to prevent moving Gaussians from being incorrectly classified as static.
