    where τ=-2\ln(ρ/α) is a threshold-dependent constant. For a ray r(t)=o+td, substituting x=o+td into this iso-surface equation yields a quadratic

    at²+bt+c=0,

    		(4)

    where

    a=dᵀΣ⁻¹d, b=2dᵀΣ⁻¹(o-μ),
    c=(o-μ)ᵀΣ⁻¹(o-μ)-τ.

    The closest valid hit is given by the smaller positive root. For our architectural study, this formulation exposes native ray–Gaussian intersection without polyhedral approximation. Its arithmetic is dominated by symmetric matrix-vector products, dot products, and a quadratic solve, directly reflecting the workload that the hardware must execute. Accordingly, the rest of this paper adopts this RaySplats-style workload model: rays are intersected directly with Gaussian primitives, and their contributions are accumulated in ray order.

    II-CWhy Hybrid Rendering Matters

    Once Gaussian rendering is expressed in a ray-tracing framework, it inherits many of the benefits of ray tracing. Prior work shows that ray-traced 3DGS can naturally support reflections, refractions, shadows, stochastic ray sampling, highly distorted cameras, and rolling-shutter effects [13, 23, 3]. It also becomes easier to combine Gaussian scene content with triangle-based geometry, mesh proxies, or standard graphics assets within the same rendering pipeline. For instance, 3DGRT demonstrates compatibility with ray-based visual effects and mesh interactions, 3DGUT performs hybrid rendering with splatted primary rays and traced secondary rays, and RaySplats shows that Gaussian scenes can be rendered together with mesh-based objects and lighting effects. These capabilities make mixed primitive support relevant even when Gaussian rendering remains the dominant workload: the architecture must handle the less frequent triangle path without duplicating an entire rendering backend.

    Hybrid scenes therefore create a genuine mixed-intersection workload: different rays may encounter Gaussian primitives, triangles, or both. Figure 11 later quantifies this behavior for perspective, fisheye, and mesh-augmented rendering. We treat this workload as an architectural requirement for unified ray–Gaussian and ray–triangle execution.

    III Motivation

    We characterize a RaySplats-style renderer at the scene, ray, and intersection levels. Its workload is shaped by spatial imbalance, redundant neighboring-ray traversal, and scene-dependent Gaussian–triangle mixtures, motivating the three components of H2-Ray.

    III-AScene-Level Challenge: Spatial Imbalance in Gaussian Distributions

    Unlike mesh scenes, 3DGS Gaussians cluster around visible surfaces, leaving empty or weakly observed regions sparsely populated. The skew varies by scene: the coefficient of variation in Table I ranges from 2.7 (Playroom) to 11.2 (Kitchen).

    This spatial skew is problematic for a conventional monolithic BVH, as shown in Figure 3. A single global hierarchy must serve dense regions with long traversal and intersection queues as well as sparse regions that underutilize ray-tracing hardware. This produces uneven per-ray cost, reducing parallel efficiency and complicating load balance as scenes grow. The imbalance also makes a single global hierarchy a poor unit for memory placement and scheduling: dense regions dominate queues and cache traffic, while sparse regions leave traversal capacity idle.

    Table I quantifies this imbalance across all eight scenes under a uniform 8³ partition. On average, 69.8% of grids are empty and another 20.9% are sparse (1–99 Gaussians), leaving only 9.3% dense (at least 100 Gaussians). Even among non-empty grids, Gaussian counts remain highly uneven (average CV of 6.7).

    III-BRay-Level Challenge: Redundant Traversal Across Neighboring Rays

    A second inefficiency remains even with a fixed acceleration structure: neighboring rays often share BVH prefixes because adjacent pixels enter the same coarse Gaussian regions before diverging near boundaries (Figure 4). This image-space coherence is especially strong at high resolution and in primary visibility.

    Current execution nevertheless fetches and tests these upper-level nodes repeatedly, even though much of the traversal state is shared. This wastes memory bandwidth and RT Core cycles in coherent workloads such as mild lens distortion and some secondary-ray queries. The wasted work is not limited to duplicate node tests; repeated address generation and state updates also increase pressure on the traversal stack and memory system.

    III-CIntersection-Level Challenge: Heterogeneous Mixed-Primitive Intersection Workloads

    The final bottleneck appears when Gaussian rendering extends to hybrid scenes with triangle meshes, proxy geometry, or conventional ray-traced effects, where rays require Gaussian tests, triangle tests, or both.

    A rigid pipeline specialized for one primitive type is therefore inefficient: a triangle-centric datapath loses efficiency when Gaussian intersections dominate, while a Gaussian-only datapath cannot serve triangle work. The challenge is both mixed execution and a dominant primitive that varies with scene, camera, and task.

    IV H2-Ray Acceleration Framework

    H2-Ray combines three mechanisms: LB-SBVH for scene partitioning, RCPR for traversal reuse, and UIE for mixed-primitive intersection. Together, they form a hybrid and hierarchical ray-tracing framework for efficient 3D Gaussian rendering.

    IV-AThe End-to-End Rendering Pipeline

    The H2-Ray pipeline reorganizes conventional ray tracing into four density-aware stages:

    Raster-Assisted Culling

    Rather than starting each ray from a cold BVH traversal, H2-Ray first runs a lightweight low-resolution rasterization pass to generate a grid hit map that records per-grid hit counts (Figure 5). The map prunes empty regions and skips rays with negligible Gaussian energy, reducing initial traversal pressure.

    Balanced Scene Partitioning

    The scene is partitioned into uniform spatial grids by LB-SBVH, with each grid classified as dense or sparse by primitive count. Dense grids are assigned dedicated local BVHs, while sparse grids store primitives in flat lists for brute-force enumeration. Culling then dispatches rays only to active grids, concentrating traversal on occupied regions with bounded local workloads.

    Coherent Path Traversal

    For each ray cluster, the RCPR unit selects a proxy ray that performs BVH node fetching and internal intersection tests. Its traversal state is broadcast to worker rays, amortizing memory bandwidth across the group.

    Adaptive Intersection & Accumulation

    When rays reach leaf nodes, the UIE selects the appropriate Gaussian or triangle mode for each primitive, using a shared pool of floating-point units with mode-multiplexed inputs. The pipeline then performs front-to-back alpha blending and color accumulation.

    IV-BLoad-Balanced Spatial BVH (LB-SBVH)

    3D Gaussian scenes are highly non-uniform, making a monolithic BVH prone to divergence and hotspots. The Load-Balanced Spatial BVH (LB-SBVH) converts this global workload into locally balanced traversal units (Figure 5 (a)).

    Density-Aware Sub-Region Construction

    LB-SBVH partitions the scene into a uniform spatial grid and chooses a representation per grid. Dense grids (N≥100 Gaussians) construct specialized shallow BVHs to accelerate traversal in regions with high primitive density. Sparse grids (0

    Coverage-Preserving Grid Bounds

    Ownership and traversal bounds are separate. Each Gaussian is assigned once by its center, avoiding duplicate occupancy counts. Each non-empty grid then builds a tight conservative AABB around the full support of its assigned Gaussians. These AABBs may expand beyond or shrink within the original cells and may overlap one another, so any ray intersecting a Gaussian support reaches its owning grid even when it misses the center cell. The local BVH or sparse list performs the exact intersection, ensuring complete coverage without duplicating Gaussians.

    Hardware Support for LB-SBVH

    LB-SBVH adds two hardware mechanisms. Hybrid Metadata Storage (HMS) combines a meta-tree with meta-bitmaps to encode BVH addresses and sub-region positions, allowing threads to locate target trees with little decoding overhead. The Raster-to-RT Forward Path (R2RFP) forwards BVH pointers directly from the Raster Engine to the RT Cores, avoiding DRAM synchronization and redundant top-level traversal.

    IV-CRay-Cluster Path Reuse (RCPR)

    For primary and coherent secondary rays, neighboring paths through the BVH are highly correlated. RCPR shares intermediate states within localized 3×3 ray tiles (Figure 5 (b)).

    Proxy-Ray-Based Cluster Traversal

    For each tile, the center proxy ray performs a full BVH traversal. When it reaches a leaf, hardware “hops back” by c levels (e.g., c=2 or 3) to define a coherence volume. The eight worker rays are dispatched to these intermediate nodes, bypassing redundant upper-level tests.

    Hardware Support for Path Reuse

    RT Cores are augmented with a Shared Prefix Memory (SPM) and a Pinned Cache. SPM stores the deepest nodes found by the proxy ray so worker rays resume from the longest shared path. Frequently accessed Gaussian primitives are pinned in L2 with a dedicated flag bit. A specialized internal Load-Store Unit (LSU) provides Direct Color Duplication, offloading copy-heavy work that would otherwise stall the warp.

    IV-DUnified Intersection Engine (UIE)

    Since the Gaussian-to-triangle ratio varies by view, scene, and ray effect, fixed hardware for one primitive type is inefficient. UIE reuses the LB-SBVH grid structure: each grid points to either a Gaussian-BVH or a triangle-BVH, keeping primitive selection local to leaf-level intersection while ray generation, culling, and blending remain unchanged.

    Structural Isomorphism Between Intersection Pipelines

    Gaussian ellipsoid intersection and Möller-Trumbore triangle intersection follow a similar algebraic flow: both transform the ray into a local frame, execute multiply-accumulate stages, and solve for the intersection distance t. Many floating-point units can therefore be shared; switching primitive types changes operands and control bits rather than the pipeline topology.

    Reconfigurable Unified Datapath

    We instantiate 78 floating-point units organized in an eight-stage feed-forward pipeline. Of these, 31 units (40%) are shared between Gaussian and triangle modes: they execute the same operation in both modes but receive different operands via mode-MUX input selection. The remaining units are dedicated to one primitive type: 32 units (41%) serve only the Gaussian path, while 15 units (19%) serve only the triangle path. The Gaussian path needs more dedicated hardware because its quadratic solve and alpha computation have no triangle analog, while Möller–Trumbore is more compact. Table II reports sharing by unit type: multipliers and reciprocal units are shared most aggressively, while adders and the square-root unit are largely path-specific.

    The active datapath is selected per intersection by the primitive-type field in the ray-intersection instruction; no runtime workload prediction is required. Once traversal reaches a leaf, UIE gates the corresponding operands into the shared pipeline, so primitive-type selection requires no software branching while the triangle path stays lightweight. Triangle-dedicated units account for 15 of the 78 floating-point units (approximately 19%); this is a unit-count fraction, not an area-overhead estimate.

    IV-EHardware Integration

    Figure 6 shows how LB-SBVH, RCPR, and UIE are integrated into the GPU pipeline. At the system level (left), each Graphics Processing Cluster (GPC) contains a Streaming Multiprocessor (SM), an H2-Ray RT Core, and a Raster Engine connected by R2RFP. The Pinned L2 Cache sits beside the DRAM controller to support RCPR. This organization leaves shader execution, memory hierarchy, and rasterization largely intact; H2-Ray adds only the paths needed to pass culling and reuse information to the RT Core. This section describes the target hardware path; the evaluation separately reports modeled RT Core behavior and measured CUDA kernels, as detailed in Section V.

    The H2-Ray RT Core (center) adds four blocks to a conventional RT Core: (1) a Raster-to-RT Interface that receives BVH pointers without a DRAM round-trip, (2) a Shared Prefix Memory (SPM) for proxy-ray path pointers, (3) a Reconfigurable Intersection Unit that switches between Gaussian and triangle logic, and (4) a Direct Color Duplication unit that offloads pixel-copy operations from the SM. These additions are placed around the existing traversal and intersection flow: R2RFP supplies the starting BVH handle, SPM changes where worker rays resume traversal, UIE changes the leaf test, and color duplication handles repeated output writes.

    Execution proceeds in two phases (right). In the Proxy Ray Phase, the Raster Engine performs low-resolution culling, forwards valid grid BVH handles through R2RFP, and the RT Core writes proxy-ray prefix pointers into SPM. In the Real Ray Phase, worker rays load these pointers, skip redundant upper-level nodes, and proceed to the Reconfigurable Intersection Unit. The two phases therefore reuse traversal state while leaving the front-to-back blending semantics unchanged; the quality impact of this approximate reuse is evaluated in Section V. The Pinned L2 Cache (bottom) protects marked cache lines from eviction so Gaussian primitives found during the proxy phase remain resident for worker rays.

    V Evaluation
item.content:encoded:
一句话：用密度感知 BVH 修负载失衡，用统一求交引擎在同一数据通路上处理高斯与三角形。

要点：

  • 负载均衡空间 BVH（LB-SBVH）把场景切成均匀网格并用密度感知表示，把极不均匀的高斯分布转成可均衡调度的任务
  • 识别相邻像素遍历路径高度相似的问题，合并冗余遍历以减少重复采样
  • 统一求交引擎用模式复用数据通路支持高斯与三角形混合求交，两类图元共享 40% 浮点单元；多视角评测相对 RaySplats 平均 PSNR 仅降 0.034dB

为什么值得看：光追 3DGS 想落地，卡点不是算法而是负载均衡与混合图元的硬件利用；这篇给出的是架构层取舍。

中文摘要：3DGS 依赖光栅化获得效率，但次级光照、强畸变相机与景深效果需要光线追踪。把光追引入 3DGS 会撞上三个难题：海量高斯基元的空间分布极不均匀，造成严重负载失衡；相邻像素发出的光线遍历路径高度相似，产生大量冗余遍历；同时支持高斯与三角形两种图元会让求交负载异构，现有 GPU 架构难以匹配。作者提出 H-Ray：负载均衡空间 BVH 把场景划成均匀网格、用密度感知表示把失衡分布转成可均衡调度的工作；针对路径相似性做遍历合并；统一求交引擎用模式复用的数据通路同时处理两类图元，共享 40% 浮点单元。在与 RaySplats 匹配的多视角评测中，平均 PSNR 仅下降 0.034dB。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

A Hybrid and Hierarchical Ray Tracing Method for Efficient 3D Gaussian Rendering

Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a powerful representation for real-time neural reconstruction and rendering. While existing 3DGS systems rely on rasterization for efficiency, recent work explores ray tracing to enable secondary lighting, highly distorted cameras, and depth-of-field effects. However, compared with rasterization, ray-traced 3DGS introduces three major challenges: (1) the highly non-uniform spatial distribution of massive numbers of Gaussian primitives creates severe load imbalance; (2) neighboring pixels often generate rays with highly similar traversal paths, leading to substantial redundant traversal overhead; and (3) supporting both Gaussian and triangle primitives yields heterogeneous intersection workloads that are not well matched to existing GPU architectures. We present H2-Ray, a hybrid and hierarchical ray tracing architecture for efficient 3D Gaussian rendering. H2-Ray introduces three techniques. Load-Balanced Spatial BVH (LB-SBVH) partitions the scene into uniform grids and uses density-aware representations to convert an imbalanced global workload into balanced local traversal units. Ray-Cluster Path Reuse (RCPR) lets a proxy ray share traversal state with neighboring rays to amortize redundant traversal. The Unified Intersection Engine (UIE) supports mixed Gaussian and triangle intersections through a mode-multiplexed datapath that shares 40% of its floating-point units across both primitive types. Across 8 scenes, H2-Ray achieves a geometric-mean speedup of 3.77× and a maximum speedup of 9.26× over RaySplats on the NVIDIA RTX A5000, combining a cycle-accurate model of the modified RT Core with measured CUDA timings.

Index Terms:

Neural Rendering, 3D Gaussian Splatting, Ray Tracing, GPU Architecture, Hardware Acceleration

I Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become a compelling scene representation for neural reconstruction and rendering, delivering high visual quality at real-time rates [8]. Its anisotropic primitives and rasterization-friendly rendering capture fine geometric and appearance details at interactive rates. However, the rasterization-centric design that makes 3DGS efficient also limits its ability to model real-world optical effects. In particular, rasterization-based Gaussian rendering struggles to support (1) secondary-lighting effects such as reflections and refractions needed for mirror-like and transparent materials [17], (2) highly distorted fisheye cameras used in autonomous-driving surround-view systems [24], (3) depth-of-field effects arising from finite-aperture camera optics [4], and other rendering modes that benefit from per-ray visibility reasoning. As summarized in Figure 1, ray tracing broadens the rendering envelope of 3DGS, but making this flexibility practical requires architectural support beyond both triangle-centric ray tracing hardware and rasterization-based 3DGS pipelines.

This gap stems from 3D Gaussian ray-tracing workloads, which differ from rasterization and triangle-based ray tracing. First, Gaussian primitives are highly non-uniform across space, so a monolithic acceleration structure must simultaneously serve extremely dense and extremely sparse regions, leading to poor traversal balance and inefficient parallelism. In rasterization, imbalance mainly arises from the number of projected fragments in 2D screen space. In ray tracing, which operates in 3D, secondary-ray effects (e.g., reflections and refractions) further amplify spatial non-uniformity, resulting in more severe load imbalance and irregular execution. Second, neighboring pixels often generate rays that traverse highly similar BVH path prefixes, so processing these rays independently causes substantial redundant traversal work. This redundancy is most pronounced at high resolutions, where dense pixel sampling induces strong spatial coherence among rays and deep BVH hierarchies lead to long shared traversal prefixes. Third, advanced effects increasingly mix ray–Gaussian and ray–triangle intersections, creating a heterogeneous workload mismatched to fixed-function specialization around one dominant primitive type. Modern GPU architectures provide dedicated hardware support for ray–triangle intersections (e.g., via RT Cores), while ray–Gaussian intersections are typically handled by general-purpose compute units, leading to an imbalance in execution efficiency. This heterogeneity limits hardware efficiency and motivates unified support for both primitives.

Recent efforts have brought ray tracing to 3D Gaussian rendering. 3DGRT [13], 3DGUT [23], and RaySplats [3] demonstrate ray-traced 3DGS with different rendering formulations, and GRTX [9] adds hardware support for Gaussian BVH traversal. However, these works target rendering formulations or single-ray traversal, leaving spatial imbalance, redundant traversal across neighboring rays, and heterogeneous intersection largely unexplored.

To address these challenges, we present H2-Ray, a hybrid and hierarchical ray tracing architecture. H2-Ray is hybrid in two senses: it combines rasterization with ray tracing for fast region-of-interest culling, and it supports mixed ray–Gaussian and ray–triangle intersection workloads. It is hierarchical because it addresses the workload at three levels: scene-level spatial partitioning, ray-level traversal reuse, and intersection-level execution adaptation. Rather than replacing modern graphics hardware, H2-Ray adopts a practical co-design approach, adding targeted support at key points in the GPU rendering pipeline. Our contributions are as follows.

  • •

    We propose Load-Balanced Spatial BVH (LB-SBVH), a density-aware spatial partitioning scheme that converts globally skewed Gaussian distributions into balanced traversal regions, achieving a microarchitectural traversal speedup of up to 1.31× over a monolithic BVH.

  • •

    We propose Ray-Cluster Path Reuse (RCPR), which shares traversal across neighboring rays to reduce redundant BVH operations. In matched multi-view evaluation, H2-Ray decreases average PSNR by only 0.034 dB relative to RaySplats.

  • •

    We design a Unified Intersection Engine (UIE) that supports both Gaussian and triangle primitives within a single reconfigurable datapath, sharing 31 of its 78 floating-point units (approximately 40%) across primitive types, with 15 units (approximately 19%) dedicated to triangles.

    • We evaluate H2-Ray on 8 scenes from Mip-NeRF 360 [2] and Deep Blending [6] (Figure 2), combining cycle-level modeling of the modified RT Core with measured RTX A5000 timings for all CUDA work. H2-Ray achieves a geometric-mean speedup of 3.77× (up to 9.26×) over RaySplats on the A5000 while enabling rendering effects beyond rasterization-based pipelines.

    II Background

    II-A3D Gaussian Splatting

    3DGS represents a scene as a set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives, where each primitive stores a mean position, covariance, opacity, and view-dependent appearance [8]. A Gaussian primitive can be written as

    Gᵢ(x)=αᵢ\exp(-1/2(x-μᵢ)ᵀΣᵢ⁻¹(x-μᵢ)),

    		(1)

    where μᵢ and Σᵢ describe the primitive’s spatial support, and αᵢ controls its contribution strength. In practice, a reconstructed scene contains a very large number of such Gaussians, and their spatial distribution is often highly non-uniform, as quantified later in Table I and Figure 3.

    Rasterization-based 3DGS projects these 3D Gaussians onto the image plane, bins them into screen-space tiles, and blends their contributions in front-to-back order. The rendered color of a pixel can be written in the standard alpha-compositing form

    C(r)=∑ᵢTᵢ α̂ᵢ cᵢ, Tᵢ=∏_j

    		(2)

    where α̂ᵢ is the projected opacity of the i-th Gaussian along ray r, cᵢ is its color, and Tᵢ is the accumulated transmittance before it. This rasterization pipeline is highly efficient for standard pinhole-camera novel-view synthesis, but it is less natural for rendering modes that require arbitrary-ray queries, secondary visibility, or tight integration with conventional ray-traced geometry.

    II-BRay Tracing for 3DGS Rendering

    Recent work revisits 3DGS rendering from a ray-based viewpoint. 3DGRT [13] builds a BVH over Gaussian primitives, encapsulates each with a stretched bounding mesh, and uses hardware ray–triangle intersection. This design improves flexibility, but traversal and ordering remain proxy-based: primitives are gathered through bounding-mesh hits, and integration follows proxy intersections rather than exact sample locations along the ray. 3DGUT [23] instead preserves splatting for primary rendering while extending 3DGS to nonlinear cameras through Unscented-Transform sigma points. 3DGUT further aligns its rendering formulation with 3DGRT so that primary rays can still be splatted efficiently while secondary rays are traced in the same representation. This bridges rasterization efficiency and ray-tracing flexibility, but primary rays still use a sigma-point approximation rather than direct ray–Gaussian intersection, while secondary rays follow the ray-traced representation. These designs emphasize rendering flexibility and camera-model support, whereas our architectural study focuses on the execution costs exposed by direct Gaussian traversal.

    RaySplats [3] moves further toward a direct ray-based formulation. Instead of using bounding polytopes as the primitive representation, RaySplats explicitly computes intersections between rays and Gaussian confidence ellipsoids, avoiding polytope approximation and remaining applicable to flat Gaussians. Importantly, this ellipsoid is not a different primitive from (1); it is an iso-surface induced by the same Gaussian after choosing a fixed density threshold. Specifically, setting Gᵢ(x)=ρ in (1) yields

    (x-μ)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x-μ)=τ,

    		(3)

    where τ=-2\ln(ρ/α) is a threshold-dependent constant. For a ray r(t)=o+td, substituting x=o+td into this iso-surface equation yields a quadratic

    at²+bt+c=0,

    		(4)

    where

    a=dᵀΣ⁻¹d, b=2dᵀΣ⁻¹(o-μ),
    c=(o-μ)ᵀΣ⁻¹(o-μ)-τ.

    The closest valid hit is given by the smaller positive root. For our architectural study, this formulation exposes native ray–Gaussian intersection without polyhedral approximation. Its arithmetic is dominated by symmetric matrix-vector products, dot products, and a quadratic solve, directly reflecting the workload that the hardware must execute. Accordingly, the rest of this paper adopts this RaySplats-style workload model: rays are intersected directly with Gaussian primitives, and their contributions are accumulated in ray order.

    II-CWhy Hybrid Rendering Matters

    Once Gaussian rendering is expressed in a ray-tracing framework, it inherits many of the benefits of ray tracing. Prior work shows that ray-traced 3DGS can naturally support reflections, refractions, shadows, stochastic ray sampling, highly distorted cameras, and rolling-shutter effects [13, 23, 3]. It also becomes easier to combine Gaussian scene content with triangle-based geometry, mesh proxies, or standard graphics assets within the same rendering pipeline. For instance, 3DGRT demonstrates compatibility with ray-based visual effects and mesh interactions, 3DGUT performs hybrid rendering with splatted primary rays and traced secondary rays, and RaySplats shows that Gaussian scenes can be rendered together with mesh-based objects and lighting effects. These capabilities make mixed primitive support relevant even when Gaussian rendering remains the dominant workload: the architecture must handle the less frequent triangle path without duplicating an entire rendering backend.

    Hybrid scenes therefore create a genuine mixed-intersection workload: different rays may encounter Gaussian primitives, triangles, or both. Figure 11 later quantifies this behavior for perspective, fisheye, and mesh-augmented rendering. We treat this workload as an architectural requirement for unified ray–Gaussian and ray–triangle execution.

    III Motivation

    We characterize a RaySplats-style renderer at the scene, ray, and intersection levels. Its workload is shaped by spatial imbalance, redundant neighboring-ray traversal, and scene-dependent Gaussian–triangle mixtures, motivating the three components of H2-Ray.

    III-AScene-Level Challenge: Spatial Imbalance in Gaussian Distributions

    Unlike mesh scenes, 3DGS Gaussians cluster around visible surfaces, leaving empty or weakly observed regions sparsely populated. The skew varies by scene: the coefficient of variation in Table I ranges from 2.7 (Playroom) to 11.2 (Kitchen).

    This spatial skew is problematic for a conventional monolithic BVH, as shown in Figure 3. A single global hierarchy must serve dense regions with long traversal and intersection queues as well as sparse regions that underutilize ray-tracing hardware. This produces uneven per-ray cost, reducing parallel efficiency and complicating load balance as scenes grow. The imbalance also makes a single global hierarchy a poor unit for memory placement and scheduling: dense regions dominate queues and cache traffic, while sparse regions leave traversal capacity idle.

    Table I quantifies this imbalance across all eight scenes under a uniform 8³ partition. On average, 69.8% of grids are empty and another 20.9% are sparse (1–99 Gaussians), leaving only 9.3% dense (at least 100 Gaussians). Even among non-empty grids, Gaussian counts remain highly uneven (average CV of 6.7).

    III-BRay-Level Challenge: Redundant Traversal Across Neighboring Rays

    A second inefficiency remains even with a fixed acceleration structure: neighboring rays often share BVH prefixes because adjacent pixels enter the same coarse Gaussian regions before diverging near boundaries (Figure 4). This image-space coherence is especially strong at high resolution and in primary visibility.

    Current execution nevertheless fetches and tests these upper-level nodes repeatedly, even though much of the traversal state is shared. This wastes memory bandwidth and RT Core cycles in coherent workloads such as mild lens distortion and some secondary-ray queries. The wasted work is not limited to duplicate node tests; repeated address generation and state updates also increase pressure on the traversal stack and memory system.

    III-CIntersection-Level Challenge: Heterogeneous Mixed-Primitive Intersection Workloads

    The final bottleneck appears when Gaussian rendering extends to hybrid scenes with triangle meshes, proxy geometry, or conventional ray-traced effects, where rays require Gaussian tests, triangle tests, or both.

    A rigid pipeline specialized for one primitive type is therefore inefficient: a triangle-centric datapath loses efficiency when Gaussian intersections dominate, while a Gaussian-only datapath cannot serve triangle work. The challenge is both mixed execution and a dominant primitive that varies with scene, camera, and task.

    IV H2-Ray Acceleration Framework

    H2-Ray combines three mechanisms: LB-SBVH for scene partitioning, RCPR for traversal reuse, and UIE for mixed-primitive intersection. Together, they form a hybrid and hierarchical ray-tracing framework for efficient 3D Gaussian rendering.

    IV-AThe End-to-End Rendering Pipeline

    The H2-Ray pipeline reorganizes conventional ray tracing into four density-aware stages:

    Raster-Assisted Culling

    Rather than starting each ray from a cold BVH traversal, H2-Ray first runs a lightweight low-resolution rasterization pass to generate a grid hit map that records per-grid hit counts (Figure 5). The map prunes empty regions and skips rays with negligible Gaussian energy, reducing initial traversal pressure.

    Balanced Scene Partitioning

    The scene is partitioned into uniform spatial grids by LB-SBVH, with each grid classified as dense or sparse by primitive count. Dense grids are assigned dedicated local BVHs, while sparse grids store primitives in flat lists for brute-force enumeration. Culling then dispatches rays only to active grids, concentrating traversal on occupied regions with bounded local workloads.

    Coherent Path Traversal

    For each ray cluster, the RCPR unit selects a proxy ray that performs BVH node fetching and internal intersection tests. Its traversal state is broadcast to worker rays, amortizing memory bandwidth across the group.

    Adaptive Intersection & Accumulation

    When rays reach leaf nodes, the UIE selects the appropriate Gaussian or triangle mode for each primitive, using a shared pool of floating-point units with mode-multiplexed inputs. The pipeline then performs front-to-back alpha blending and color accumulation.

    IV-BLoad-Balanced Spatial BVH (LB-SBVH)

    3D Gaussian scenes are highly non-uniform, making a monolithic BVH prone to divergence and hotspots. The Load-Balanced Spatial BVH (LB-SBVH) converts this global workload into locally balanced traversal units (Figure 5 (a)).

    Density-Aware Sub-Region Construction

    LB-SBVH partitions the scene into a uniform spatial grid and chooses a representation per grid. Dense grids (N≥100 Gaussians) construct specialized shallow BVHs to accelerate traversal in regions with high primitive density. Sparse grids (0

    Coverage-Preserving Grid Bounds

    Ownership and traversal bounds are separate. Each Gaussian is assigned once by its center, avoiding duplicate occupancy counts. Each non-empty grid then builds a tight conservative AABB around the full support of its assigned Gaussians. These AABBs may expand beyond or shrink within the original cells and may overlap one another, so any ray intersecting a Gaussian support reaches its owning grid even when it misses the center cell. The local BVH or sparse list performs the exact intersection, ensuring complete coverage without duplicating Gaussians.

    Hardware Support for LB-SBVH

    LB-SBVH adds two hardware mechanisms. Hybrid Metadata Storage (HMS) combines a meta-tree with meta-bitmaps to encode BVH addresses and sub-region positions, allowing threads to locate target trees with little decoding overhead. The Raster-to-RT Forward Path (R2RFP) forwards BVH pointers directly from the Raster Engine to the RT Cores, avoiding DRAM synchronization and redundant top-level traversal.

    IV-CRay-Cluster Path Reuse (RCPR)

    For primary and coherent secondary rays, neighboring paths through the BVH are highly correlated. RCPR shares intermediate states within localized 3×3 ray tiles (Figure 5 (b)).

    Proxy-Ray-Based Cluster Traversal

    For each tile, the center proxy ray performs a full BVH traversal. When it reaches a leaf, hardware “hops back” by c levels (e.g., c=2 or 3) to define a coherence volume. The eight worker rays are dispatched to these intermediate nodes, bypassing redundant upper-level tests.

    Hardware Support for Path Reuse

    RT Cores are augmented with a Shared Prefix Memory (SPM) and a Pinned Cache. SPM stores the deepest nodes found by the proxy ray so worker rays resume from the longest shared path. Frequently accessed Gaussian primitives are pinned in L2 with a dedicated flag bit. A specialized internal Load-Store Unit (LSU) provides Direct Color Duplication, offloading copy-heavy work that would otherwise stall the warp.

    IV-DUnified Intersection Engine (UIE)

    Since the Gaussian-to-triangle ratio varies by view, scene, and ray effect, fixed hardware for one primitive type is inefficient. UIE reuses the LB-SBVH grid structure: each grid points to either a Gaussian-BVH or a triangle-BVH, keeping primitive selection local to leaf-level intersection while ray generation, culling, and blending remain unchanged.

    Structural Isomorphism Between Intersection Pipelines

    Gaussian ellipsoid intersection and Möller-Trumbore triangle intersection follow a similar algebraic flow: both transform the ray into a local frame, execute multiply-accumulate stages, and solve for the intersection distance t. Many floating-point units can therefore be shared; switching primitive types changes operands and control bits rather than the pipeline topology.

    Reconfigurable Unified Datapath

    We instantiate 78 floating-point units organized in an eight-stage feed-forward pipeline. Of these, 31 units (40%) are shared between Gaussian and triangle modes: they execute the same operation in both modes but receive different operands via mode-MUX input selection. The remaining units are dedicated to one primitive type: 32 units (41%) serve only the Gaussian path, while 15 units (19%) serve only the triangle path. The Gaussian path needs more dedicated hardware because its quadratic solve and alpha computation have no triangle analog, while Möller–Trumbore is more compact. Table II reports sharing by unit type: multipliers and reciprocal units are shared most aggressively, while adders and the square-root unit are largely path-specific.

    The active datapath is selected per intersection by the primitive-type field in the ray-intersection instruction; no runtime workload prediction is required. Once traversal reaches a leaf, UIE gates the corresponding operands into the shared pipeline, so primitive-type selection requires no software branching while the triangle path stays lightweight. Triangle-dedicated units account for 15 of the 78 floating-point units (approximately 19%); this is a unit-count fraction, not an area-overhead estimate.

    IV-EHardware Integration

    Figure 6 shows how LB-SBVH, RCPR, and UIE are integrated into the GPU pipeline. At the system level (left), each Graphics Processing Cluster (GPC) contains a Streaming Multiprocessor (SM), an H2-Ray RT Core, and a Raster Engine connected by R2RFP. The Pinned L2 Cache sits beside the DRAM controller to support RCPR. This organization leaves shader execution, memory hierarchy, and rasterization largely intact; H2-Ray adds only the paths needed to pass culling and reuse information to the RT Core. This section describes the target hardware path; the evaluation separately reports modeled RT Core behavior and measured CUDA kernels, as detailed in Section V.

    The H2-Ray RT Core (center) adds four blocks to a conventional RT Core: (1) a Raster-to-RT Interface that receives BVH pointers without a DRAM round-trip, (2) a Shared Prefix Memory (SPM) for proxy-ray path pointers, (3) a Reconfigurable Intersection Unit that switches between Gaussian and triangle logic, and (4) a Direct Color Duplication unit that offloads pixel-copy operations from the SM. These additions are placed around the existing traversal and intersection flow: R2RFP supplies the starting BVH handle, SPM changes where worker rays resume traversal, UIE changes the leaf test, and color duplication handles repeated output writes.

    Execution proceeds in two phases (right). In the Proxy Ray Phase, the Raster Engine performs low-resolution culling, forwards valid grid BVH handles through R2RFP, and the RT Core writes proxy-ray prefix pointers into SPM. In the Real Ray Phase, worker rays load these pointers, skip redundant upper-level nodes, and proceed to the Reconfigurable Intersection Unit. The two phases therefore reuse traversal state while leaving the front-to-back blending semantics unchanged; the quality impact of this approximate reuse is evaluated in Section V. The Pinned L2 Cache (bottom) protects marked cache lines from eviction so Gaussian primitives found during the proxy phase remain resident for worker rays.

    V Evaluation

item.title: TETRIS-4DGS：几秒完成、压缩率 40 倍以上的 4D 高斯后训练压缩 ｜ TETRIS-4DGS: Efficient Post-Training Compression of 4D Gaussian Splatting
item.description:
一句话：不再逐场景优化，直接把 4DGS 属性排成编解码器友好的 2D 图，秒级压到 1/40。

要点：

  • 把 4DGS 压缩从「逐场景优化问题」改成通用后训练框架，直接复用现有图像与视频编解码器
  • 按高斯重要性做自适应量化，重新分配码率，同时保持与现有 codec 完全兼容
  • 利用 4DGS 的统计特性做运动与重要性感知的打包，把属性重排成编解码友好的 2D 图；压缩率超 40 倍且只需数秒

为什么值得看：动态 3DGS 的存储是部署死穴，能直接吃现成 codec、还能秒级完成，才谈得上流式加载与在线分发。

中文摘要：4D 高斯泼溅能实时高质量渲染动态场景，但存储开销高得难以部署。现有压缩方法多把压缩当成逐场景优化问题，泛化性差，也无法满足低延迟压缩的场景。TETRIS-4DGS 改用通用后训练框架：直接借助成熟的图像与视频编解码器，先按重要性水平对高斯做自适应量化，从而细化码率分配，并保持与现有 codec 完全兼容；再利用 4DGS 的统计特性，提出运动与重要性感知的打包方式，把高斯属性重排成对编解码器友好的 2D 图。实验显示它能在数秒内完成压缩、达到 40 倍以上的压缩率，同时保持较高质量。对需要把动态高斯内容分发到端侧的应用，这种「不训练、只用 codec」的路线工程成本最低。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

TETRIS-4DGS: Efficient Post-Training Compression of 4D Gaussian Splatting

Abstract

4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) has emerged as a powerful dynamic scene representation, supporting real-time high quality rendering but suffers from prohibitive storage overhead. Existing methods typically attempt to solve this by treating compression as a per-scene optimization problem, limiting generalizability and applicability where low-latency compression is required. In this work, we leverage existing image and video codecs and propose a generalized post-training compression framework for 4DGS to address these issues. Specifically, we apply importance-based adaptive quantization to Gaussians according to their importance levels, effectively refining bitrate allocation while remaining fully compatible with existing codecs. To further improve compression efficiency, we utilize the statistical properties of 4DGS and propose motion- and importance-aware packing to reorganize attributes into codec-friendly 2D maps. Our approach can achieve over 40× compression rate in seconds while maintaining high quality, facilitating the practical deployment of 4DGS.

Index Terms:

4D Gaussian Splatting, 4D Gaussian Splatting Compression, Post-Training Compression

I Introduction

With photorealistic and fast rendering, dynamic Gaussian Splatting is a promising pathway toward free-viewpoint video, enabling immersive visual applications. Existing paradigms for dynamic Gaussian Splatting can be categorized into three classes: per-frame 3DGS methods [11, 4], deformable Gaussians with canonical space [13, 16], and 4D Gaussian representations [15, 9]. Practical deployment of dynamic Gaussians requires both efficient rendering and lightweight representation. The former makes canonical-space deformable Gaussians less practical, since neural inference for deformation slows down rendering. The latter makes per-frame 3DGS less attractive due to its large storage footprint. 4D Gaussian representations—exemplified by 4DGS [15]—offer a more favorable balance between rendering efficiency and model compactness.

While striking a balance, 4D Gaussian still suffer from its raw data volume, highlighting the need for effective compression. One line of work reduces the number of parameters per primitive by modifying the representation for compression, as in MEGA and CSTG. However, introducing neural networks into the representation enable memory-efficient representation but increases rendering complexity. Another line of work achieves compression by pruning low-contribution primitives, such as 4DGS-1K and the masking strategy in CSTG. These methods require costly pruning-score computation and fine-tuning. Despite their effectiveness in terms of rate-distortion performance, these methods still treat compression as a scene-specific optimization tightly coupled with 4D Gaussian training. This tight coupling demands costly re-training when the content is not generated using the same training pipeline and becomes impractical for low-latency compression.

We target 4DGS [15] representation and aim to achieve strong rate–distortion performance for 4DGS compression with short encoding and decoding time. As shown in Fig. 1, we propose TETRIS-4DGS, an efficient post-training compression scheme for 4DGS that packs Gaussians into different blocks like Tetris. The key principle behind the scheme is to leverage off-the-shelf standard image and video codecs that are widely available across devices for efficient compression.

4DGS attributes that affect primitive positions are seen as distortion-sensitive and encoded with lossless image codecs, while the remaining majority, distortion-robust attributes are encoded with lossy video codecs. To efficiently compress the latter, we introduce two techniques: 1) importance-based adaptive quantization, and 2) motion- and importance-aware packing. The former achieves adaptive bit allocation across primitives with different importance scores, without modifying the existing video codec implementation. Unlike existing time-consuming importance calculation methods, we train a generalizable importance estimator that predicts importance scores in a feed-forward pass. Guided by the motion statistics and importance of 4DGS, our packing method first partitions primitives into groups and then places primitives from the same group into spatially contiguous regions. This produces codec-friendly 2D attribute maps that can be efficiently compressed by standard video codecs.

Our method achieves over 40× compression ratio while maintaining high visual quality, with only 12s for encoding and 2s for decoding a 300-frame dynamic scene, offering a strong rate–distortion–runtime trade-off.

II Related Works

II-AGaussians Primitives Pruning

Existing methods typically address primitive redundancy by pruning Gaussians based on per-point importance metrics, which are mainly obtained in two ways: (1) leveraging rendering kernels to calculate each primitive’s rendering contribution or uncertainty [1, 2, 3, 17]; and (2) learning per-point scores or masks through rate–distortion optimization [12]. While effective in improving RD performance, these methods incur substantial computational overhead and GPU memory consumption, limiting their practicality. More recently, an MPEG contribution [14] proposed predicting per-point importance from Gaussian features using a generalized MLP, achieving competitive RD performance with reduced runtime. However, both this method and prior approaches categorize Gaussians into only two groups—pruned or retained—overlooking the fact that Gaussians can be more finely stratified into multiple importance levels to further exploit redundancy.

II-B4D Gaussian Compression

Even though 4D Gaussian representations achieved favorable balance between model compactness and rendering efficiency, it still suffers from significant storage overhead. To mitigate this issue, MEGA [19] enlarges each Gaussian’s influence range via entropy-constrained deformation, reducing the number of primitives, and replaces spherical harmonics with a color predictor for decoding. 4DGS-1K [17] ranks 4D Gaussians by spatial–temporal variation, pruning up to 80% of primitives to lower storage and proceeds fine-tuning to recover quality. CSTG [6] prunes Gaussians using learnable per-point masks and compresses attributes with residual vector quantization. Though effective in terms of RD performance, these methods still tightly couple optimization with compression, lacking generalizability to pre-generated Gaussian models and making them unsuitable for low-latency compression.

III Method

In order to achieve strong rate–distortion–runtime trade-off on the 4DGS [15] representation, we propose Importance-Based Adaptive Quantization (Sec. III-B) and Motion- and Importance-Aware Packing (Sec. III-C) for 4DGS compression. Fig. 2 illustrates the overall workflow of our method.

III-APreliminary

Each 4DGS [15] primitive is defined by the following attributes: (i) 4D mean vector μ_4D=(μₓ,μ_y,μ_z,μₜ)∈ℝ⁴; (ii) 4D rotation R_4D, parameterized by a pair of isotropic quaternions, qₗ∈ℝ⁴ and qᵣ∈ℝ⁴; (iii) 4D scaling factor s_4D=(sₓ,s_y,s_z,sₜ)∈ℝ⁴; (iv) spatial and temporal spherical harmonics (SH) sh∈ℝ^3(kᵥ+1)²(kₜ+1) with view degrees of freedom kᵥ and time degrees of freedom kₜ; (v) opacity o∈[0,1]. Given the above attributes, the covariance matrix Σ_4D of a 4DGS can be constructed as:

Σ_4D=R_4DS_4DS_4DᵀR_4Dᵀ=\beginpmatrixU&V Vᵀ&W\endpmatrix,

(1)

where U∈ℝ^3×3, V∈ℝ^3×1, and W∈ℝ^1×1 represent the decomposed sub-matrices of the covariance.

For rendering, 4D Gaussians are projected into 3D space, where Σ_3D=U-VVᵀ/W denotes the 3D covariance matrix and σ(t)=e^-(t-μₜ)²/2W models the temporal decay of opacity. Furthermore, the 3D centers of Gaussians are defined as μ_3D(t)=μ_3D+(t-μₜ)V/W, approximating Gaussian trajectories as uniform linear motions. Following the projection of 4DGS into 3D space, differentiable rasterization is applied to the projected 3D Gaussians to synthesize the final image.

According to the above formulation, the spherical harmonics and opacity of 4DGS are distortion-robust for they do not affect the Gaussian position, whereas the remaining attributes influence their positions to some extent. Our work focuses on efficiently compressing the former group—which constitutes the majority of attribute channels—using lossy video codecs, as these attributes contain greater redundancy.

III-BImportance-Based Adaptive Quantization

While current pruning-based methods reduce the primitive redundancy among 4DGS, they treat all surviving Gaussians equally. This binary approach is inefficient for primitives of borderline importance: pruning them degrades quality, yet storing them at full precision wastes bits. These primitives should be treated in a more delicate way, for which we propose importance-based adaptive quantization.

Importance-Based Adaptive Quantization for Attributes: We assign each Gaussian attribute a specific bit width and then uniformly quantize it using its per-channel minimum and maximum values, where we propose an importance-guided attribute rescaling. Specifically, each Gaussian is associated with an importance score φ∈(0,1), predicted by a generalized importance score estimator, which is described in the following paragraph. We then divide the importance score φ into L importance levels l:

l(φ)=\begincases0,&φ∈(0,φₜₕᵣₑₛ), 1+⌊(L-1)·\dfracφ-φₜₕᵣₑₛ1-φₜₕᵣₑₛ⌋,&φ∈[φₜₕᵣₑₛ,1),\endcases

(2)

where l∈{0,1,2,...,L-1} denotes the assigned importance level and φₜₕᵣₑₛ denotes a preset score threshold which will be explained later. With the importance level of each primitive determined, we define the corresponding attribute rescale ratio φ̂_L as:

φ̂ₗ=\begincases0,&l=0, [6.0pt] φₗ^\max,&l∈{1,2,...,L-2}, [6.0pt] 1,&l=L-1,\endcases

(3)

where φₗ^\max denotes the maximum score value of level l importance scores.

Next, the distortion-robust Gaussian attributes A are multiplied by their respective rescale ratios φ̂ₗ before quantization, forming adjusted attribute value A^′: A^′=A·φ̂ₗ. During decoding, the original attribute values will be restored by dividing their own rescale ratio: Â=Â^′/φ̂ₗ. Through this process, while Gaussian attributes share the same per-channel quantization range and bit width, the value ranges of attributes from less important Gaussians are narrowed down, equivalent to being quantized at a lower precision. When combined with subsequent video coding, this strategy plays a role analogous to the rate–distortion optimization process in video codecs, while requiring no major modifications to existing codec architectures.

It is worth noting that Gaussians assigned to the lowest importance level are permanently discarded, as their attributes are multiplied by zero and can no longer be restored. This process is equivalent to pruning and can be controlled by adjusting a predefined lowest importance ratio, which in turn determines the corresponding score threshold φₜₕᵣₑₛ.

Generalized Importance Score Estimator: We now explain how to train a generalized score estimator to predict the aforementioned importance score φ. The score estimator we propose takes features that describe each primitive’s spatial and temporal properties as input, and outputs a per-point predicted importance score.

We extract seven feature types from each 4D primitive: the average KNN distance d, computed at the midpoint of its uniform linear motion; the 4D Gaussian scales (sₓ,s_y,s_z,sₜ); the 4D volume V=sₓs_ys_zsₜ; the opacity α; the color anisotropy A, defined as the ratio of color variance to squared mean over M sampled directions on the bounding sphere; the motion magnitude v; and the lifespan T, measured as the temporal interval where the opacity decay σ(t) exceeds a threshold τ. Given the resulting 10-channel feature set {d,sₓ,s_y,s_z,sₜ,V,α,A,v,T} and the K nearest neighbors of each Gaussian, we standardize each feature both globally across all features and locally within its neighborhood, and concatenate the resulting features to feed into the score estimator.

With the input of the score estimator prepared, we then obtain the corresponding supervision by training per-point importance scores in a rate-distortion optimization manner on the training dataset. Specifically, we assign a sigmoid function constrained importance score φˢ∈(0,1) to each Gaussian. Based on the score, we proceed simulation of importance-based adaptive quantization, where the quantization step size Δ is defined as:

Δ(φˢ)=Δ₀/φˢ

(4)

Here, Δ₀ denotes the base quantization step size. Through this design, Gaussians have their quantization step size adjusted according to their respective importance score, effectively simulating the possible perturbation caused by adaptive quantization. Additionally, the least important Gaussian attributes will all be quantized to zero to faithfully simulate the effect of discarding them. Quantization is simulated using a straight-through estimator (STE) to enable gradient propagation, as quantization is inherently a discrete operation.

For optimization, we introduce a rendering quality loss to preserve representation accuracy, as defined in Eq. (5), and a sparsity loss to encourage smaller importance scores, defined in Eq. (6). The two terms formulate a rate–distortion joint training objective, enabling to learn rate–distortion–efficient importance scores as supervisions.

L_render=\lVertI-I_gt\rVert₁+λ_dssim(1-SSIM(I,I_gt)).

(5)

L_sparcity=1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^Nφᵢˢ,

(6)

With both the input features and supervision scores prepared, we train a lightweight MLP as a score estimator on the training scenes. Once trained, the estimator generalizes well to unseen scenes, producing accurate and robust importance scores efficiently to guide importance-based adaptive quantization.

III-CMotion- and Importance-Aware Packing

Based on 4D primitives’ predicted importance and their spatial-temporal properties, we propose Importance-based Packing and Motion-Aware Packing to make 4DGS attributes more amendable for existing codecs.

Importance-based Packing: During importance-based adaptive quantization, the distortion-robust Gaussian attributes are rescaled. Therefore, attributes at different importance levels exhibit distinct statistical distributions. This necessitates separate handling when reorganizing 4DGS attributes into 2D attribute maps for image and video coding. Specifically, we apply Morton sorting to the trajectory centers μ̄_3D of 4DGS within each importance level, evaluated at the time of maximum opacity. After obtaining the 1D Morton order for each level, we concatenate them into a unified 1D ordering. Based on this ordering, we reorganize 4DGS attributes into a 2D pixel grid using row-major layout, which balances packing efficiency and spatial locality. Finally, the reorganized 2D maps of distortion-sensitive attributes are compressed using PNG. For distortion-robust attributes, higher-order SH maps are concatenated into a multi-frame video, while opacity and zeroth-order SH maps form single-frame videos; both are compressed using HEVC via FFmpeg.   Through this design, Gaussians of different importance levels are placed in separate regions, allowing less important attributes’ region to be smoother and easier for video codes to encode. It is worth noting that the importance map, doesn’t have to be encoded and transmitted for restoring the rescaled attribute values. Instead, thanks to the reorganization method described above, it suffices to store and transmit only the coordinates of the L-2 pixels that mark the boundaries between the L-1 regions in the importance map, along with the L-1 regions corresponding rescale ratio φ̂ₗ.

Motion-Aware Packing: To exploit the spatial-temporal characteristics of 4DGS for compression, we analyze the motion statistics of 4D primitives and observe a Laplacian-like distribution: most Gaussians exhibit near-zero motion, while only a small fraction move rapidly. Further analysis reveals a consistent difference in attribute distributions between these two groups. For example, Fig. 3 shows that the high-order spherical harmonics coefficients (shN) of dynamic Gaussians lie in a significantly narrower range than those of near-static ones. This is because dynamic Gaussians are observed under fewer stable view directions, which suppresses high-frequency angular variations. This observation generalizes to other attribute channels like zero-order spherical harmonics and the imaginary parts of both quaternions.   Based on this observation, we partition 4DGS into near-static Gaussians, whose motion magnitudes along all axes are below a threshold vₜₕ, and dynamic Gaussians, where at least one axis exceeds this threshold. We then apply motion-aware packing by processing these two groups independently. Each group is reorganized into separate attribute maps and quantized using group-specific minimum and maximum values, while sharing the same bit width. As dynamic Gaussians occupy a smaller value range, this strategy effectively increases quantization precision, leading to improved rate-distortion performance without additional cost.

IV Experiments

IV-AExperiment Settings

Datasets: For training, we select three representative scenes in the MeetRoom [7] dataset to reconstruct 4DGS and derive per-point importance scores, serving as the supervision targets for the importance score estimator. For evaluation, we conduct experiments on the Neural 3D Video [8] dataset, using the initial 300 frames of each scene for all evaluations.

Implementation Details: We adopt the official implementation of 4DGS [15] to train 4DGS models on the two datasets. Notably, we do not employ the extremely redundant temporal spherical harmonics proposed in the original work. Instead, we use 48 channel spherical harmonics following Inria 3DGS [5] and are able to reproduce the reported rendering quality. After obtaining the per-point importance scores as supervision, we train an MLP-based score estimator, whose layer dimensions are [256, 128, 64, 64, 32], to regress importance values. We set the number of importance levels L to 5 in our experiments.

Baselines: Post-training compression for 4DGS remains largely unexplored, and no dedicated baselines currently exist. To enable a comprehensive evaluation, we compare our method against two categories of approaches. (1) Post-training compression methods. We include D-FCGS [18], a post-training compression framework designed for dynamic Gaussian representations that operates on per-frame 3DGS sequences rather than 4DGS. We further adapt representative 3D or 4D compression methods to the post-training setting to compress the same 4DGS data for fair comparison. Specifically, we consider 4DGS-1K PC, adapted from 4DGS-1K [17] by removing the post-pruning fine-tuning stage, and SOGS [10], which we extend to 4DGS by sorting 4D Gaussians into 2D image layouts using its proposed sorting strategy. (2) Optimization-based compression methods. We also compare with approaches that integrate compression into the reconstruction pipeline, including MEGA [19], 4DGS-1K [17], Spacetime Gaussians [9], and the original 4DGS [15] as a reference. These methods jointly optimize reconstruction and compression through end-to-end training or extensive per-scene fine-tuning, whereas our approach focuses on post-training compression without retraining.

IV-BComparison with State-of-the-Art Methods

Table IV reports rate–distortion (RD) performance in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS, together with rendering FPS and encoding/decoding time on the Neural 3D Video dataset. Fig. 4 further shows PSNR–bitrate and encoding-time comparisons. Our method achieves superior RD performance over most post-training compression approaches while requiring substantially less encoding time. Compared with state-of-the-art optimization-based methods such as MEGA, our approach attains comparable RD performance while delivering significantly higher rendering FPS, as it avoids feature decoding during rendering. Moreover, our method is more flexible across devices with different GPU memory budgets, since the MLP-based importance prediction does not require processing all Gaussians simultaneously, unlike rendering-based scoring methods. Qualitative results in Fig. 5 further demonstrate that our method preserves visual quality comparable to the 4DGS baseline while achieving a 33× compression ratio.

IV-CAblation Study

To assess the effectiveness of our method, we perform ablation studies on the Neural 3D Video dataset focusing on the following three components:

Generalized Score Estimator: We assess our score estimator based on pruning guidance effectiveness, GPU memory usage, and computational time. We first compare our generalized importance score with the spatiotemporal variation score proposed in 4DGS-1K, which requires rendering all training views and computing importance from opacity and lifespan. Fig. 6(a) shows the PSNR–pruning ratio curves, where our approach achieves better performance using an efficient, generalizable importance estimator. Note that here we set our importance level number L to 2 for fair comparison with 4DGS-1K.

Next, we evaluate the flexibility of our method in terms of GPU memory usage and computational efficiency in Table IV-C, using the Coffee Martini scene with approximately 4.5 million primitives. While 4DGS-1K incurs high GPU memory consumption by loading all active primitives into the rendering pipeline simultaneously, our method allows for flexibly adjusting the input feature batch size to match available device memory. In terms of runtime, our approach completes in 4 seconds, whereas 4DGS-1K requires approximately 3 minutes due to the need to render all training views.

Importance-Based Adaptive Quantization for Attributes: In this section, we evaluate the rate-distortion performance improvements achieved by the proposed importance-based adaptive quantization, as well as the effect of simulating this strategy during the supervision training of the generalized score estimator. The RD comparisons are presented in Fig. 6(b). To assess the effectiveness of adaptive quantization, we compare two settings with different numbers of importance levels: L=2 (Ours w/o Adaptive Quantization) and L=5 (Ours). Our method achieves an approximate 12% bitrate reduction at the highest bitrate point with no PSNR drop, indicating that it effectively removes redundancy among Gaussians while maintaining quality.

Furthermore, we analyze the contribution of adaptive quantization simulation during supervision training. When adaptive quantization is not simulated during training (i.e., only pruning is simulated with L=2), but adaptive quantization is still applied during post-training processing with L=5, a noticeable degradation in rendering quality is observed. This behavior suggests that simulating adaptive quantization during training leads to importance scores that are more robust to adaptive quantization at compression time, thereby alleviating the quality loss introduced by this process.

Motion-Aware Packing: Our separate packing strategy maintains the same quantization bit width for both dynamic and near-static Gaussians. As a result, dynamic Gaussian attributes are quantized with higher precision without introducing additional bit width due to their reduced value range. We further assign a higher QP to the high-order spherical harmonics of dynamic Gaussians when encoded with video codecs to optimize bitrate allocation. This leads to a clear improvement in RD performance, as demonstrated in Fig. 6(b).

V Conclusion

This paper introduces a generalized post-training compression framework for 4DGS that achieves competitive rate-distortion performance with minimal encoding and decoding time. Through importance-based adaptive quantization and motion- and importance-aware packing, guided by a lightweight and generalizable importance estimator, we effectively exploit redundancy in the 4DGS representation. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach delivers a strong rate–distortion trade-off with very short runtime and high flexibility across GPU memory constraints.

Acknowledgment

This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China under Grant 62441223 and 62571485.

（参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：不再逐场景优化，直接把 4DGS 属性排成编解码器友好的 2D 图，秒级压到 1/40。

要点：

  • 把 4DGS 压缩从「逐场景优化问题」改成通用后训练框架，直接复用现有图像与视频编解码器
  • 按高斯重要性做自适应量化，重新分配码率，同时保持与现有 codec 完全兼容
  • 利用 4DGS 的统计特性做运动与重要性感知的打包，把属性重排成编解码友好的 2D 图；压缩率超 40 倍且只需数秒

为什么值得看：动态 3DGS 的存储是部署死穴，能直接吃现成 codec、还能秒级完成，才谈得上流式加载与在线分发。

中文摘要：4D 高斯泼溅能实时高质量渲染动态场景，但存储开销高得难以部署。现有压缩方法多把压缩当成逐场景优化问题，泛化性差，也无法满足低延迟压缩的场景。TETRIS-4DGS 改用通用后训练框架：直接借助成熟的图像与视频编解码器，先按重要性水平对高斯做自适应量化，从而细化码率分配，并保持与现有 codec 完全兼容；再利用 4DGS 的统计特性，提出运动与重要性感知的打包方式，把高斯属性重排成对编解码器友好的 2D 图。实验显示它能在数秒内完成压缩、达到 40 倍以上的压缩率，同时保持较高质量。对需要把动态高斯内容分发到端侧的应用，这种「不训练、只用 codec」的路线工程成本最低。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

TETRIS-4DGS: Efficient Post-Training Compression of 4D Gaussian Splatting

Abstract

4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) has emerged as a powerful dynamic scene representation, supporting real-time high quality rendering but suffers from prohibitive storage overhead. Existing methods typically attempt to solve this by treating compression as a per-scene optimization problem, limiting generalizability and applicability where low-latency compression is required. In this work, we leverage existing image and video codecs and propose a generalized post-training compression framework for 4DGS to address these issues. Specifically, we apply importance-based adaptive quantization to Gaussians according to their importance levels, effectively refining bitrate allocation while remaining fully compatible with existing codecs. To further improve compression efficiency, we utilize the statistical properties of 4DGS and propose motion- and importance-aware packing to reorganize attributes into codec-friendly 2D maps. Our approach can achieve over 40× compression rate in seconds while maintaining high quality, facilitating the practical deployment of 4DGS.

Index Terms:

4D Gaussian Splatting, 4D Gaussian Splatting Compression, Post-Training Compression

I Introduction

With photorealistic and fast rendering, dynamic Gaussian Splatting is a promising pathway toward free-viewpoint video, enabling immersive visual applications. Existing paradigms for dynamic Gaussian Splatting can be categorized into three classes: per-frame 3DGS methods [11, 4], deformable Gaussians with canonical space [13, 16], and 4D Gaussian representations [15, 9]. Practical deployment of dynamic Gaussians requires both efficient rendering and lightweight representation. The former makes canonical-space deformable Gaussians less practical, since neural inference for deformation slows down rendering. The latter makes per-frame 3DGS less attractive due to its large storage footprint. 4D Gaussian representations—exemplified by 4DGS [15]—offer a more favorable balance between rendering efficiency and model compactness.

While striking a balance, 4D Gaussian still suffer from its raw data volume, highlighting the need for effective compression. One line of work reduces the number of parameters per primitive by modifying the representation for compression, as in MEGA and CSTG. However, introducing neural networks into the representation enable memory-efficient representation but increases rendering complexity. Another line of work achieves compression by pruning low-contribution primitives, such as 4DGS-1K and the masking strategy in CSTG. These methods require costly pruning-score computation and fine-tuning. Despite their effectiveness in terms of rate-distortion performance, these methods still treat compression as a scene-specific optimization tightly coupled with 4D Gaussian training. This tight coupling demands costly re-training when the content is not generated using the same training pipeline and becomes impractical for low-latency compression.

We target 4DGS [15] representation and aim to achieve strong rate–distortion performance for 4DGS compression with short encoding and decoding time. As shown in Fig. 1, we propose TETRIS-4DGS, an efficient post-training compression scheme for 4DGS that packs Gaussians into different blocks like Tetris. The key principle behind the scheme is to leverage off-the-shelf standard image and video codecs that are widely available across devices for efficient compression.

4DGS attributes that affect primitive positions are seen as distortion-sensitive and encoded with lossless image codecs, while the remaining majority, distortion-robust attributes are encoded with lossy video codecs. To efficiently compress the latter, we introduce two techniques: 1) importance-based adaptive quantization, and 2) motion- and importance-aware packing. The former achieves adaptive bit allocation across primitives with different importance scores, without modifying the existing video codec implementation. Unlike existing time-consuming importance calculation methods, we train a generalizable importance estimator that predicts importance scores in a feed-forward pass. Guided by the motion statistics and importance of 4DGS, our packing method first partitions primitives into groups and then places primitives from the same group into spatially contiguous regions. This produces codec-friendly 2D attribute maps that can be efficiently compressed by standard video codecs.

Our method achieves over 40× compression ratio while maintaining high visual quality, with only 12s for encoding and 2s for decoding a 300-frame dynamic scene, offering a strong rate–distortion–runtime trade-off.

We extract seven feature types from each 4D primitive: the average KNN distance d, computed at the midpoint of its uniform linear motion; the 4D Gaussian scales (sₓ,s_y,s_z,sₜ); the 4D volume V=sₓs_ys_zsₜ; the opacity α; the color anisotropy A, defined as the ratio of color variance to squared mean over M sampled directions on the bounding sphere; the motion magnitude v; and the lifespan T, measured as the temporal interval where the opacity decay σ(t) exceeds a threshold τ. Given the resulting 10-channel feature set {d,sₓ,s_y,s_z,sₜ,V,α,A,v,T} and the K nearest neighbors of each Gaussian, we standardize each feature both globally across all features and locally within its neighborhood, and concatenate the resulting features to feed into the score estimator.

With the input of the score estimator prepared, we then obtain the corresponding supervision by training per-point importance scores in a rate-distortion optimization manner on the training dataset. Specifically, we assign a sigmoid function constrained importance score φˢ∈(0,1) to each Gaussian. Based on the score, we proceed simulation of importance-based adaptive quantization, where the quantization step size Δ is defined as:

Δ(φˢ)=Δ₀/φˢ

(4)

Here, Δ₀ denotes the base quantization step size. Through this design, Gaussians have their quantization step size adjusted according to their respective importance score, effectively simulating the possible perturbation caused by adaptive quantization. Additionally, the least important Gaussian attributes will all be quantized to zero to faithfully simulate the effect of discarding them. Quantization is simulated using a straight-through estimator (STE) to enable gradient propagation, as quantization is inherently a discrete operation.

For optimization, we introduce a rendering quality loss to preserve representation accuracy, as defined in Eq. (5), and a sparsity loss to encourage smaller importance scores, defined in Eq. (6). The two terms formulate a rate–distortion joint training objective, enabling to learn rate–distortion–efficient importance scores as supervisions.

L_render=\lVertI-I_gt\rVert₁+λ_dssim(1-SSIM(I,I_gt)).

(5)

L_sparcity=1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^Nφᵢˢ,

(6)

With both the input features and supervision scores prepared, we train a lightweight MLP as a score estimator on the training scenes. Once trained, the estimator generalizes well to unseen scenes, producing accurate and robust importance scores efficiently to guide importance-based adaptive quantization.

III-CMotion- and Importance-Aware Packing

Based on 4D primitives’ predicted importance and their spatial-temporal properties, we propose Importance-based Packing and Motion-Aware Packing to make 4DGS attributes more amendable for existing codecs.

Importance-based Packing: During importance-based adaptive quantization, the distortion-robust Gaussian attributes are rescaled. Therefore, attributes at different importance levels exhibit distinct statistical distributions. This necessitates separate handling when reorganizing 4DGS attributes into 2D attribute maps for image and video coding. Specifically, we apply Morton sorting to the trajectory centers μ̄_3D of 4DGS within each importance level, evaluated at the time of maximum opacity. After obtaining the 1D Morton order for each level, we concatenate them into a unified 1D ordering. Based on this ordering, we reorganize 4DGS attributes into a 2D pixel grid using row-major layout, which balances packing efficiency and spatial locality. Finally, the reorganized 2D maps of distortion-sensitive attributes are compressed using PNG. For distortion-robust attributes, higher-order SH maps are concatenated into a multi-frame video, while opacity and zeroth-order SH maps form single-frame videos; both are compressed using HEVC via FFmpeg.   Through this design, Gaussians of different importance levels are placed in separate regions, allowing less important attributes’ region to be smoother and easier for video codes to encode. It is worth noting that the importance map, doesn’t have to be encoded and transmitted for restoring the rescaled attribute values. Instead, thanks to the reorganization method described above, it suffices to store and transmit only the coordinates of the L-2 pixels that mark the boundaries between the L-1 regions in the importance map, along with the L-1 regions corresponding rescale ratio φ̂ₗ.

Motion-Aware Packing: To exploit the spatial-temporal characteristics of 4DGS for compression, we analyze the motion statistics of 4D primitives and observe a Laplacian-like distribution: most Gaussians exhibit near-zero motion, while only a small fraction move rapidly. Further analysis reveals a consistent difference in attribute distributions between these two groups. For example, Fig. 3 shows that the high-order spherical harmonics coefficients (shN) of dynamic Gaussians lie in a significantly narrower range than those of near-static ones. This is because dynamic Gaussians are observed under fewer stable view directions, which suppresses high-frequency angular variations. This observation generalizes to other attribute channels like zero-order spherical harmonics and the imaginary parts of both quaternions.   Based on this observation, we partition 4DGS into near-static Gaussians, whose motion magnitudes along all axes are below a threshold vₜₕ, and dynamic Gaussians, where at least one axis exceeds this threshold. We then apply motion-aware packing by processing these two groups independently. Each group is reorganized into separate attribute maps and quantized using group-specific minimum and maximum values, while sharing the same bit width. As dynamic Gaussians occupy a smaller value range, this strategy effectively increases quantization precision, leading to improved rate-distortion performance without additional cost.

IV Experiments

IV-AExperiment Settings

Datasets: For training, we select three representative scenes in the MeetRoom [7] dataset to reconstruct 4DGS and derive per-point importance scores, serving as the supervision targets for the importance score estimator. For evaluation, we conduct experiments on the Neural 3D Video [8] dataset, using the initial 300 frames of each scene for all evaluations.

Implementation Details: We adopt the official implementation of 4DGS [15] to train 4DGS models on the two datasets. Notably, we do not employ the extremely redundant temporal spherical harmonics proposed in the original work. Instead, we use 48 channel spherical harmonics following Inria 3DGS [5] and are able to reproduce the reported rendering quality. After obtaining the per-point importance scores as supervision, we train an MLP-based score estimator, whose layer dimensions are [256, 128, 64, 64, 32], to regress importance values. We set the number of importance levels L to 5 in our experiments.

Baselines: Post-training compression for 4DGS remains largely unexplored, and no dedicated baselines currently exist. To enable a comprehensive evaluation, we compare our method against two categories of approaches. (1) Post-training compression methods. We include D-FCGS [18], a post-training compression framework designed for dynamic Gaussian representations that operates on per-frame 3DGS sequences rather than 4DGS. We further adapt representative 3D or 4D compression methods to the post-training setting to compress the same 4DGS data for fair comparison. Specifically, we consider 4DGS-1K PC, adapted from 4DGS-1K [17] by removing the post-pruning fine-tuning stage, and SOGS [10], which we extend to 4DGS by sorting 4D Gaussians into 2D image layouts using its proposed sorting strategy. (2) Optimization-based compression methods. We also compare with approaches that integrate compression into the reconstruction pipeline, including MEGA [19], 4DGS-1K [17], Spacetime Gaussians [9], and the original 4DGS [15] as a reference. These methods jointly optimize reconstruction and compression through end-to-end training or extensive per-scene fine-tuning, whereas our approach focuses on post-training compression without retraining.

IV-BComparison with State-of-the-Art Methods

Table IV reports rate–distortion (RD) performance in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS, together with rendering FPS and encoding/decoding time on the Neural 3D Video dataset. Fig. 4 further shows PSNR–bitrate and encoding-time comparisons. Our method achieves superior RD performance over most post-training compression approaches while requiring substantially less encoding time. Compared with state-of-the-art optimization-based methods such as MEGA, our approach attains comparable RD performance while delivering significantly higher rendering FPS, as it avoids feature decoding during rendering. Moreover, our method is more flexible across devices with different GPU memory budgets, since the MLP-based importance prediction does not require processing all Gaussians simultaneously, unlike rendering-based scoring methods. Qualitative results in Fig. 5 further demonstrate that our method preserves visual quality comparable to the 4DGS baseline while achieving a 33× compression ratio.

IV-CAblation Study

To assess the effectiveness of our method, we perform ablation studies on the Neural 3D Video dataset focusing on the following three components:

Generalized Score Estimator: We assess our score estimator based on pruning guidance effectiveness, GPU memory usage, and computational time. We first compare our generalized importance score with the spatiotemporal variation score proposed in 4DGS-1K, which requires rendering all training views and computing importance from opacity and lifespan. Fig. 6(a) shows the PSNR–pruning ratio curves, where our approach achieves better performance using an efficient, generalizable importance estimator. Note that here we set our importance level number L to 2 for fair comparison with 4DGS-1K.

Next, we evaluate the flexibility of our method in terms of GPU memory usage and computational efficiency in Table IV-C, using the Coffee Martini scene with approximately 4.5 million primitives. While 4DGS-1K incurs high GPU memory consumption by loading all active primitives into the rendering pipeline simultaneously, our method allows for flexibly adjusting the input feature batch size to match available device memory. In terms of runtime, our approach completes in 4 seconds, whereas 4DGS-1K requires approximately 3 minutes due to the need to render all training views.

Importance-Based Adaptive Quantization for Attributes: In this section, we evaluate the rate-distortion performance improvements achieved by the proposed importance-based adaptive quantization, as well as the effect of simulating this strategy during the supervision training of the generalized score estimator. The RD comparisons are presented in Fig. 6(b). To assess the effectiveness of adaptive quantization, we compare two settings with different numbers of importance levels: L=2 (Ours w/o Adaptive Quantization) and L=5 (Ours). Our method achieves an approximate 12% bitrate reduction at the highest bitrate point with no PSNR drop, indicating that it effectively removes redundancy among Gaussians while maintaining quality.

Furthermore, we analyze the contribution of adaptive quantization simulation during supervision training.
