When adaptive quantization is not simulated during training (i.e., only pruning is simulated with L=2), but adaptive quantization is still applied during post-training processing with L=5, a noticeable degradation in rendering quality is observed. This behavior suggests that simulating adaptive quantization during training leads to importance scores that are more robust to adaptive quantization at compression time, thereby alleviating the quality loss introduced by this process.

Motion-Aware Packing: Our separate packing strategy maintains the same quantization bit width for both dynamic and near-static Gaussians. As a result, dynamic Gaussian attributes are quantized with higher precision without introducing additional bit width due to their reduced value range. We further assign a higher QP to the high-order spherical harmonics of dynamic Gaussians when encoded with video codecs to optimize bitrate allocation. This leads to a clear improvement in RD performance, as demonstrated in Fig. 6(b).

V Conclusion

This paper introduces a generalized post-training compression framework for 4DGS that achieves competitive rate-distortion performance with minimal encoding and decoding time. Through importance-based adaptive quantization and motion- and importance-aware packing, guided by a lightweight and generalizable importance estimator, we effectively exploit redundancy in the 4DGS representation. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach delivers a strong rate–distortion trade-off with very short runtime and high flexibility across GPU memory constraints.

Acknowledgment

This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China under Grant 62441223 and 62571485.

（参考文献见原文。）

item.title: RDCompGS：把 3DGS 压缩当成率失真优化问题 ｜ RDCompGS: Rate–Distortion Optimization for Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting with Image Codecs
item.description:
一句话：把高斯属性映射成 2D 图后用可微率估计联合优化，BD-Rate 平均降 37.8%（HEVC）/49.3%（JPEG XL）。

要点：

  • 在把高斯属性排成 2D 图交给图像编解码器时，显式引入可微率估计模型，让码率与渲染失真一起进优化目标
  • 平均 BD-Rate 相对基线降低 37.84%（H.265/HEVC）与 49.31%（JPEG XL），渲染质量持平
  • 核心洞察是量化步长变大时率梯度幅值会衰减，需要按压缩条件动态调节率与失真的权重

为什么值得看：「压完画质崩」多半是压缩目标与渲染目标不一致，把率失真放进优化里最省事。

中文摘要：3DGS 渲染又快又好，但存储与传输代价高。把高斯属性映射到 2D 表示可以借用成熟的图像编解码器，问题是这样做之后率失真性能并不能自动对齐渲染质量——压缩优化的目标通常是降低表示误差，而不是降低渲染误差。RDCompGS 显式引入可微率估计模型，把估计码率与渲染失真一起纳入优化，并按不同压缩条件调节二者权重。作者还分析了量化步长增大时率梯度幅值会衰减这一现象，据此设计调整策略。在三个基准数据集上，方法在渲染质量持平的前提下取得平均 37.84%（H.265/HEVC）与 49.31%（JPEG XL）的 BD-Rate 降低；与剪枝结合时收益还能进一步叠加。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

RDCompGS: Rate–Distortion Optimization for Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting with Image Codecs

Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis but requires significant storage and transmission resources. Mapping Gaussian attributes to 2D representations enables efficient compression using mature image codecs. However, Gaussian representations that achieve comparable rendering quality are generally treated similarly during optimization, despite substantial differences in coding rate, leading to limited rate-distortion (R-D) performance after compression. To address this limitation, we propose RDCompGS, a 3DGS compression method that enables overall R-D optimization of Gaussian representations with respect to subsequent coding. A differentiable estimate of the coding rate is incorporated into the R-D optimization with rendering distortion. The rate constraint adjustment model further regulates the R-D trade-off across different compression conditions. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that RDCompGS achieves average Bjøntegaard Delta Rate reductions of 37.84% and 49.31% with H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL, respectively. The estimated rate also shows a strong correlation with the actual bit-rate under different compression conditions.

Index Terms:

3D Gaussian Splatting, 3DGS compression, rate-distortion optimization, image codecs.

I Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [1] is an important approach for novel view synthesis. By representing scenes with explicit anisotropic 3D Gaussians and rendering them through α-blending, 3DGS achieves high rendering quality and real-time performance. 3DGS is an active research topic and is relevant to areas such as autonomous driving, multimedia interaction, virtual reality, cultural heritage digitization, and digital twinning [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. However, representing a 3D scene with 3DGS typically requires millions of Gaussian primitives, leading to significant storage and memory overhead [7, 8]. Existing studies on 3DGS compression mainly focus on two aspects.

The first aspect directly compresses the native 3D Gaussian representation. We broadly classify current approaches into Gaussian parameter and attribute compression [9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17], anchor-based compression [18, 19, 20, 21, 22], and Gaussian primitive compactification [23, 17, 3, 24, 25, 26]. These strategies are not mutually exclusive and are often combined to reduce redundancy.

The second aspect converts 3DGS into 2D representations and compresses them using mature image codecs [27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32]. This direction enables 3DGS compression to directly leverage established coding standards and their existing software and hardware support, providing a practical solution for 3DGS storage and transmission. As shown in Fig. 1, the general pipeline consists of 3DGS generation and compression. The scene is first represented by Gaussian primitives and then mapped into 2D representations for coding.

However, in 3DGS compression through image codecs, Gaussian optimization is usually separated from subsequent coding. Specifically, Gaussian optimization evaluates attributes according to their contribution to rendered views, while subsequent compression is performed considering both the coding distortion and the corresponding bit-rate as the cost. As the result, Gaussian representations with comparable rendering quality are generally treated similarly during optimization even when their coding rates differ substantially. Therefore, the rate-distortion (R-D) performance cannot be optimized for compression if reducing the rendering distortion is the optimization goal. Since the actual bit-rate produced by the codec is also not differentiable, it is not feasible to be directly incorporated into Gaussian optimization.

Moreover, the balance between coding rate and rendering distortion changes across compression conditions. Therefore, applying a single rate constraint to all compression conditions cannot maintain an appropriate R-D trade-off, which limits the R-D performance after compression.

To address the above issues, we propose RDCompGS, a 3DGS compression method that enables overall R-D optimization in which Gaussian generation and subsequent coding are treated as a whole. During Gaussian optimization, rendering distortion and the coding rate associated with subsequent compression are jointly optimized to improve the R-D performance after compression. To incorporate the coding rate into Gaussian optimization, RDCompGS introduces differentiable rate estimation based on the statistical distribution of transformed coefficients and their quantization probabilities. Different from prior approaches that optimize under a prescribed rate or distortion setting, the rate constraint adjustment model characterizes the relative strength of the estimated rate and rendering distortion and adjusts their balance across different compression conditions. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that RDCompGS achieves average BD-Rate reductions of 37.84% and 49.31% with H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL, respectively, while maintaining comparable rendering quality.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows.

  • •

    We consider Gaussian generation and subsequent coding as a whole for 3DGS compression and formulate the compression of Gaussian representations as an overall R-D optimization with respect to subsequent coding.

  • •

    Based on this formulation, we propose RDCompGS, which derives a differentiable estimate of the coding rate from transformed Gaussian attributes and introduces the rate constraint adjustment model to regulate the rate constraint under different coding conditions.

  • •

    We validate RDCompGS on three benchmark datasets using both H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL, showing consistent R-D improvements across different coding conditions. Additional experiments combining Gaussian pruning with image codec compression further confirm the effectiveness of RDCompGS.

    • The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the related work. Section III introduces the proposed method. Section IV reports the experimental results and analysis. Finally, Section V concludes this paper.

    II Related Work

    Based on the Gaussian representation used during compression, we divide existing 3DGS compression methods into two types: compression of 3D Gaussian representations and compression of 3DGS with 2D representations.

    II-ACompression of 3D Gaussian Representations

    We broadly classify methods for compressing 3D Gaussian representations into Gaussian parameter and attribute compression, anchor-based compression, and Gaussian primitive compactification.

    Gaussian parameter and attribute compression reduces storage by making the representation of individual Gaussians more compact while retaining the native 3D Gaussian structure. Representative approaches include quantization, which reduces storage by lowering precision [9, 10, 11, 12, 13], entropy coding based on symbol probabilities to reduce the coded length [14, 15], and spherical harmonics (SH) reduction [17, 16].

    Anchor-based methods reduce 3DGS redundancy by organizing local Gaussians around sparse anchors while exploiting relationships among anchors and their associated attributes. Representative methods include Scaffold-GS [18], HAC [19], HAC++ [20], ContextGS [21], and CAT-3DGS [22], which exploit attribute prediction, contextual dependencies, hierarchical relationships, and spatial correlations for compression.

    Gaussian primitive compactification reduces redundancy by controlling the number or distribution of Gaussians. Representative methods include PUP 3D-GS [23], LightGaussian [17], APNet [3], visibility-based geometry pruning [24], REFINE [25], and SPARE-GS [26]. These methods exploit spatial sensitivity scores, global significance scores, view-dependent masks and Rasterization Weight Sampling, multi-view visibility, rendering-aware importance, and global budget allocation to reduce redundant Gaussians or regulate their spatial distribution.

    Although these methods effectively reduce redundancy in native 3D Gaussian representations, they mainly compress Gaussian primitives in their original representation form. Another direction incorporates 2D representations into 3DGS compression, enabling the use of established image codecs for compression.

    II-BCompression of 3DGS with 2D Representations

    We broadly divide existing 3DGS compression methods based on 2D representations according to when the 2D representation is introduced: during or after the Gaussian optimization process.

    Methods that introduce 2D representations after Gaussian optimization adopt different mapping strategies. LGSCV [27] first applies a 3D Morton scan to order Gaussian primitives and then uses a 2D Morton scan to map them into blockwise 2D maps, which are compressed using H.265/HEVC. To improve performance at medium and low bit-rates, it further applies Principal Component Analysis to SH coefficients and introduces MiniPLAS for local primitive permutation. Zhu et al. [28] propose a Dual-Hilbert scan algorithm that uses a 3D Hilbert curve to preserve spatial locality and a 2D Hilbert curve to map the ordered Gaussian primitives into 2D grids for subsequent H.265/HEVC compression. 3DGCoding [29] sorts Gaussian primitives in z-order according to their positions, maps the quantized attributes onto 2D planes, and compresses the attribute planes of static Gaussians using lossless PNG and those of dynamic Gaussians using H.265/HEVC. V3[32] sorts Gaussian primitives using Morton order, maps Gaussian attributes into video frames, and compresses them using H.264/AVC.

    For methods that introduce 2D representations during Gaussian optimization, CodecGS [30] redesigns the explicit Gaussian representation using progressive tri-plane features and employs a multilayer perceptron to predict Gaussian attributes. The feature plane channels are then concatenated into frames and compressed using H.265/HEVC. Compared with CodecGS, SOG [31] retains explicit Gaussian attributes and directly organizes them into aligned 2D grids using Parallel Linear Assignment Sorting (PLAS).

    Specifically, PLAS improves the local smoothness of the grids by constructing a smoothed target with a Gaussian filter and performing parallel blockwise assignments to update the arrangement of Gaussian primitives. The optimized Gaussian parameters are then quantized and compressed using JPEG XL.

    To summarize, organizing Gaussian parameters into 2D representations provides a structured form that can be compressed using image codecs. However, Gaussian optimization remains separated from subsequent coding, which limits the overall R-D performance.

    III Methodology

    To address the mismatch between Gaussian attribute optimization and subsequent coding and the limitation of using a single rate constraint across different coding conditions, we propose RDCompGS, as shown in Fig. 2. RDCompGS introduces two main components. (a) Differentiable rate estimation constructs a differentiable rate term for Gaussian optimization (Section III-A). (b) The rate constraint adjustment model regulates the influence of the estimated rate under different coding conditions (Section III-B). The weighted rate term is then combined with the rendering distortion for Gaussian optimization (Section III-C). The optimized Gaussian attributes are subsequently compressed using image codecs.

    III-ADifferentiable Rate Estimation Model

    Natural images generally exhibit strong spatial correlation, which is exploited by image codecs to reduce spatial redundancy. PLAS organizes Gaussian attributes into 2D grids and places Gaussians with similar attribute values at nearby positions. As shown in Fig. 3, PLAS improves the spatial correlation of the Gaussian attribute grids, but a difference from natural images still remains. To further reduce redundancy for subsequent compression while maintaining rendering quality, RDCompGS performs overall R-D optimization of Gaussian representations with respect to subsequent coding.

    To incorporate the coding rate into the overall R-D optimization, we introduce differentiable rate estimation for the non-position Gaussian attributes. The non-position attributes are first normalized and transformed using an 8×8 block-based Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), while the position attributes are excluded to preserve scene geometry. The statistical analysis in [33] motivates modeling the transformed coefficients using a zero-mean Laplace distribution. Fig. 4 further shows that the transformed coefficients exhibit distributions that are consistent with the Laplace model.

    Let xᵢ denote the i-th DCT coefficient and bᵢ>0 its scale parameter. The Laplace probability density function is

    p(xᵢ|bᵢ)=1/2bᵢ\exp(-(|xᵢ|)/(bᵢ)).

    		(1)

    For a uniform scalar quantizer with step size Δ, the quantized coefficient is

    qᵢ=round(xᵢ/Δ).

    		(2)

    The probability of obtaining qᵢ is

    Pᵢ=∫_(qᵢ-1/2)Δ^(qᵢ+1/2)Δp(t|bᵢ) dt.

    		(3)

    Under the high-resolution scalar quantization approximation, the probability density is approximately constant within each quantization interval. Therefore, Eq. (3) can be approximated as

    Pᵢ≈Δp(xᵢ|bᵢ).

    		(4)

    Based on self-information, we define rᵢ=-\log₂Pᵢ. Using Eqs. (4) and (1), we obtain

    rᵢ≈\log₂(2bᵢ/Δ)+(|xᵢ|)/(bᵢ\ln2).

    		(5)

    Since the scale parameter bᵢ is unknown during Gaussian optimization, we eliminate it by minimizing Eq. (5) with respect to bᵢ. For xᵢ≠0, the minimizing solution is

    bᵢ^⋆=|xᵢ|.

    		(6)

    Substituting Eq. (6) into Eq. (5) yields

    rᵢ≈\log₂((2e|xᵢ|)/(Δ)).

    		(7)

    To make the rate term differentiable and nonnegative during Gaussian optimization, we define

    rᵢ=\log₂(1+(2e√xᵢ²+ε)/(Δ)), ε=10⁻⁶.

    		(8)

    The estimated rate is obtained by accumulating rᵢ over the DCT coefficients of the non-position Gaussian attributes:

    Lᵣₐₜₑ=k∑ᵢ₌₁^Nrᵢ=k∑ᵢ₌₁^N\log₂(1+(2e√xᵢ²+ε)/(Δ)),

    		(9)

    where N denotes the total number of DCT coefficients included in the rate term, and k is a conversion coefficient that scales the accumulated rate to kbps.

    III-BThe Rate Constraint Adjustment Model

    During Gaussian optimization, the rendering distortion and the weighted estimated rate are jointly used to update the Gaussian parameters. Since the gradient magnitude of the estimated rate varies with the quantization step, a single rate constraint cannot maintain an appropriate balance between the estimated rate and rendering distortion across different compression conditions. As illustrated in Fig. 5, using a single rate constraint provides only limited improvements in the high-bit-rate region. RDCompGS therefore introduces the rate constraint adjustment model to adjust the rate constraint according to the quantization step.

    We first analyze how the quantization step affects the rate gradient that is backpropagated to the Gaussian parameters. According to Eq. (9), the gradient of the estimated rate with respect to the i-th DCT coefficient is

    (∂Lᵣₐₜₑ)/(∂xᵢ)=(2ekxᵢ)/(\ln2 √xᵢ²+ε(Δ+2e√xᵢ²+ε)).

    		(10)

    For a fixed DCT coefficient xᵢ, Eq. (10) shows that increasing the quantization step reduces the gradient magnitude. When

    2e√xᵢ²+ε≪Δ,

    		(11)

    the dependence on Δ can be approximated as

    |(∂Lᵣₐₜₑ)/(∂xᵢ)|∝Δ⁻¹.

    		(12)

    Let θ denote the Gaussian parameters and let x=F(θ) denote the DCT coefficients obtained from the non-position Gaussian parameters. By the chain rule,

    ∇_θLᵣₐₜₑ=J_Fᵀ∇ₓLᵣₐₜₑ,

    		(13)

    where J_F denotes the Jacobian of F(θ) with respect to θ. Since the mapping from the Gaussian parameters to the DCT coefficients does not explicitly depend on Δ, the dependence of ∇_θLᵣₐₜₑ on the quantization step is introduced through ∇ₓLᵣₐₜₑ. According to Eq. (12), the rate gradient with respect to the Gaussian parameters therefore approximately satisfies

    ∇_θLᵣₐₜₑ(θ,Δ)≈(Δ_ref)/(Δ)∇_θLᵣₐₜₑ(θ,Δ_ref),

    		(14)

    where Δ_ref denotes a reference quantization step.

    To characterize the magnitude of the rate gradient, we define

    G_R(θ,Δ)=\lVert∇_θLᵣₐₜₑ(θ,Δ)\rVert₂.

    		(15)

    The corresponding magnitude at Δ_ref is denoted by

    G_R,ref=G_R(θ,Δ_ref).

    		(16)

    Taking the L₂ norm on both sides of Eq. (14) gives

    (G_R(θ,Δ))/(G_R,ref)≈(Δ_ref)/(Δ).

    		(17)

    The same Gaussian parameters are also updated by the rendering distortion. We therefore define

    G_D(θ)=\lVert∇_θL_D(θ)\rVert₂,

    		(18)

    where G_D denotes the magnitude of the rendering distortion gradient with respect to the Gaussian parameters.

    To characterize the influence of the estimated rate relative to the rendering distortion, we define

    ρ(Δ)=(λᵣₐₜₑ(Δ)G_R(θ,Δ))/(G_D(θ)),

    		(19)

    where λᵣₐₜₑ(Δ) denotes the rate constraint at Δ, and ρ(Δ) represents the relative rate constraint strength with respect to the rendering distortion. The reference value of the relative rate constraint strength is defined as

    ρ_ref=(λ_refG_R,ref)/(G_D(θ)),

    		(20)

    where λ_ref denotes the rate constraint at Δ_ref.

    Combining Eqs. (19), (20), and (17) gives

    (ρ(Δ))/(ρ_ref)≈(λᵣₐₜₑ(Δ))/(λ_ref)(Δ_ref)/(Δ).

    		(21)

    If the rate constraint is adjusted only to compensate for the reduction in the rate gradient magnitude as Δ increases, ρ(Δ) should remain approximately unchanged. However, this does not reflect the different compression requirements across quantization steps. A smaller Δ places more emphasis on rendering quality, whereas a larger Δ requires greater emphasis on reducing redundancy in Gaussian attributes. Accordingly, we let ρ(Δ) increase with Δ as

    (ρ(Δ))/(ρ_ref)=((Δ)/(Δ_ref))^β, β>0,

    		(22)

    where β controls the sensitivity of ρ(Δ) to the quantization step.

    Combining Eq. (22) with Eq. (21), the rate constraint is defined as

    λᵣₐₜₑ(Δ)=λ_ref((Δ)/(Δ_ref))^1+β.

    		(23)

    III-CTotal Training Loss

    Following 3DGS [1], the rendering distortion is defined as

    L_D=(1-λ_dssim)L_L1+λ_dssimL_D-SSIM,

    		(24)

    where λ_dssim=0.2.

    The distortion considered in RDCompGS refers to the rendering distortion defined above, while the distortion introduced by compression is not explicitly modeled in the optimization process.

    Before densification ends, the Gaussian representation is optimized using only L_D. After densification, the estimated rate in Eq. (9) is incorporated into Gaussian optimization using λᵣₐₜₑ(Δ) in Eq. (23). The total training loss is

    Lₜₒₜₐₗ=L_D+λᵣₐₜₑ(Δ)Lᵣₐₜₑ.

    		(25)

    By jointly incorporating the estimated rate and rendering distortion, RDCompGS connects Gaussian optimization with subsequent coding to achieve overall R-D optimization for 3DGS compression. The R-D optimization procedure in RDCompGS is summarized in Algorithm 1.

    IV Experiments

    IV-AExperimental Setup

    IV-A1 Datasets and Evaluation Metrics

    We conduct experiments on three datasets: Tanks and Temples [34], Deep Blending [35], and Mip-NeRF 360 [36]. These datasets contain diverse indoor and outdoor scenes with complex geometry and texture details. We evaluate rendering quality using Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) [37], and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) [38]. The encoded data sizes generated by H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL are used for compression evaluation. The coding performance is evaluated in terms of the Bjøntegaard delta rate (BD-Rate) [39].

    IV-A2 Implementation Details

    The proposed method is implemented in PyTorch. Experiments are conducted on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Ti GPU. During training, PLAS is applied after Gaussian initialization and after each densification step to organize the Gaussian parameters into 2D representations. After the densification stage, differentiable rate estimation is introduced into Gaussian optimization.

    Following the settings in V3[32] and SOG [31], Gaussian attributes are first quantized and then compressed using image codecs. The position attributes are quantized to 16-bit values and split into high and low 8-bit components, which are represented as two three-channel RGB images. The remaining attributes are quantized to 8-bit values. Specifically, the opacity attribute and the w component of the rotation quaternion are represented as single-channel grayscale images, whereas the scale attribute, the xyz components of the rotation quaternion, and the SH coefficients are represented as three-channel RGB images. These attribute images are then compressed using H.265/HEVC [40] (all intra coding) or JPEG XL [41], where the position attributes are encoded losslessly and the remaining attributes are encoded using lossy compression.

    For H.265/HEVC compression, the quantization parameter (QP) values are set to 4, 10, 16, and 22. The corresponding quantization step size Δ is calculated following [42]. Higher QP values are not considered because they cause severe degradation in rendering quality. To determine the JPEG XL distance value, we select 260 3DGS attribute images from the three datasets. The position attribute images are excluded. For each H.265/HEVC QP, we use binary search to determine the JPEG XL distance value that produces the same bits per pixel. The resulting distance values are 0.1005, 0.2157, 0.4511, and 0.9363 for QP values of 4, 10, 16, and 22, respectively. For SOG, the SH attributes are compressed using JPEG XL with quality levels of 95, 90, 70, and 50, while the default compression settings are used for all other attributes. The coefficient k=1/40 is derived from the encoder frame rate of 25 frames per second.

    Based on the parameter analysis conducted on the Truck scene from Tanks and Temples, we set Δ_ref=8, λ_ref=1×10⁻⁷, and β=0.2. Since the Truck scene is used to determine the reference parameters, it is excluded from all subsequent R-D evaluations to avoid potential bias. The exceptions are the validation of the rate estimation model in Section IV-C and the analysis of the rate constraint adjustment model in Section IV-D, where the Truck scene is retained.

    IV-BCompression Performance

    We evaluate RDCompGS by compressing the optimized Gaussian representations using JPEG XL and H.265/HEVC, and compare the resulting R-D performance with SOG. Tables I and II report the results with JPEG XL and H.265/HEVC, respectively. The BD-Rate results show consistent R-D improvements across the three datasets. With JPEG XL, RDCompGS obtains BD-Rate reductions of 30.44%, 60.94%, and 56.55% on Tanks & Temples, Deep Blending, and Mip-NeRF 360, respectively, corresponding to an average reduction of 49.31%. Similar improvements are observed with H.265/HEVC, where the corresponding BD-Rate reductions are 15.44%, 50.48%, and 47.61%, with an average reduction of 37.84%.

    Fig. 6 further compares the R-D performance of SOG and RDCompGS compressed using JPEG XL in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. For PSNR and SSIM, the RDCompGS curves are generally located above and to the left of those of SOG, indicating improved R-D performance across the three datasets, although SOG achieves slightly lower LPIPS in the high-bit-rate region on Tanks & Temples and Mip-NeRF 360.

    Fig. 7 presents visual comparisons on the Train, Playroom, and Bonsai scenes. RDCompGS achieves higher PSNR than SOG with smaller compressed sizes across the three scenes. The enlarged regions further show that RDCompGS better preserves the sky appearance in Train, the paper box details in Playroom, and the floor textures in Bonsai.

    IV-CValidation of Rate Estimation Model

    Having established the R-D improvements, we further evaluate the correlation between the estimated rate and the actual bit-rate. We use 260 non-position Gaussian attribute images generated after PLAS sorting. For each image, the estimated rate is compared with the actual bit-rate obtained by encoding the same image with H.265/HEVC.

    As shown in Fig. 8, the estimated rate exhibits a strong linear correlation with the actual bit-rate across all tested QP values. At QP values of 4, 10, 16, and 22, the Pearson correlation coefficients are 0.997, 0.996, 0.990, and 0.973, respectively.

    IV-DAnalysis of the Rate Constraint Adjustment Model

    The parameter settings of the rate constraint adjustment model are analyzed in this section. The reference quantization step is set to Δ_ref=8. According to Eq. (23), using a relatively large Δ_ref keeps the rate constraint small at small quantization steps, avoiding an excessive rate constraint in the high-bit-rate region. The effects of λ_ref and β are evaluated on the Truck scene, and the selected values are used in the subsequent experiments.

    IV-D1 Selection of λ_ref

    Fig. 9 presents the R-D curves obtained with different λ_ref values. As λ_ref increases, the compressed size generally decreases, showing that a larger rate coefficient places a stronger constraint on the estimated rate during Gaussian optimization. For relatively small λ_ref values, the reduction in compressed size is limited, while the rendering quality remains relatively stable. Increasing λ_ref to 1×10⁻⁷ provides a more evident size reduction without noticeable degradation in the three quality metrics. Further increasing λ_ref results in only limited additional size reduction, while PSNR and SSIM decrease and LPIPS increases more noticeably. Considering these trends, λ_ref=1×10⁻⁷ provides a favorable trade-off between compression efficiency and rendering quality and is therefore adopted in the subsequent experiments.

    IV-D2 Selection of β

    Fig. 10 evaluates the sensitivity of the rate constraint adjustment model to different β values, using Gaussian optimization without the rate constraint as the reference. Clear BD-Rate reductions are observed for all tested settings, while β=0.2 achieves the lowest BD-Rate of -62.31%. Therefore, β=0.2 is adopted in the subsequent experiments.

    IV-ECombination with Gaussian Pruning

    Gaussian pruning can be incorporated into the 3DGS compression pipeline using image codecs. To evaluate RDCompGS under this setting, we first adopt the pruning procedure in LightGaussian and optimize the Gaussian representation using RDCompGS. In this process, pruning reduces the number of Gaussian primitives, while RDCompGS performs R-D optimization of the remaining Gaussian representation with respect to subsequent coding.

    As shown in Table III, the combination of RDCompGS with Gaussian pruning achieves consistent R-D improvements over LightGaussian on all three datasets. The BD-Rate reductions are 38.83%, 67.19%, and 54.54% on Tanks & Temples, Deep Blending, and Mip-NeRF 360, respectively, corresponding to an average reduction of 53.52%. Across different QPs, RDCompGS substantially reduces the compressed size while maintaining comparable or slightly higher PSNR and SSIM, with LPIPS remaining generally comparable to that of LightGaussian. These results demonstrate that RDCompGS remains effective when combined with Gaussian pruning, providing additional R-D gains for the pruned Gaussian representation.

    IV-FAblation Studies

    We conduct ablation studies to evaluate the two main components of RDCompGS, including differentiable rate estimation and the rate constraint adjustment model. Their effects are evaluated separately under H.265/HEVC compression.

    IV-F1 Effectiveness of Differentiable Rate Estimation

    To evaluate the effectiveness of differentiable rate estimation, we remove the estimated rate term from Gaussian optimization while keeping the other settings unchanged. As shown in Table IV, incorporating rate estimation consistently improves the R-D performance across all three datasets, with BD-Rate reductions exceeding 50%. In particular, the reduction reaches 62.32% on Deep Blending, while positive BD-PSNR gains are obtained on all three datasets. These results demonstrate that differentiable rate estimation effectively connects Gaussian representation optimization with subsequent coding, leading to substantial R-D improvements.

    IV-F2 Effectiveness of the Rate Constraint Adjustment Model

    We further evaluate the rate constraint adjustment model while retaining differentiable rate estimation. Specifically, a single rate constraint with λᵣₐₜₑ=1×10⁻⁷ is used across all compression conditions instead of the adjustment model, while the remaining settings are kept unchanged.

    As shown in Table V, the rate constraint adjustment model provides non-negative BD-PSNR gains on all three datasets and improves the overall BD-Rate performance. Although the BD-Rate increases slightly by 0.77% on the Train scene, reductions are obtained on Deep Blending and Mip-NeRF 360, with the latter reaching 5.46%. Averaged over the three datasets, the adjustment model achieves a BD-Rate reduction of 1.76%. These results indicate that the adjustment model provides a more appropriate rate constraint under different compression conditions, leading to a more favorable overall R-D trade-off than using a single rate constraint.

    V Conclusion

    In this work, we revisit 3DGS compression with 2D representations from the perspective of R-D optimization, with the aim of better aligning Gaussian attribute optimization with subsequent coding. We introduce RDCompGS, which combines rate estimation with the rate constraint adjustment model to balance compression and rendering quality under different coding conditions. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent R-D improvements across different codec settings, and RDCompGS remains effective when Gaussian pruning is incorporated into compression with image codecs.

    Future work will further explore joint modeling of coding rate and compression distortion. Extending RDCompGS to dynamic scenes is also an important direction for future research.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：把高斯属性映射成 2D 图后用可微率估计联合优化，BD-Rate 平均降 37.8%（HEVC）/49.3%（JPEG XL）。

要点：

  • 在把高斯属性排成 2D 图交给图像编解码器时，显式引入可微率估计模型，让码率与渲染失真一起进优化目标
  • 平均 BD-Rate 相对基线降低 37.84%（H.265/HEVC）与 49.31%（JPEG XL），渲染质量持平
  • 核心洞察是量化步长变大时率梯度幅值会衰减，需要按压缩条件动态调节率与失真的权重

为什么值得看：「压完画质崩」多半是压缩目标与渲染目标不一致，把率失真放进优化里最省事。

中文摘要：3DGS 渲染又快又好，但存储与传输代价高。把高斯属性映射到 2D 表示可以借用成熟的图像编解码器，问题是这样做之后率失真性能并不能自动对齐渲染质量——压缩优化的目标通常是降低表示误差，而不是降低渲染误差。RDCompGS 显式引入可微率估计模型，把估计码率与渲染失真一起纳入优化，并按不同压缩条件调节二者权重。作者还分析了量化步长增大时率梯度幅值会衰减这一现象，据此设计调整策略。在三个基准数据集上，方法在渲染质量持平的前提下取得平均 37.84%（H.265/HEVC）与 49.31%（JPEG XL）的 BD-Rate 降低；与剪枝结合时收益还能进一步叠加。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

RDCompGS: Rate–Distortion Optimization for Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting with Image Codecs

Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis but requires significant storage and transmission resources. Mapping Gaussian attributes to 2D representations enables efficient compression using mature image codecs. However, Gaussian representations that achieve comparable rendering quality are generally treated similarly during optimization, despite substantial differences in coding rate, leading to limited rate-distortion (R-D) performance after compression. To address this limitation, we propose RDCompGS, a 3DGS compression method that enables overall R-D optimization of Gaussian representations with respect to subsequent coding. A differentiable estimate of the coding rate is incorporated into the R-D optimization with rendering distortion. The rate constraint adjustment model further regulates the R-D trade-off across different compression conditions. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that RDCompGS achieves average Bjøntegaard Delta Rate reductions of 37.84% and 49.31% with H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL, respectively. The estimated rate also shows a strong correlation with the actual bit-rate under different compression conditions.

Index Terms:

3D Gaussian Splatting, 3DGS compression, rate-distortion optimization, image codecs.

I Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [1] is an important approach for novel view synthesis. By representing scenes with explicit anisotropic 3D Gaussians and rendering them through α-blending, 3DGS achieves high rendering quality and real-time performance. 3DGS is an active research topic and is relevant to areas such as autonomous driving, multimedia interaction, virtual reality, cultural heritage digitization, and digital twinning [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. However, representing a 3D scene with 3DGS typically requires millions of Gaussian primitives, leading to significant storage and memory overhead [7, 8]. Existing studies on 3DGS compression mainly focus on two aspects.

The first aspect directly compresses the native 3D Gaussian representation. We broadly classify current approaches into Gaussian parameter and attribute compression [9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17], anchor-based compression [18, 19, 20, 21, 22], and Gaussian primitive compactification [23, 17, 3, 24, 25, 26]. These strategies are not mutually exclusive and are often combined to reduce redundancy.

The second aspect converts 3DGS into 2D representations and compresses them using mature image codecs [27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32]. This direction enables 3DGS compression to directly leverage established coding standards and their existing software and hardware support, providing a practical solution for 3DGS storage and transmission. As shown in Fig. 1, the general pipeline consists of 3DGS generation and compression. The scene is first represented by Gaussian primitives and then mapped into 2D representations for coding.

However, in 3DGS compression through image codecs, Gaussian optimization is usually separated from subsequent coding. Specifically, Gaussian optimization evaluates attributes according to their contribution to rendered views, while subsequent compression is performed considering both the coding distortion and the corresponding bit-rate as the cost. As the result, Gaussian representations with comparable rendering quality are generally treated similarly during optimization even when their coding rates differ substantially. Therefore, the rate-distortion (R-D) performance cannot be optimized for compression if reducing the rendering distortion is the optimization goal. Since the actual bit-rate produced by the codec is also not differentiable, it is not feasible to be directly incorporated into Gaussian optimization.

Moreover, the balance between coding rate and rendering distortion changes across compression conditions. Therefore, applying a single rate constraint to all compression conditions cannot maintain an appropriate R-D trade-off, which limits the R-D performance after compression.

To address the above issues, we propose RDCompGS, a 3DGS compression method that enables overall R-D optimization in which Gaussian generation and subsequent coding are treated as a whole. During Gaussian optimization, rendering distortion and the coding rate associated with subsequent compression are jointly optimized to improve the R-D performance after compression. To incorporate the coding rate into Gaussian optimization, RDCompGS introduces differentiable rate estimation based on the statistical distribution of transformed coefficients and their quantization probabilities. Different from prior approaches that optimize under a prescribed rate or distortion setting, the rate constraint adjustment model characterizes the relative strength of the estimated rate and rendering distortion and adjusts their balance across different compression conditions. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that RDCompGS achieves average BD-Rate reductions of 37.84% and 49.31% with H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL, respectively, while maintaining comparable rendering quality.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows.

  • •

    We consider Gaussian generation and subsequent coding as a whole for 3DGS compression and formulate the compression of Gaussian representations as an overall R-D optimization with respect to subsequent coding.

  • •

    Based on this formulation, we propose RDCompGS, which derives a differentiable estimate of the coding rate from transformed Gaussian attributes and introduces the rate constraint adjustment model to regulate the rate constraint under different coding conditions.

  • •

    We validate RDCompGS on three benchmark datasets using both H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL, showing consistent R-D improvements across different coding conditions. Additional experiments combining Gaussian pruning with image codec compression further confirm the effectiveness of RDCompGS.

    • The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the related work. Section III introduces the proposed method. Section IV reports the experimental results and analysis. Finally, Section V concludes this paper.

    II Related Work

    Based on the Gaussian representation used during compression, we divide existing 3DGS compression methods into two types: compression of 3D Gaussian representations and compression of 3DGS with 2D representations.

    II-ACompression of 3D Gaussian Representations

    We broadly classify methods for compressing 3D Gaussian representations into Gaussian parameter and attribute compression, anchor-based compression, and Gaussian primitive compactification.

    Gaussian parameter and attribute compression reduces storage by making the representation of individual Gaussians more compact while retaining the native 3D Gaussian structure. Representative approaches include quantization, which reduces storage by lowering precision [9, 10, 11, 12, 13], entropy coding based on symbol probabilities to reduce the coded length [14, 15], and spherical harmonics (SH) reduction [17, 16].

    Anchor-based methods reduce 3DGS redundancy by organizing local Gaussians around sparse anchors while exploiting relationships among anchors and their associated attributes. Representative methods include Scaffold-GS [18], HAC [19], HAC++ [20], ContextGS [21], and CAT-3DGS [22], which exploit attribute prediction, contextual dependencies, hierarchical relationships, and spatial correlations for compression.

    Gaussian primitive compactification reduces redundancy by controlling the number or distribution of Gaussians. Representative methods include PUP 3D-GS [23], LightGaussian [17], APNet [3], visibility-based geometry pruning [24], REFINE [25], and SPARE-GS [26]. These methods exploit spatial sensitivity scores, global significance scores, view-dependent masks and Rasterization Weight Sampling, multi-view visibility, rendering-aware importance, and global budget allocation to reduce redundant Gaussians or regulate their spatial distribution.

    Although these methods effectively reduce redundancy in native 3D Gaussian representations, they mainly compress Gaussian primitives in their original representation form. Another direction incorporates 2D representations into 3DGS compression, enabling the use of established image codecs for compression.

    II-BCompression of 3DGS with 2D Representations

    We broadly divide existing 3DGS compression methods based on 2D representations according to when the 2D representation is introduced: during or after the Gaussian optimization process.

    Methods that introduce 2D representations after Gaussian optimization adopt different mapping strategies. LGSCV [27] first applies a 3D Morton scan to order Gaussian primitives and then uses a 2D Morton scan to map them into blockwise 2D maps, which are compressed using H.265/HEVC. To improve performance at medium and low bit-rates, it further applies Principal Component Analysis to SH coefficients and introduces MiniPLAS for local primitive permutation. Zhu et al. [28] propose a Dual-Hilbert scan algorithm that uses a 3D Hilbert curve to preserve spatial locality and a 2D Hilbert curve to map the ordered Gaussian primitives into 2D grids for subsequent H.265/HEVC compression. 3DGCoding [29] sorts Gaussian primitives in z-order according to their positions, maps the quantized attributes onto 2D planes, and compresses the attribute planes of static Gaussians using lossless PNG and those of dynamic Gaussians using H.265/HEVC. V3[32] sorts Gaussian primitives using Morton order, maps Gaussian attributes into video frames, and compresses them using H.264/AVC.

    For methods that introduce 2D representations during Gaussian optimization, CodecGS [30] redesigns the explicit Gaussian representation using progressive tri-plane features and employs a multilayer perceptron to predict Gaussian attributes. The feature plane channels are then concatenated into frames and compressed using H.265/HEVC. Compared with CodecGS, SOG [31] retains explicit Gaussian attributes and directly organizes them into aligned 2D grids using Parallel Linear Assignment Sorting (PLAS).

    Specifically, PLAS improves the local smoothness of the grids by constructing a smoothed target with a Gaussian filter and performing parallel blockwise assignments to update the arrangement of Gaussian primitives. The optimized Gaussian parameters are then quantized and compressed using JPEG XL.

    To summarize, organizing Gaussian parameters into 2D representations provides a structured form that can be compressed using image codecs. However, Gaussian optimization remains separated from subsequent coding, which limits the overall R-D performance.

    III Methodology

    To address the mismatch between Gaussian attribute optimization and subsequent coding and the limitation of using a single rate constraint across different coding conditions, we propose RDCompGS, as shown in Fig. 2. RDCompGS introduces two main components. (a) Differentiable rate estimation constructs a differentiable rate term for Gaussian optimization (Section III-A). (b) The rate constraint adjustment model regulates the influence of the estimated rate under different coding conditions (Section III-B). The weighted rate term is then combined with the rendering distortion for Gaussian optimization (Section III-C). The optimized Gaussian attributes are subsequently compressed using image codecs.

    III-ADifferentiable Rate Estimation Model

    Natural images generally exhibit strong spatial correlation, which is exploited by image codecs to reduce spatial redundancy. PLAS organizes Gaussian attributes into 2D grids and places Gaussians with similar attribute values at nearby positions. As shown in Fig. 3, PLAS improves the spatial correlation of the Gaussian attribute grids, but a difference from natural images still remains. To further reduce redundancy for subsequent compression while maintaining rendering quality, RDCompGS performs overall R-D optimization of Gaussian representations with respect to subsequent coding.

    To incorporate the coding rate into the overall R-D optimization, we introduce differentiable rate estimation for the non-position Gaussian attributes. The non-position attributes are first normalized and transformed using an 8×8 block-based Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), while the position attributes are excluded to preserve scene geometry. The statistical analysis in [33] motivates modeling the transformed coefficients using a zero-mean Laplace distribution. Fig. 4 further shows that the transformed coefficients exhibit distributions that are consistent with the Laplace model.

    Let xᵢ denote the i-th DCT coefficient and bᵢ>0 its scale parameter. The Laplace probability density function is

    p(xᵢ|bᵢ)=1/2bᵢ\exp(-(|xᵢ|)/(bᵢ)).

    		(1)

    For a uniform scalar quantizer with step size Δ, the quantized coefficient is

    qᵢ=round(xᵢ/Δ).

    		(2)

    The probability of obtaining qᵢ is

    Pᵢ=∫_(qᵢ-1/2)Δ^(qᵢ+1/2)Δp(t|bᵢ) dt.

    		(3)

    Under the high-resolution scalar quantization approximation, the probability density is approximately constant within each quantization interval. Therefore, Eq. (3) can be approximated as

    Pᵢ≈Δp(xᵢ|bᵢ).

    		(4)

    Based on self-information, we define rᵢ=-\log₂Pᵢ. Using Eqs. (4) and (1), we obtain

    rᵢ≈\log₂(2bᵢ/Δ)+(|xᵢ|)/(bᵢ\ln2).

    		(5)

    Since the scale parameter bᵢ is unknown during Gaussian optimization, we eliminate it by minimizing Eq. (5) with respect to bᵢ. For xᵢ≠0, the minimizing solution is

    bᵢ^⋆=|xᵢ|.

    		(6)

    Substituting Eq. (6) into Eq. (5) yields

    rᵢ≈\log₂((2e|xᵢ|)/(Δ)).

    		(7)

    To make the rate term differentiable and nonnegative during Gaussian optimization, we define

    rᵢ=\log₂(1+(2e√xᵢ²+ε)/(Δ)), ε=10⁻⁶.

    		(8)

    The estimated rate is obtained by accumulating rᵢ over the DCT coefficients of the non-position Gaussian attributes:

    Lᵣₐₜₑ=k∑ᵢ₌₁^Nrᵢ=k∑ᵢ₌₁^N\log₂(1+(2e√xᵢ²+ε)/(Δ)),

    		(9)

    where N denotes the total number of DCT coefficients included in the rate term, and k is a conversion coefficient that scales the accumulated rate to kbps.

    III-BThe Rate Constraint Adjustment Model

    During Gaussian optimization, the rendering distortion and the weighted estimated rate are jointly used to update the Gaussian parameters. Since the gradient magnitude of the estimated rate varies with the quantization step, a single rate constraint cannot maintain an appropriate balance between the estimated rate and rendering distortion across different compression conditions. As illustrated in Fig. 5, using a single rate constraint provides only limited improvements in the high-bit-rate region. RDCompGS therefore introduces the rate constraint adjustment model to adjust the rate constraint according to the quantization step.

    We first analyze how the quantization step affects the rate gradient that is backpropagated to the Gaussian parameters. According to Eq. (9), the gradient of the estimated rate with respect to the i-th DCT coefficient is

    (∂Lᵣₐₜₑ)/(∂xᵢ)=(2ekxᵢ)/(\ln2 √xᵢ²+ε(Δ+2e√xᵢ²+ε)).

    		(10)

    For a fixed DCT coefficient xᵢ, Eq. (10) shows that increasing the quantization step reduces the gradient magnitude. When

    2e√xᵢ²+ε≪Δ,

    		(11)

    the dependence on Δ can be approximated as

    |(∂Lᵣₐₜₑ)/(∂xᵢ)|∝Δ⁻¹.

    		(12)

    Let θ denote the Gaussian parameters and let x=F(θ) denote the DCT coefficients obtained from the non-position Gaussian parameters. By the chain rule,

    ∇_θLᵣₐₜₑ=J_Fᵀ∇ₓLᵣₐₜₑ,

    		(13)

    where J_F denotes the Jacobian of F(θ) with respect to θ. Since the mapping from the Gaussian parameters to the DCT coefficients does not explicitly depend on Δ, the dependence of ∇_θLᵣₐₜₑ on the quantization step is introduced through ∇ₓLᵣₐₜₑ. According to Eq. (12), the rate gradient with respect to the Gaussian parameters therefore approximately satisfies

    ∇_θLᵣₐₜₑ(θ,Δ)≈(Δ_ref)/(Δ)∇_θLᵣₐₜₑ(θ,Δ_ref),

    		(14)

    where Δ_ref denotes a reference quantization step.

    To characterize the magnitude of the rate gradient, we define

    G_R(θ,Δ)=\lVert∇_θLᵣₐₜₑ(θ,Δ)\rVert₂.

    		(15)

    The corresponding magnitude at Δ_ref is denoted by

    G_R,ref=G_R(θ,Δ_ref).

    		(16)

    Taking the L₂ norm on both sides of Eq. (14) gives

    (G_R(θ,Δ))/(G_R,ref)≈(Δ_ref)/(Δ).

    		(17)

    The same Gaussian parameters are also updated by the rendering distortion. We therefore define

    G_D(θ)=\lVert∇_θL_D(θ)\rVert₂,

    		(18)

    where G_D denotes the magnitude of the rendering distortion gradient with respect to the Gaussian parameters.

    To characterize the influence of the estimated rate relative to the rendering distortion, we define

    ρ(Δ)=(λᵣₐₜₑ(Δ)G_R(θ,Δ))/(G_D(θ)),

    		(19)

    where λᵣₐₜₑ(Δ) denotes the rate constraint at Δ, and ρ(Δ) represents the relative rate constraint strength with respect to the rendering distortion. The reference value of the relative rate constraint strength is defined as

    ρ_ref=(λ_refG_R,ref)/(G_D(θ)),

    		(20)

    where λ_ref denotes the rate constraint at Δ_ref.

    Combining Eqs. (19), (20), and (17) gives

    (ρ(Δ))/(ρ_ref)≈(λᵣₐₜₑ(Δ))/(λ_ref)(Δ_ref)/(Δ).

    		(21)

    If the rate constraint is adjusted only to compensate for the reduction in the rate gradient magnitude as Δ increases, ρ(Δ) should remain approximately unchanged. However, this does not reflect the different compression requirements across quantization steps. A smaller Δ places more emphasis on rendering quality, whereas a larger Δ requires greater emphasis on reducing redundancy in Gaussian attributes. Accordingly, we let ρ(Δ) increase with Δ as

    (ρ(Δ))/(ρ_ref)=((Δ)/(Δ_ref))^β, β>0,

    		(22)

    where β controls the sensitivity of ρ(Δ) to the quantization step.

    Combining Eq. (22) with Eq. (21), the rate constraint is defined as

    λᵣₐₜₑ(Δ)=λ_ref((Δ)/(Δ_ref))^1+β.

    		(23)

    III-CTotal Training Loss

    Following 3DGS [1], the rendering distortion is defined as

    L_D=(1-λ_dssim)L_L1+λ_dssimL_D-SSIM,

    		(24)

    where λ_dssim=0.2.

    The distortion considered in RDCompGS refers to the rendering distortion defined above, while the distortion introduced by compression is not explicitly modeled in the optimization process.

    Before densification ends, the Gaussian representation is optimized using only L_D. After densification, the estimated rate in Eq. (9) is incorporated into Gaussian optimization using λᵣₐₜₑ(Δ) in Eq. (23). The total training loss is

    Lₜₒₜₐₗ=L_D+λᵣₐₜₑ(Δ)Lᵣₐₜₑ.

    		(25)

    By jointly incorporating the estimated rate and rendering distortion, RDCompGS connects Gaussian optimization with subsequent coding to achieve overall R-D optimization for 3DGS compression. The R-D optimization procedure in RDCompGS is summarized in Algorithm 1.

    IV Experiments

    IV-AExperimental Setup

    IV-A1 Datasets and Evaluation Metrics

    We conduct experiments on three datasets: Tanks and Temples [34], Deep Blending [35], and Mip-NeRF 360 [36]. These datasets contain diverse indoor and outdoor scenes with complex geometry and texture details. We evaluate rendering quality using Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) [37], and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) [38]. The encoded data sizes generated by H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL are used for compression evaluation. The coding performance is evaluated in terms of the Bjøntegaard delta rate (BD-Rate) [39].

    IV-A2 Implementation Details

    The proposed method is implemented in PyTorch. Experiments are conducted on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Ti GPU. During training, PLAS is applied after Gaussian initialization and after each densification step to organize the Gaussian parameters into 2D representations. After the densification stage, differentiable rate estimation is introduced into Gaussian optimization.

    Following the settings in V3[32] and SOG [31], Gaussian attributes are first quantized and then compressed using image codecs. The position attributes are quantized to 16-bit values and split into high and low 8-bit components, which are represented as two three-channel RGB images. The remaining attributes are quantized to 8-bit values. Specifically, the opacity attribute and the w component of the rotation quaternion are represented as single-channel grayscale images, whereas the scale attribute, the xyz components of the rotation quaternion, and the SH coefficients are represented as three-channel RGB images. These attribute images are then compressed using H.265/HEVC [40] (all intra coding) or JPEG XL [41], where the position attributes are encoded losslessly and the remaining attributes are encoded using lossy compression.

    For H.265/HEVC compression, the quantization parameter (QP) values are set to 4, 10, 16, and 22. The corresponding quantization step size Δ is calculated following [42]. Higher QP values are not considered because they cause severe degradation in rendering quality. To determine the JPEG XL distance value, we select 260 3DGS attribute images from the three datasets. The position attribute images are excluded. For each H.265/HEVC QP, we use binary search to determine the JPEG XL distance value that produces the same bits per pixel. The resulting distance values are 0.1005, 0.2157, 0.4511, and 0.9363 for QP values of 4, 10, 16, and 22, respectively. For SOG, the SH attributes are compressed using JPEG XL with quality levels of 95, 90, 70, and 50, while the default compression settings are used for all other attributes. The coefficient k=1/40 is derived from the encoder frame rate of 25 frames per second.

    Based on the parameter analysis conducted on the Truck scene from Tanks and Temples, we set Δ_ref=8, λ_ref=1×10⁻⁷, and β=0.2. Since the Truck scene is used to determine the reference parameters, it is excluded from all subsequent R-D evaluations to avoid potential bias. The exceptions are the validation of the rate estimation model in Section IV-C and the analysis of the rate constraint adjustment model in Section IV-D, where the Truck scene is retained.

    IV-BCompression Performance

    We evaluate RDCompGS by compressing the optimized Gaussian representations using JPEG XL and H.265/HEVC, and compare the resulting R-D performance with SOG. Tables I and II report the results with JPEG XL and H.265/HEVC, respectively. The BD-Rate results show consistent R-D improvements across the three datasets. With JPEG XL, RDCompGS obtains BD-Rate reductions of 30.44%, 60.94%, and 56.55% on Tanks & Temples, Deep Blending, and Mip-NeRF 360, respectively, corresponding to an average reduction of 49.31%. Similar improvements are observed with H.265/HEVC, where the corresponding BD-Rate reductions are 15.44%, 50.48%, and 47.61%, with an average reduction of 37.84%.

    Fig. 6 further compares the R-D performance of SOG and RDCompGS compressed using JPEG XL in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. For PSNR and SSIM, the RDCompGS curves are generally located above and to the left of those of SOG, indicating improved R-D performance across the three datasets, although SOG achieves slightly lower LPIPS in the high-bit-rate region on Tanks & Temples and Mip-NeRF 360.

    Fig. 7 presents visual comparisons on the Train, Playroom, and Bonsai scenes. RDCompGS achieves higher PSNR than SOG with smaller compressed sizes across the three scenes. The enlarged regions further show that RDCompGS better preserves the sky appearance in Train, the paper box details in Playroom, and the floor textures in Bonsai.

    IV-CValidation of Rate Estimation Model

    Having established the R-D improvements, we further evaluate the correlation between the estimated rate and the actual bit-rate. We use 260 non-position Gaussian attribute images generated after PLAS sorting. For each image, the estimated rate is compared with the actual bit-rate obtained by encoding the same image with H.265/HEVC.

    As shown in Fig. 8, the estimated rate exhibits a strong linear correlation with the actual bit-rate across all tested QP values. At QP values of 4, 10, 16, and 22, the Pearson correlation coefficients are 0.997, 0.996, 0.990, and 0.973, respectively.

    IV-DAnalysis of the Rate Constraint Adjustment Model

    The parameter settings of the rate constraint adjustment model are analyzed in this section. The reference quantization step is set to Δ_ref=8. According to Eq. (23), using a relatively large Δ_ref keeps the rate constraint small at small quantization steps, avoiding an excessive rate constraint in the high-bit-rate region. The effects of λ_ref and β are evaluated on the Truck scene, and the selected values are used in the subsequent experiments.

    IV-D1 Selection of λ_ref

    Fig. 9 presents the R-D curves obtained with different λ_ref values. As λ_ref increases, the compressed size generally decreases, showing that a larger rate coefficient places a stronger constraint on the estimated rate during Gaussian optimization. For relatively small λ_ref values, the reduction in compressed size is limited, while the rendering quality remains relatively stable. Increasing λ_ref to 1×10⁻⁷ provides a more evident size reduction without noticeable degradation in the three quality metrics. Further increasing λ_ref results in only limited additional size reduction, while PSNR and SSIM decrease and LPIPS increases more noticeably. Considering these trends, λ_ref=1×10⁻⁷ provides a favorable trade-off between compression efficiency and rendering quality and is therefore adopted in the subsequent experiments.

    IV-D2 Selection of β

    Fig. 10 evaluates the sensitivity of the rate constraint adjustment model to different β values, using Gaussian optimization without the rate constraint as the reference. Clear BD-Rate reductions are observed for all tested settings, while β=0.2 achieves the lowest BD-Rate of -62.31%. Therefore, β=0.2 is adopted in the subsequent experiments.

    IV-ECombination with Gaussian Pruning

    Gaussian pruning can be incorporated into the 3DGS compression pipeline using image codecs. To evaluate RDCompGS under this setting, we first adopt the pruning procedure in LightGaussian and optimize the Gaussian representation using RDCompGS. In this process, pruning reduces the number of Gaussian primitives, while RDCompGS performs R-D optimization of the remaining Gaussian representation with respect to subsequent coding.

    As shown in Table III, the combination of RDCompGS with Gaussian pruning achieves consistent R-D improvements over LightGaussian on all three datasets. The BD-Rate reductions are 38.83%, 67.19%, and 54.54% on Tanks & Temples, Deep Blending, and Mip-NeRF 360, respectively, corresponding to an average reduction of 53.52%. Across different QPs, RDCompGS substantially reduces the compressed size while maintaining comparable or slightly higher PSNR and SSIM, with LPIPS remaining generally comparable to that of LightGaussian. These results demonstrate that RDCompGS remains effective when combined with Gaussian pruning, providing additional R-D gains for the pruned Gaussian representation.

    IV-FAblation Studies

    We conduct ablation studies to evaluate the two main components of RDCompGS, including differentiable rate estimation and the rate constraint adjustment model. Their effects are evaluated separately under H.265/HEVC compression.

    IV-F1 Effectiveness of Differentiable Rate Estimation

    To evaluate the effectiveness of differentiable rate estimation, we remove the estimated rate term from Gaussian optimization while keeping the other settings unchanged. As shown in Table IV, incorporating rate estimation consistently improves the R-D performance across all three datasets, with BD-Rate reductions exceeding 50%. In particular, the reduction reaches 62.32% on Deep Blending, while positive BD-PSNR gains are obtained on all three datasets. These results demonstrate that differentiable rate estimation effectively connects Gaussian representation optimization with subsequent coding, leading to substantial R-D improvements.

    IV-F2 Effectiveness of the Rate Constraint Adjustment Model

    We further evaluate the rate constraint adjustment model while retaining differentiable rate estimation. Specifically, a single rate constraint with λᵣₐₜₑ=1×10⁻⁷ is used across all compression conditions instead of the adjustment model, while the remaining settings are kept unchanged.

    As shown in Table V, the rate constraint adjustment model provides non-negative BD-PSNR gains on all three datasets and improves the overall BD-Rate performance. Although the BD-Rate increases slightly by 0.77% on the Train scene, reductions are obtained on Deep Blending and Mip-NeRF 360, with the latter reaching 5.46%. Averaged over the three datasets, the adjustment model achieves a BD-Rate reduction of 1.76%. These results indicate that the adjustment model provides a more appropriate rate constraint under different compression conditions, leading to a more favorable overall R-D trade-off than using a single rate constraint.

    V Conclusion

    In this work, we revisit 3DGS compression with 2D representations from the perspective of R-D optimization, with the aim of better aligning Gaussian attribute optimization with subsequent coding. We introduce RDCompGS, which combines rate estimation with the rate constraint adjustment model to balance compression and rendering quality under different coding conditions. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent R-D improvements across different codec settings, and RDCompGS remains effective when Gaussian pruning is incorporated into compression with image codecs.

    Future work will further explore joint modeling of coding rate and compression distortion. Extending RDCompGS to dynamic scenes is also an important direction for future research.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: Make It Flow：给静态 3DGS 场景里的水面加上运动 ｜ Make It Flow: Animating Water in 3D Gaussian Splatting Scenes
item.description:
一句话：从参考图估 2D 光流、提升成 3D 欧拉运动场，再把运动场直接作用到高斯基元上。

要点：

  • 从参考图像或模型渲染结果估计 2D 光流，再提升为一致的 3D 欧拉运动场
  • 用类似 Cinemagraph 的算法把运动场施加到高斯基元上做形变，生成时间上无缝的循环动画
  • 不需要动态采集、也不需要物理仿真，结果仍保持实时渲染与自由视角浏览

为什么值得看：随手拍出来的 3DGS 场景最缺的就是动起来的水，这条路绕开了高速多视角采集与流体仿真两条重成本路线。

中文摘要：显式 3D 表示让 3DGS 实现了高质量实时新视角合成，但这些方法默认场景是静态的，遇到现实中随处可见的动态现象就失真。人流车流这类相干运动还能通过动态重建捕捉，而流动的水这种高频效应，在随手拍摄条件下根本无法采集——既没有密集多视角，也没有高速采集。作者提出一种在静态 3DGS 场景中「让水动起来」的方法：先从参考图像或模型渲染结果估计 2D 光流，再把它提升为一致的 3D 欧拉运动场；然后用受 Cinemagraph 启发的算法，把该运动场作用于高斯基元使其形变，得到时间上无缝循环的动画。整个流程不需要动态采集也不需要物理仿真，结果保持实时渲染性能与自由视角一致性，同时明显提升感知真实感。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

Make It Flow: Animating Water in 3D Gaussian Splatting Scenes

Abstract

Explicit 3D scene representations such as 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have recently enabled high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis. However, these methods assume static scenes, limiting realism in the presence of dynamic phenomena ubiquitous in real-world environments. While coherent motion (e.g., humans or vehicles) can be captured and reconstructed, high-frequency effects such as flowing water remain intractable under casual capture conditions, where dense multi-view, high-speed acquisition is not feasible. We present a method to animate water in static 3DGS scenes, enabling visually plausible motion without requiring dynamic capture or physical simulation. Our approach estimates 2D optical flow from reference images or model renderings and lifts it into a consistent 3D Eulerian motion field. We propose a cinemagraph-inspired algorithm that applies this motion field to deform Gaussian primitives, producing temporally seamless looping animations. The resulting representation retains real-time rendering performance, significantly enhances perceptual realism, and preserves free-viewpoint navigation within the scene. We evaluate our method on a newly captured dataset of in-the-wild waterfall scenes and demonstrate clear improvements over prior work in dynamic Gaussian splatting and 3D cinemagraph generation in visual quality and computational efficiency.

1 Introduction

Novel view synthesis has significantly advanced the reconstruction and interactive exploration of real-world environments. Recent progress in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [KKLD23] combines the visual fidelity of neural radiance field approaches [MST∗20] with the efficiency of point-based rendering, enabling high-quality real-time rendering even on resource-constrained platforms. Despite these advances, reconstructed scenes remain predominantly static and often fail to capture dynamic phenomena that are essential for visual realism. This limitation is particularly evident in fluid regions, where 3D Gaussian primitives frequently produce temporally inconsistent or structurally unstable reconstructions. As a result, phenomena such as flowing water often appear unnaturally frozen. In this work, we show that introducing plausible motion specifically in these regions can substantially enhance the perceived realism and liveliness of reconstructed scenes.

Recent dynamic Gaussian Splatting methods have made substantial progress toward extending static reconstruction frameworks to dynamic scenes, but primarily focus on explicitly moving foreground objects [LKLR24, WYF∗24, YYPZ24]. In contrast, subtle continuous background phenomena such as rivers or waterfalls remain largely underexplored. Moreover, many dynamic reconstruction approaches rely on multi-view synchronized capture setups, limiting their applicability to casually captured or in-the-wild data. An alternative direction augments static 3DGS reconstructions with synthesized dynamics. While physics-based methods [XZQ∗24] can produce convincing simulations across materials including fluids, they incur substantial computational cost and are difficult to apply in real-time or casual capture settings. Instead of targeting physically accurate simulation, which is often unnecessary for visual realism, we aim to generate visually plausible motion that improves scene perception while remaining efficient.

To this end, we draw inspiration from cinemagraphs, which introduce temporally looping motion into otherwise static imagery and are particularly effective for fluid phenomena in 2D [HCSS21]. Prior work extending cinemagraphs to 3D either combines layered depth representations with neural networks [LCS∗23], resulting in slow rendering and limited free-viewpoint capability, or relies on self-similarity in Gaussian point clouds [LCW∗24], which provides insufficient structure to recover realistic fluid motion. These limitations motivate a more efficient approach for visually plausible water animation in static 3DGS scenes.

Given a 3DGS model and its training views (or alternatively model renderings), we estimate per-view fluid flow with an existing pretrained network [MK22]. Our first contribution is lifting these multi-view estimates into a grid-based 3D Eulerian motion field via depth-based reprojection, refined via static/dynamic voxel hit ratios and view-hit thresholding. Second, we adopt the concept of symmetric warping from 2D cinemagraphs [HCSS21], which is defined for pixels, and reformulate it for 3D Gaussians treated as Lagrangian particles: volume-aware covariance propagation, density-preserving opacity blending, and randomized per-Gaussian temporal offsets replace the feature warping and inpainting used in 2D. The resulting method integrates directly into the 3DGS rendering pipeline, enabling real-time animation of static scenes with low overhead and allowing interactive exploration of dynamically enhanced environments (cf. ).

For evaluation, we introduce a new dataset of seven casually captured 3DGS scenes containing fluid phenomena such as waterfalls. We compare against dynamic Gaussian Splatting [YYPZ24] and recent 3D cinemagraph methods [LCS∗23, LCW∗24] qualitatively and in terms of efficiency. As evident in our video, our method produces more realistic and temporally coherent novel view renderings while remaining computationally efficient.

In summary, we make the following contributions:

  • •

    The first method to animate fluid regions in a static 3DGS scene, without dynamic capture, retraining, or simulation.

  • •

    An efficient, 3DGS-based approach for lifting multi-view optical flow into a 3D Eulerian motion field.

  • •

    A deformation framework for temporally looping, visually plausible fluid animation, integrated into a real-time 3DGS rendering system for interactive exploration of animated scenes.

  • •

    A curated dataset of seven casual scenes with fluid motion.

    • We will release our full implementation, including preprocessing scripts, interactive GUI, and dataset.

    2 Related Work

    Our work extends novel view synthesis by integrating cinemagraph-inspired motion into static 3D scene representations, with a focus on efficient and perceptually plausible fluid animation.

    2.1 Novel View Synthesis

    Early image-based rendering and light field methods [DTM96, GGSC96, LH96] are limited by sparse viewpoint coverage. Neural radiance fields (NeRF) [MST∗20] significantly advanced novel view synthesis, but are expensive to train and render, which motivated more efficient scene parameterizations [FKYT∗22, SSC22, MESK22, CXG∗22]. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [KKLD23] models scenes as anisotropic Gaussians optimized for real-time rasterization and forms the basis of our approach.

    Extensions of both NeRF and 3DGS to dynamic scenes introduce temporal variation either through explicit time-conditioned representations or learned deformation fields [PCPMMN21, PSB∗21, CJ23, FKMW∗23, FYW∗22, LDZY24, YYPZ24, WYF∗24]. These methods achieve compelling results for structured and well-observed motion such as humans or rigid objects, but typically assume controlled multi-view capture setups or availability of strong data-driven priors. Such assumptions restrict their applicability to casually captured or in-the-wild scenes. Moreover, they are less suitable for subtle, continuous background phenomena such as water, where motion is locally smooth, temporally repetitive, and driven more by perceptual consistency than strict geometric reconstruction.

    2.2 Cinemagraphs and Motion Synthesis

    Cinemagraphs and the closely related video textures [SSSE00] introduce looping motion into static imagery while preserving spatial consistency. Early work focused on manual or semi-automatic creation, followed by numerous methods for automatic loop synthesis and fluid animation in videos [LJH13, LFH15, TPSK11]. These techniques have demonstrated that fluid regions such as waterfalls are particularly well-suited for perceptually convincing motion synthesis.

    Recent learning-based approaches extend cinemagraph generation to single-image or sparse-input settings using generative models or optical flow prediction [HHB18, GXG18, EKK19]. More recently, diffusion-based image-to-video models have enabled controllable cinemagraph synthesis with localized motion editing and user-guided spatial constraints [LIM∗26]. While visually compelling, these approaches remain computationally expensive and typically require repeated inference for long-duration or seamlessly looping animations, limiting interactivity and real-time applicability.

    To address this, recent works learn static or quasi-static motion fields that enable efficient looping animations [HCSS21, MK22, HHV∗21]. These approaches are effective for synthesizing fluid motion and form the foundation of our motion generation framework.

    Recent work has further explored lifting cinemagraph synthesis into 3D scene representations. Approaches based on layered depth images or multi-view video synthesis project 2D motion into 3D representations, but remain limited in viewpoint flexibility or reconstruction quality [LCS∗23, MLLS23]. More recent methods leverage neural or Gaussian-based scene representations to synthesize motion directly in 3D [LCW∗24, JMG∗25]. However, these methods often rely on appearance-based similarity, specialized motion priors, or computationally expensive learned pipelines, which work well for their specific application but limit their ability to model coherent directional fluid motion in unconstrained scenes.

    Related approaches also augment static Gaussian scenes with specialized scene dynamics such as snowfall using physics-guided diffusion models [FAEB26], or fluids using physics-based simulation with artificially added fluid particles rather than animating reconstructed water [FFS∗25]. Physics-based methods incur substantial computational cost, require careful per-scene setup, or noticeably alter scene appearance. Recent methods targeting oscillatory scene dynamics, such as swaying vegetation, employ specifically tailored motion models [SHK∗24, LGB∗26, THM∗26]. While effective for such structured oscillatory motion, these assumptions do not readily generalize to fluid phenomena.

    In contrast to dynamic reconstruction, learned 3D cinemagraph approaches and physics-based simulation, we augment static 3DGS scenes using motion derived from 2D flow priors, enabling efficient and controllable fluid animation without reconstructing a fully dynamic scene.

    3 Method

    We propose an end-to-end pipeline for animating fluid regions in a static 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [KKLD23] reconstruction (cf. Fig.1). In contrast to previous methods [LCS∗23, MLLS23], our objective is a complete animated 3D scene observable from arbitrary viewing directions. Besides its real-time rendering capabilities, 3DGS offers an explicit scene representation based on a set of points G with anisotropic Gaussian extent that are straightforward to animate. Specifically, each Gaussian is described by its mean μ∈ℝ³, 3D covariance Σ∈ℝ^3×3, opacity o∈[0,1], and view-dependent color c∈ℝ³ computed from Spherical Harmonics coefficients ∈ℝ⁴⁸. This representation is then optimized from multi-view RGB images I_1,⋯,N with known camera poses. To render an image, 3DGS linearly approximates the perspective projection onto the image plane at a point x (usually μ) [ZPvBG01]:

    J_n, x=\beginpmatrix(f)/(x̂₃)&0&-(fx̂₁)/((x̂₃)²) 0&(f)/(x̂₃)&-(fx̂₂)/((x̂₃)²)\endpmatrixRₙ, with x̂=Rₙx+tₙ

    		(1)

    where x̂ᵢ denotes the i-th component of x̂, (Rₙ,tₙ) the world-to-camera transformation of the n-th view, and f the focal length. Optionally, I_1,⋯,N can be extended by renderings from user defined camera poses. For each pixel p in a rendered image Iₙ, color is accumulated by alpha blending Gaussian contributions:

    Iₙ(p)=∑ᵢ₌₁^McᵢTᵢoᵢgᵢ(p) with Tᵢ=∏ⱼ₌₁ⁱ⁻¹(1-oⱼgⱼ(p)),

    		(2)

    where gᵢ(p) is the i-th Gaussian value at the pixel p. Since our method assumes G and I_1,⋯,N are provided as input, no training modifications and minimal renderer changes (see Sec.3.3.3) are required. In the following subsections, we describe each step in our pipeline for animating fluids in such 3DGS models.

    3.1 Optical Flow Estimation

    To construct a 3D motion field, we first estimate 2D optical flow F_1,⋯,N for each input view. Since the input images are static and non-time-consecutive, conventional optical flow methods [TD20] are not applicable. Instead, following prior cinemagraph approaches [HCSS21, MK22], we employ a specialized neural network trained on fluid motion. For improved controllability and cross-view consistency, the network is guided by user-defined motion hints and segmentation masks.

    We define a set of global 3D motion hints H={(pₗ,dₗ)}ₗ₌₁^L interactively within the 3DGS scene using our GUI. Each hint consists of a 3D position pₗ∈ℝ³ and a motion direction dₗ∈ℝ³, where \lVertdₗ\rVert₂ controls motion strength. Defining hints directly in 3D ensures consistent motion guidance across views. The hints are projected into each camera view using the projection operator πₙ, resulting in sparse 2D flow hints Hₙ={(πₙ(p),πₙ(p+d)-πₙ(p))|(p,d)∈H} that are converted to sparse flow maps:

    Fˢᵖᵃʳˢᵉₙ(x)=\begincasesd/r^H,&if∃ dwith(x,d)∈Hₙ 0,&otherwise\endcases ,

    		(3)

    with a regulation factor r^H=median{\lVertd\rVert₂|(p,d)∈Hₙ} to limit the extent of projected motion hints in screen space.

    To restrict motion to fluid regions, we additionally compute binary segmentation masks S_1,⋯,N for all input images using the promptable segmentation model SAM3 [CGH∗26]. These masks are used both to guide the motion synthesis network and to constrain subsequent 3D motion field fusion. In practice, simple prompts such as “water” or “waterfall” are sufficient for robust segmentation in most scenes. For cases requiring additional user control, we use an interactive segmentation tool [COP∗24].

    Following Mahapatra and Kulkarni [MK22], the sparse flow maps are converted into dense flow maps Fᵈᵉⁿˢᵉ_1,⋯,N via distance-weighted interpolation within the segmented regions (see AppendixA). Finally, a learned flow refinement network takes RGB images I_1,⋯,N, segmentation masks S_1,⋯,N, and dense flow maps Fᵈᵉⁿˢᵉ_1,⋯,N as input to generate high-quality fluid flow maps F_1,⋯,N. We adopt the SPADE-based U-Net architecture of Mahapatra and Kulkarni [MK22] using the implementation and pretrained weights provided by Li et al. [LCS∗23].

    3.2 3D Motion Field

    In contrast to motion estimated from Gaussian self-similarity [LCW∗24], which suits subtle motion such as swaying vegetation but not dense directional fluid flow, or to flow projected onto a single-view layered depth image [LCS∗23], we project multi-view optical flow into the 3DGS scene to obtain a coherent 3D motion field M.

    Depth Rendering.

    In order to reproject 2D optical flow into the scene, depth information is required. To this end, we render depth maps D_1,⋯,N from the 3DGS model for all input views. We compute the depth of each pixel via alpha blending as defined in Eq.2, where the color of each Gaussian is replaced by its depth μ̂₃ (cf. Eq.1). Note that we divide by the final alpha value of the pixel to obtain meaningful depth for semi-transparent pixels. We further highlight that using depth renderings of the underlying 3DGS model aligns the motion field with Gaussians that can be animated.

    Multi-View Reprojection.
