Although Gaussian Splatting can provide real-time rendering, rendering an existing representation is distinct from constructing, updating, or maintaining the scene itself. In this survey, we synthesize current literature, categorize them and provide a connection of current approaches and tools towards an end-to-end pipeline. Explicitly, we categorize GS scene reconstruction into five overlapping families: single-shot generation, dynamic representations, efficiency and compression, streaming and immersive systems, and Gaussian Splatting SLAM. We distinguish render-only throughput from task-specific scene generation, update, tracking, mapping, and optimization costs, and combine controlled sparse-view benchmarking with native evaluations to identify cross-family quality, latency, memory, and update-cost trade-offs.

Keywords:

Gaussian Splatting , 3D Scene Representation , Novel View Synthesis , Neural Rendering , Multi-View Geometry

1 Introduction

Kerbl et al. [19] introduced 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) as an explicit scene representation capable of high-quality interactive novel-view rendering. Subsequent work rapidly extended this formulation beyond static per-scene reconstruction. Deformable 3DGS [67] and 4DGaussians [61] introduced temporal deformation and spatiotemporal representations, while later methods explored feed-forward sparse-view generation [4, 5], efficiency and compression, streaming, and Gaussian-based SLAM. These developments increasingly shift the systems bottleneck from rendering an existing representation toward constructing, updating, transmitting, or maintaining the Gaussian scene. This distinction is important for applications such as free-viewpoint video, immersive media, online mapping, and robotics. In these settings, interactive rendering alone is insufficient when scene construction, temporal updates, or map maintenance remain substantially slower than rasterization.

Several surveys have reviewed 3DGS from broader perspectives. Wu et al. [62] organize the field by 3D reconstruction, editing, and downstream applications; Fei et al. [10] use taxonomies based on characteristics and applications; and Bao et al. [2] examine optimization, applications, extensions, and recurring technical modules. More focused surveys address compression and compaction [1] and robotics [80]. As summarized in Table 1, our focus is different: we organize Gaussian Splatting as a reconstruction pipeline and study which task-specific costs limit real-time deployment.

In this survey, real-time is task specific. We distinguish render-only throughput from scene generation, dynamic or streaming updates, SLAM tracking and mapping, and offline optimization. These quantities are compared only when their unit of work and timing boundary are aligned, as defined in Section2.7.

We formulate real-time Gaussian scene reconstruction from the pipeline perspective illustrated in Figure1. We organize the literature into five overlapping families according to the stage containing the dominant contribution: single-shot generation, dynamic representations, efficiency and compression, streaming and immersive systems, and Gaussian Splatting SLAM. This pipeline-centric view exposes where geometry, pose estimation, temporal updates, memory, and rendering costs arise across otherwise different GS systems.

We summarize the scope, organization, and contributions of this survey as follows:

  • 1.

    Pipeline-centric taxonomy: We organize GS research into five overlapping families according to the dominant stage of the reconstruction pipeline, supported by a compact tag schema for structured comparison (Figures2 and 3).

  • 2.

    Task-specific real-time framework: We distinguish render-only throughput, scene generation, temporal updates, SLAM tracking and mapping, and offline optimization using explicit units of work and timing boundaries (Sections2.7, 4.2 and 4.3).

  • 3.

    Quantitative and algorithmic evaluation: We provide a controlled comparison of compatible sparse-view methods and complementary native evaluations across the remaining families, with explicit comparability boundaries and mechanism-level analysis (Section 6).

  • 4.

    Cross-family synthesis: We connect algorithmic choices to quality, latency, memory, update cost, and deployment suitability, and identify remaining barriers toward end-to-end real-time systems (Section 6 and Section7).

    • 2 Preliminaries

    Figure1 summarizes the end-to-end Gaussian Splatting reconstruction pipeline and where our five taxonomy families intervene. This section fixes terminology and notation, summarizes the core 3DGS representation and rasterization/compositing used for real-time rendering, and defines the training regimes, input/supervision assumptions, and the real-time criterion used throughout. We conclude with a compact tag schema used to structure the taxonomy and method comparisons.

    2.1 Scope and Terms

    We use Gaussian Splatting to refer to modern 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [19]: an explicit set of 3D Gaussian primitives parameterized in world space and rendered by fast (typically differentiable) screen-space splatting with rasterization/compositing. Under this scope, the primary object is a Gaussian scene representation (centers, covariances, opacities, and appearance parameters), and the key efficiency advantage comes from rasterizing a finite set of primitives rather than volumetric ray marching. We do not survey NeRFs [34] as a primary topic. We cite NeRF-related work only when necessary for context (e.g., datasets/metrics) or when a method explicitly transfers radiance-field ideas into Gaussian representations.

    Finally, we use real-time scene reconstruction in a task-specific sense rather than through a universal FPS threshold. Rendering, scene generation, dynamic or streaming updates, and SLAM are evaluated using their corresponding units of work and timing boundaries, as defined in Section2.7.

    2.2 Notations

    Table2 lists the main symbols used in the survey. For dynamic scenes, quantities are indexed by time t and the Gaussian set at time t is denoted Gₜ. Unless stated otherwise, each primitive is represented by (μⱼ,Σⱼ,αⱼ,cⱼ), where cⱼ may be RGB, spherical harmonics coefficients, or learned features depending on the method.

    2.3 Gaussian Representation

    Gaussian Splatting represents a scene as G={gⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^N, a set of N anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives in world coordinates. Each gⱼ is defined by a mean μⱼ∈ℝ³, covariance Σⱼ∈ℝ^3×3 (commonly parameterized via rotation and per-axis scales for stability), opacity αⱼ∈[0,1], and appearance parameters cⱼ. This explicit primitive-based representation enables high-throughput rasterization pipelines compared to radiance-field rendering [19].

    Methods primarily differ in (i) which parameters are optimized vs. predicted, and (ii) how time is modeled. Static pipelines often optimize all parameters per scene with SfM/MVS/depth-based initialization; dynamic extensions introduce time dependence via explicit per-frame parameters, deformation models, or static/dynamic partitions. Online/SLAM-style systems additionally constrain updates to bounded latency and control representation growth via pruning, keyframes, and local refinement.

    Representation complexity and real-time knobs

    Runtime and memory are dominated by the number of primitives N and the appearance bandwidth (e.g., SH degree or feature dimensionality). Dynamic/streaming settings add growth over time, so many systems explicitly regulate N and appearance parameters to meet real-time targets.

    Representation vs. serialization (file formats)

    Gaussian scenes may be stored in different encodings (e.g., PLY-like formats or .splat-style binaries). These typically change serialization/layout and attribute encoding (e.g., quantization, SH/features) rather than the underlying representation {(μⱼ,Σⱼ,αⱼ,cⱼ)}ⱼ₌₁^N.

    2.4 Rasterization

    Given camera intrinsics K and pose T=(R,t), each mean μⱼ projects to

    μ̂ⱼ=π (K,T;μⱼ)∈ℝ²,

    		(1)

    and its 3D covariance Σⱼ induces an elliptical screen-space footprint (2D covariance) Σ^2Dⱼ. Rendering composites projected splats in approximate front-to-back order using alpha/transmittance blending [19]. Modern implementations use GPU tiled rasterization and sorting so only splats overlapping a pixel/tile are processed, which is central to real-time performance [70]. Approximate visibility/sorting can cause artifacts in dense or dynamic regions [20], motivating improved compositing and hardware/system optimizations [73, 52, 12].

    2.5 Training

    We group common regimes by when optimization/learning happens: per-scene/per-sequence optimization (offline fitting), amortized feed-forward generation via pretrained models, and dynamic/online settings where temporal modeling and incremental updates impose bounded-latency constraints. Per-scene optimization fits {(μⱼ,Σⱼ,αⱼ,cⱼ)} for a specific sequence [19]; amortized methods predict Gaussians at inference time (optionally followed by brief test-time refinement) [63, 5, 4, 30]. Dynamic methods often introduce time-dependent parameterizations or deformations and are frequently optimized per sequence [61, 11, 67], while online/SLAM pipelines prioritize training-free or pretrained components at runtime with efficient map maintenance.

    2.6 Inputs and Supervision

    We categorize input modalities as multi-view captures, monocular video, and RGB-D or sensor-augmented streams (e.g., events). Pose assumptions range from known (calibration/SfM) to estimated/refined (tracked or jointly optimized) to pose-free. Supervision is often self-supervised via photometric consistency, but many pipelines incorporate pretrained priors (especially depth/MVS) to stabilize geometry and accelerate initialization.

    2.7 Task-Specific Real-Time Definition

    The term real-time is used differently across Gaussian Splatting methods. Rendering, scene generation, streaming updates, and SLAM correspond to different tasks and should therefore not share a single throughput definition. We use approximately 24 FPS only as a reference for interactive playback, not as a universal threshold for reconstruction or scene updates.

    Let all latency values be expressed in milliseconds. Render-only throughput is defined as

    rFPS=(1000)/(t_render),

    		(2)

    where t_render is the time required to render one frame from an existing Gaussian representation. For a reconstruction or update task, the pipeline latency can be written as

    tₚᵢₚₑ=tₚᵣₑ+tₚₒₛₑ+t_depth/fusion+tᵢₙᵢₜ+t_update+t_render,

    		(3)

    where only stages relevant to the evaluated task are included. The corresponding task throughput is

    R_T=(1000)/(t_T).

    		(4)

    Accordingly, we report scene throughput for feed-forward reconstruction, update throughput for dynamic and streaming methods, and tracking or mapping throughput for SLAM systems. Offline optimization is reported using training or optimization time rather than scenes per second. These quantities are compared only when the task, unit of work, and timing boundary are aligned.

    2.8 Summary of Tags

    To compare methods consistently across our taxonomy, we annotate each paper using a compact tag set capturing input assumptions, regime, temporal scope, and runtime setting. Table3 summarizes the master schema and family-specific extensions.

    3 Methodology

    We survey Gaussian Splatting (GS) research toward real-time scene reconstruction using the task-specific definitions in Section2.7. Our workflow is: (i) collect papers broadly, (ii) apply inclusion criteria aligned with the GS reconstruction pipeline, (iii) assign a pipeline-centric taxonomy with consistent tags, and (iv) interpret reported efficiency using end-to-end-aware conventions.

    3.1 Literature Collection and Inclusion Criteria

    We prioritize recent work (2023–2025) while retaining foundational baselines needed for context (datasets, metrics, and core dynamic/NVS references). Literature was identified primarily through Google Scholar and the proceedings of CVPR, ICCV, ECCV, NeurIPS, and ICLR. Seed queries included Gaussian splatting, Gaussian splatting for SLAM, efficient Gaussian splatting, fast Gaussian splatting, sparse-view Gaussian splatting, and zero-shot Gaussian splatting, together with closely related variants for dynamic reconstruction, streaming, compression, pose-free reconstruction, and real-time reconstruction. Reference lists of relevant papers were also inspected to identify related and foundational work (backward citation snowballing). We include methods whose primary scene representation is an explicit Gaussian-based model (or a direct extension) and that materially affect one or more stages of a GS reconstruction pipeline (initialization/generation, temporal modeling, map maintenance, streaming/delivery, compositing, or tracking-and-mapping). We exclude NeRF-style methods as a primary focus, citing them only when necessary for context or when they explicitly bridge into Gaussian representations. Duplicate versions and works outside the surveyed reconstruction/system scope are excluded; dataset, metric, and foundational papers are retained as supporting references rather than surveyed GS methods. Because the literature search evolved iteratively during preparation of the survey, intermediate retrieval and screening counts were not recorded prospectively and are therefore not reconstructed retrospectively.

    3.2 Tagging and Taxonomy Assignment

    Each paper is annotated using the master tag schema in Table 3 (input/pose/depth cues, regime, temporal scope, runtime setting, and efficiency levers). We assign each method to one primary family based on its dominant contribution, while noting meaningful overlaps when a method intervenes in multiple pipeline stages. The five families in Fig. 2 are constructed to reflect where methods intervene operationally in the end-to-end pipeline (Fig. 1), enabling consistent comparison across tables and sections.

    3.3 Interpreting Performance Claims

    To avoid conflating rendering speed with reconstruction throughput, runtime evidence is interpreted according to the task being measured rather than through a universal FPS or SPS quantity. Render-only results, scene generation, dynamic or streaming updates, SLAM, and offline optimization follow the timing boundaries defined in Section2.7. Results are treated as directly comparable only when the dataset, input protocol, resolution, hardware, unit of work, and timing boundary are sufficiently aligned; otherwise, they are treated as method-specific evidence. When code, pretrained models, or timing scripts are available, we prioritize these artifacts over high-level paper claims for interpreting runtime and memory. For methods evaluated in Section 6, repository configurations, checkpoints, native schedules, and evaluation procedures are used where available to establish the reported operating conditions.

    4 Datasets and Evaluation Protocols

    This section summarizes the datasets, quality metrics, and evaluation protocols used throughout the survey. Runtime comparisons follow the task-specific definitions introduced in Section 2.7.

    4.1 Datasets and Quality Metrics

    Datasets (representative regimes)

    Although datasets are not the main focus of this survey, they strongly influence what claims are comparable. Across the literature, benchmarks cluster into five recurring regimes. (i) Multi-view dome/studio captures provide calibrated multi-camera observations and controlled dynamics, commonly used for high-fidelity dynamic reconstruction (e.g., Technicolor Light Field [45], Neu3DV [27], Replay [48], NeRSemble [22], PKU-DyMVHumans [77], DiVa-360 [32]). (ii) Monocular/handheld sequences emphasize pose uncertainty, motion blur, and in-the-wild dynamics, often inherited from dynamic NeRF benchmarks (e.g., NSFF Dynamic [29], D-NeRF [42], Nerfies [40], HyperNeRF [39]) and more recent GS/video-generation settings (e.g., Splat4D [72]). (iii) Event+RGB settings target fast motion and low-light where conventional frames degrade, using event streams as additional supervision or cues (e.g., Dynamic EventNeRF [44], E-4DGS [11]). (iv) Outdoor/driving/drone captures evaluate scalability and SLAM-like conditions, often with LiDAR/SLAM pose supervision and dynamic agents (e.g., MTGS [28], DroneSplat [53], Wide-Range-4D [66]). (v) Synthetic/physics-based datasets provide controllable dynamics and/or ground-truth structure for stress-testing temporal modeling (e.g., Deep3D Mask Volume [31], PhysGaia [21], Hybrid 3D-4DGS [37], DynaSplat [7]).

    Image fidelity and temporal stability

    Most works report standard per-frame fidelity using PSNR, SSIM [59], and LPIPS [74], typically averaged over time for dynamic sequences. To reflect temporal stability, several papers additionally report flow-warped temporal errors or flow-based temporal discrepancy scores [6]. Some works also use video metrics such as FVD [55], although these are less consistently reported.

    4.2 Task-Specific Runtime Metrics

    Runtime is reported according to the task being measured. Render FPS (rFPS) refers only to rendering an existing Gaussian representation. Feed-forward methods use scene throughput, dynamic and streaming methods use update throughput, and SLAM methods use tracking or mapping throughput. Offline optimization is reported using training or optimization time. These quantities are compared only when they measure the same task under the same timing boundary.

    4.3 Evaluation Protocol

    Quantitative comparisons require aligned datasets, input settings, resolution, hardware, and timing boundaries. When these conditions are not aligned, results are treated as method-specific evidence rather than direct comparisons. We therefore report both quality and runtime together with the experimental conditions under which they were measured.

    5 Taxonomy

    We organize Gaussian Splatting work for real-time reconstruction into five pipeline-centric families, defined by the primary stage a method intervenes in (capture/training, representation, rendering, system delivery, or online estimation). Because many methods are multi-faceted, we allow secondary overlaps but assign each paper a single primary family based on its dominant technical contribution.

    Figure 3 shows the chronological development of representative methods across these families, illustrating how work following 3DGS progressively expanded toward amortized generation, temporal modeling, efficiency, streaming, and online mapping.

    Single-shot / amortized Gaussian generation

    Feed-forward construction of a usable Gaussian scene from one or few images, often using depth/MVS priors or learned regularizers, optionally followed by brief refinement. Poses may be known, refined, or pose-free, but the defining feature is replacing heavy per-scene iterative fitting with amortized inference from limited views.

    Dynamic representations beyond 4DGS

    Methods that treat time as a first-class variable in the scene model (e.g., time-conditioned parameters, deformation/warp fields, key-time primitives, canonical-plus-delta factorization) or explicitly mitigate dynamic failure modes such as ghosting, identity swaps, occlusion/disocclusion artifacts, and temporal flicker. The emphasis is modeling temporal change, not merely delivering or replaying content over time.

    Efficiency and compression

    Works whose central goal is reducing compute, memory, or storage/bandwidth while preserving real-time operation, via levers such as pruning/sparsification, quantization/packing, view-adaptive LoD selection, or system/hardware acceleration. We place a method here when efficiency is the primary objective rather than a side effect.

    Streaming and immersive video systems

    Long-duration capture and interactive free-viewpoint playback under latency/bandwidth constraints, enabled by explicit delivery mechanisms (progressive transmission, caching/tiling/segmenting, rate control, bandwidth-aware loading, or continual update protocols). The core contribution is system delivery and interactivity over time, not new temporal scene parameterizations.

    SLAM with Gaussian Splatting

    Online tracking-and-mapping where camera poses are estimated incrementally and the Gaussian map is updated under bounded latency/compute, typically using keyframes, map maintenance/pruning, robustness to blur/occlusions, and (when relevant) loop-consistency considerations. We place a method here when meeting tracking deadlines and maintaining a bounded-cost map are central to the design.

    6 Quantitative Evaluation and Synthesis

    6.1 Single-Shot and Sparse-View Generation

    For calibrated sparse-view methods, Gaussian construction can be expressed as depth inference followed by unprojection,

    μᵢ(u)=π⁻¹ (u,d̂ᵢ(u);Kᵢ,Tᵢ), (Σᵢ,αᵢ,cᵢ)=H_θ (fᵢ(u)).

    		(5)

    MVSplat [5] estimates d̂ᵢ from a plane-sweep cost volume,

    Cᵢ(u,dₖ)=Agg_m≠i⟨Fᵢ(u),W_m→i(Fₘ;dₖ)⟩, d̂ᵢ=∑ₖsoftmax(Cᵢ)ₖdₖ,

    		(6)

    so geometry is determined primarily by cross-view correspondence. DepthSplat [63] instead augments the multi-view matching representation with pretrained monocular depth features,

    C̃ᵢ=Φ_θ (Cᵢ,Fᵢᵐᵒⁿᵒ),

    		(7)

    before depth regression and Gaussian unprojection. This additional geometric prior corresponds to the highest PSNR/SSIM and lowest LPIPS in table5, but also increases model-stage latency and memory relative to MVSplat. pixelSplat [4] avoids committing directly to one depth by predicting pᵢ(d|u) and differentiably sampling

    dᵢ∼pᵢ(d|u), μᵢ(u)=π⁻¹(u,dᵢ;Kᵢ,Tᵢ).

    		(8)

    Its more flexible treatment of geometric ambiguity is accompanied by the largest construction latency and memory footprint in the controlled experiment. Thus, table5 shows that the mechanism used to estimate μⱼ directly affects both reconstruction quality and construction cost; in this experiment, augmenting multi-view matching with monocular depth features gives the strongest quality, while the lighter cost-volume formulation gives the lowest latency.

    The native methods in table6 remove the calibrated-pose assumption in different ways. Splatt3R [49] extends MASt3R [25] with a Gaussian prediction head, which can be summarized as

    (xⱼ, Δxⱼ, qⱼ, sⱼ, αⱼ, cⱼ)=H_θ(I₁,I₂), μⱼ=xⱼ+Δxⱼ,

    		(9)

    with Σⱼ obtained from the predicted rotation qⱼ and scale sⱼ. The scene is therefore produced directly from an uncalibrated pair without optimizing camera variables. InstantSplat  [9] instead uses dense stereo priors to initialize both geometry and cameras and then performs Gaussian Bundle Adjustment,

    \min_G, {Tᵢ}∑ᵢLₚₕₒₜₒ(Iᵢ,Î(G,Tᵢ)),

    		(10)

    jointly updating the Gaussian parameters and poses. This distinction is visible quantitatively: Splatt3R requires 1.10 s for measured construction/export, whereas InstantSplat uses 16.01 s for initialization followed by 35.02 s of optimization. Hence the former admits a construction throughput, while the latter is an optimization problem whose runtime depends on the refinement budget. In both cases, the much larger decoder-only rFPS reported in table5 remains a separate quantity from the cost of constructing G. Recent feed-forward generalists broaden this regime to unconstrained input views and unified geometry-to-Gaussian prediction, as exemplified by AnySplat and YoNoSplat [18, 68]. These systems relax capture assumptions, but move additional latency and memory pressure into their learned geometry backbones and cross-view fusion.

    6.2 Dynamic Representations

    Let qⱼ and sⱼ denote the rotation and scale parameterization of Σⱼ. Dynamic deformation can then be written as

    (Δμⱼ,Δqⱼ,Δsⱼ)=F_θ(μⱼ,t), μⱼ(t)=μⱼ+Δμⱼ,

    		(11)

    with the predicted rotation and scale determining Σⱼ(t). Deformable-3D-Gaussians [67] uses an MLP deformation field conditioned directly on canonical position and time. 4DGaussians [61] instead obtains the deformation from factorized spatio-temporal features, using a HexPlane-style  [3] 4D encoding followed by a lightweight decoder. Thus, the former places motion complexity in the continuous deformation network, whereas the latter shifts part of it into an explicit space–time feature structure. In table7, both reach similar quality on D-NeRF bouncingballs: 41.38 dB for Deformable-3D-Gaussians and 40.81 dB for 4DGaussians. These values show that both deformation parameterizations can represent the same synthetic motion regime at high fidelity. 4DGaussians additionally renders at 36.03 rFPS in the measured native setup, showing that the deformation representation can remain compatible with interactive rendering after optimization.

item.title: 一套基就够动所有人：用高斯混合形状蒸馏做实时数字人 ｜ One Basis to Animate Them All: Gaussian Blendshape Distillation for Real-Time Avatars
item.description:
一句话：把每帧重型神经解码换成「浅层 MLP 预测系数 + 线性混合」，移动端跑到 60fps。

要点：

  • 发现预训练高斯数字人的动画可被与身份无关的 blendshape 线性组合紧密近似
  • 用浅层 MLP 预测 blendshape 系数再做线性混合，替换逐帧神经解码，且无需重训原始模型
  • 基用 block-local PCA 在渲染感知度量与显存预算下构建；宿主模型的 CPU 动画速度显著提升，移动端达 60fps

为什么值得看：数字人卡在每帧神经推理，线性近似把成本从「跑网络」降到「查系数」，是移动端可落地的那条路。

中文摘要：3D 高斯数字人能快速渲染，但实时动画常被昂贵的神经推理卡住。作者发现一个有用的结构性质：预训练数字人模型的动画结果，可以被一组与身份无关的 blendshape 的线性组合相当接近地近似。据此提出 GALA（Gaussian Animation via Linear Approximation）蒸馏方法：用一个浅层系数预测网络加线性混合，替代每帧的重型神经解码，并且可以直接作用在已有动画架构上、不需要重训原模型。为了兼顾保真度与显存，基的构建采用分块局部 PCA，在渲染感知的度量下、受显存预算约束地挑选。实验验证了这种共享线性结构确实存在，并把宿主模型的 CPU 动画速度大幅提升，使移动端设备上跑出 60fps 的写实 3D 动画成为可能。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

One Basis to Animate Them All: Gaussian Blendshape Distillation for Real-Time Avatars

Abstract

3D Gaussian avatars support fast rendering, however, their real-time animation is often challenged by the costly neural inference. We address this bottleneck and show that the animation of pretrained avatar models can be closely approximated by a linear combination of identity-independent blendshapes. Building on this finding, we introduce GALA (Gaussian Animation via Linear Approximation), a distillation method that replaces per-frame heavy neural decoding with a shallow coefficient predictor and a linear blend. To improve fidelity and reduce memory requirements, we propose to construct the basis using block-local PCA under a rendering-aware metric and a memory budget. Our method learns a shallow MLP network to predict blendshape coefficients and applies to various animation architectures without retraining original models. We validate GALA by accelerating the inference of three distinct avatar models for 3D animation of facial expressions and full-bodies with clothing dynamics. Across these models, our distillation generalizes to held-out identities and reduces CPU animation cost by up to three orders of magnitude while preserving most of the rendering quality. Excellent results of our method confirm the shared linear structure of learned avatar representations and enable highly efficient and accurate animation at frame rates reaching up to 60fps on mobile devices. Project page: https://ramazan793.github.io/gala/

1 Introduction

Recent advances in neural avatars have substantially improved the generation, reconstruction, and animation of photorealistic digital humans. Representations based on 3D Gaussians are particularly attractive because their explicit primitives support efficient rendering [(Kerbl et al., 2023)], and they underlie models for head generation, reconstruction from a single image, and full-body animation with clothing dynamics [(Yu et al., 2025; Fazylov et al., 2025; Kirschstein et al., 2026; Kwon et al., 2026)]. However, efficient rendering does not imply efficient animation. Many models evaluate a substantial neural network at every frame to update Gaussian attributes from expression or pose parameters, and this per-frame computation, which we call the model’s animation path, can dominate inference cost and limits deployment on CPUs and mobile devices.

The cost of neural animation raises the question of how much of the computation performed by a pretrained avatar model is necessary at inference time. The complexity of its nonlinear decoder does not establish that its outputs require an equally complex representation, and deformations across identities may share a compact linear structure even when the architecture and the training objective do not impose one. In this work, we show that the animation outputs of diverse pretrained Gaussian avatar models can be closely approximated by an identity-specific neutral avatar and a linear combination of identity-independent blendshapes, which we obtain by analyzing Gaussian attribute residuals relative to the neutral state across identities and driving signals. Crucially, a basis extracted once from a model also captures the animation of identities excluded from basis construction, since identity-dependent motion is retained through the blendshape coefficients while the deformation basis is shared.

Linear representations have a long history in face and body modeling [(Blanz & Vetter, 1999; Li et al., 2017b)]. More recently, Gaussian blendshape methods have demonstrated efficient photorealistic animation with bases fitted to individual subjects [(Ma et al., 2024; Zielonka et al., 2025)], while systems such as LAM adopt a predefined animation rig [(He et al., 2025)]. Our work investigates a different setting, extracting a reusable basis from a trained model that represents many identities (Table 1). The basis approximates deformations learned by the original network and can be reused for new subjects without reconstructing it, where identity independence refers to sharing within one pretrained model.

Building on this finding, we introduce a Gaussian blendshape distillation strategy, which we call GALA (Gaussian Animation via Linear Approximation). Our method constructs separate bases for Gaussian attribute groups and spatial regions using block-local principal component analysis under a rendering-aware metric, which prioritizes deformations that matter for visual fidelity, and allocates components within a memory budget according to their estimated image-space error reduction per stored byte. A shallow coefficient predictor, conditioned on identity and driving signals, then learns to control the extracted basis, so that animation requires only coefficient prediction and a linear blend added to the cached neutral avatar. The procedure requires no retraining of the original model.

We apply our approach to three existing models with distinct architectures and training objectives, the hosts of our distillation: AGORA [(Fazylov et al., 2025)] for head generation, FlexAvatar [(Kirschstein et al., 2026)] for one-shot head reconstruction, and DynaAvatar [(Kwon et al., 2026)] for full-body reconstruction with clothing dynamics. GALA closely approaches animation accuracy of approximated host models and consistently outperforms other baselines on respective benchmarks. Crucially, our method increases CPU animation speed of host models by up to three orders of magnitude and enables on-device photorealistic 3D animation at 60 fps. Figure 1 illustrates qualitative results of our method. In summary, our contributions are threefold:

  • 1.

    Identity-independent linearization of neural animation. We demonstrate that animation produced by complex pretrained Gaussian avatar networks can be closely approximated using a shared linear blendshape basis that generalizes to identities unseen during extraction.

  • 2.

    A method for basis construction and animation control. We introduce GALA, combining rendering-aware, block-local basis construction under a memory budget with a shallow network that predicts blendshape coefficients from the identity and the driving signals.

  • 3.

    Extensive experimental validation. We apply our method to three existing models for head and full-body animation and demonstrate significant improvements when compared to the state of the art and compact neural baselines.

    • 2 Related Work

    Animatable avatar models. Recent work on photorealistic avatars explores several approaches. 3D-aware GANs trained from unstructured images collections generate heads as triplanes [(Chan et al., 2022)] or Gaussians [(Kirschstein et al., 2024; Hyun & Heo, 2024; Barthel et al., 2025)], and their animatable versions condition generation on the parameters of morphable models through deformation fields or expression branches [(Sun et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2023; Bergman et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2025; Fazylov et al., 2025)]. One-shot reconstruction methods regress an animatable head from a single image, either by using 3D GANs during training [(Deng et al., 2024a; Deng et al., 2024b; Tran et al., 2024)] or by direct supervised reconstruction from tracked video [(Chu et al., 2024; Chu & Harada, 2024; He et al., 2025; Kirschstein et al., 2026)], and diffusion priors pursue the same goal with synthesised supervision [(Taubner et al., 2025b; Taubner et al., 2025a)]. Per-subject methods optimise Gaussian avatars from videos of particular people [(Qian et al., 2024; Giebenhain et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024)]. Work on full-body animation follows similar approaches. One-shot full-body reconstruction methods [(Qiu et al., 2025; Zhuang et al., 2025; Sim & Moon, 2025)] articulate Gaussians by SMPL-X skinning [(Pavlakos et al., 2019)], while DynaAvatar [(Kwon et al., 2026)] adds pose-dependent clothing dynamics using a transformer conditioned on pose history. We apply our approach to two recent host models for head animation AGORA [(Fazylov et al., 2025)], FlexAvatar [(Kirschstein et al., 2026)] and one host model for full-body animation DynaAvatar [(Kwon et al., 2026)], and demonstrate significant improvement of their inference speed.

    Linear face and body models. Linear representations have a long history in modeling human shape and appearance. Eigenfaces represent facial images in a low-dimensional PCA subspace [(Sirovich & Kirby, 1987; Turk & Pentland, 1991)], while active appearance models capture variations in shape and texture [(Cootes et al., 2001)]. Three-dimensional morphable models extend this principle to facial geometry and appearance learned from scans [(Blanz & Vetter, 1999)]. For animation, blendshape models express deformations as weighted combinations of offsets from a neutral shape [(Parke, 1972; Lewis et al., 2014)], and multilinear models disentangle identity and expression variation [(Vlasic et al., 2005; Cao et al., 2014)]. Modern parametric models, including FLAME [(Li et al., 2017b)] and SMPL-X [(Pavlakos et al., 2019)], combine learned shape and corrective blendshapes with articulated skinning to represent expressive faces and bodies; see [Egger et al. (2020)] for a review of 3D morphable face models. These representations provide the driving parameters for the avatar models considered in our work. We show that the resulting neural animation outputs themselves admit a compact linear approximation: an identity-shared blendshape basis over Gaussian attributes, extracted from a pretrained network without direct fitting to scans.

    Photorealistic blendshape models. Recent work extends blendshape representations to photorealistic Gaussian avatars. Methods such as 3D Gaussian Blendshapes [(Ma et al., 2024)], HeadGaS [(Dhamo et al., 2024)], Gaussian Déjà-vu [(Yan et al., 2025)], RGBAvatar [(Li et al., 2025)], GEM [(Zielonka et al., 2025)] and WebAvatar [(Zhan et al., 2026)] learn subject-specific bases over Gaussian attributes or latent features from monocular or multi-view observations. RGBAvatar predicts blending coefficients from tracked expression parameters, while GEM extracts a basis from a trained subject-specific avatar network and predicts its coefficients from images. Similarly, SqueezeMe [(Iandola et al., 2025)] distils per-subject full-body Gaussian avatars into linear corrective bases for efficient headset rendering. These methods establish the effectiveness of linear representations for individual avatars, but require a separate basis for each subject. Fixed-rig approaches such as LAM [(He et al., 2025)] instead support efficient animation through a predefined FLAME-based articulation model. Differently from previous work, our method extracts a shared identity-agnostic blendshape basis from a pretrained neural model. The basis captures deformations learned by that model and is reused unchanged for identities unseen during extraction, extending Gaussian blendshape distillation from individual subjects to models of diverse identities.

    3 Method

    Our goal is to accelerate pretrained Gaussian avatar models (host models) by replacing their per-frame neural decoding with a fast inference based on linear blendshape representations. We first introduce a generic host model and its animation parameters in Section 3.1. Section 3.2 then presents main parts of our method, namely the construction of identity-shared basis and prediction of its coefficients from animation parameters.

    3.1 Preliminaries

    We consider avatar models that represent a subject using n 3D Gaussians rendered by differentiable splatting [(Kerbl et al., 2023)]. Each Gaussian is described by a d-dimensional attribute vector, which includes position, scale, rotation, opacity, and appearance, with additional skinning weights where required. Avatar animation is controlled by parameters derived from parametric face or body models such as FLAME [(Li et al., 2017b)] or SMPL-X [(Pavlakos et al., 2019)]. We denote the animation driving input by θ and its neutral setting by θ₀. For models with temporal conditioning, θ includes the required motion history. An identity descriptor w, either supplied directly or extracted from an input image, remains fixed throughout an animation sequence. We define pretrained host models as A(w,θ)→G∈ℝⁿᵈ, where the output concatenates the attribute vectors of the n Gaussians. Importantly, Gaussian indices in the model output G must have consistent correspondence across variations in identity and animation parameters. This constraint is typically satisfied by existing models which initialize Gaussians on a shared UV grid or template-anchored point [(Kirschstein et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2025; Fazylov et al., 2025; Kwon et al., 2026)].

    3.2 Gaussian Blendshape Distillation

    In this section we present our method that aims to approximate the costly neural animation of the original host model G=A(w,θ) by a simpler model

    Ĝ=A(w,θ₀)+Uc(w,θ),

    		(1)

    where A(w,θ₀) is the representation of a neutral avatar estimated only once per animation sequence, U is a linear basis and c is a vector of basis coefficients. The rest of this section explains our approach to construct the basis U and to efficiently estimate its coefficients c(w,θ). Figure 2 gives an overview of our method.

    3.2.1 Simple PCA basis

    Given a pretrained model A(w,θ) and the neutral pose θ₀, we compute residuals r for a large set of N samples corresponding to identities wᵢ and animation parameters θᵢ as

    rᵢ=A(wᵢ,θᵢ)-A(wᵢ,θ₀).

    		(2)

    We stack the residuals as columns of R=[r₁,…,r_N]∈ℝ^nd×N. A rank-K basis can then be obtained by solving

    \min_U,{cᵢ}∑ᵢ₌₁^N∥rᵢ-Ucᵢ∥₂², U^⊤U=I.

    		(3)

    By the Eckart–Young theorem [(Eckart & Young, 1936)], the solution is the truncated singular value decomposition R≈UΣV^⊤, whose columns of U are the top K left singular vectors of R, with coefficients cᵢ^⋆=U^⊤rᵢ. We refer to this construction as uncentered PCA: residuals are measured relative to each identity’s neutral avatar, and no additional mean offset is introduced. Consequently, zero coefficients recover the neutral avatar exactly.

    Because residuals from different identities are factorized jointly, the resulting basis describes shared animation variation. It can also be applied to identities excluded from extraction, provided that Gaussian indices retain the correspondence specified in Section 3.1. However, this simple construction has three limitations. Attribute groups have different units and scales, global components incur storage costs even for localized deformations, and Euclidean attribute error does not directly reflect rendering quality. We address these limitations through the following modifications.

    3.2.2 Improved PCA basis

    Per-attribute and spatially local decomposition.

    We first separate Gaussian attributes into groups a, each containing dₐ channels, such as position, scale, rotation, opacity, and appearance. Constructing a separate basis for each group avoids coupling attributes with different scales and allows their representation capacities to be selected independently.

    Since animation deformations are often spatially localized, a global basis wastes memory storing components over the entire avatar when only a small region contributes to the motion. Following this intuition, we partition the Gaussians into B spatial blocks using k-means such that the Gaussians within clusters share similar 3D locations. For attribute group a and block j, containing nⱼ Gaussians, we construct a basis

    U_a,j∈ℝ^nⱼdₐ×K_a,j

    		(4)

    with K_a,j components. The complete basis U is formed by assembling these local bases in block-diagonal form after reordering the attributes. Each local component stores nⱼdₐ values instead of ndₐ and encodes a specific spatial region of the avatar. To limit the size of the increased basis U, we reduce the number of components K_a,j in U_a,j allowing the memory budget to be concentrated on regions with significant variations and complex motion, see below.

    Rendering-aware PCA.

    Standard PCA allocates representation capacity to directions with the largest variation in Gaussian attribute space. To prioritize deformations that affect visual quality, we replace the Euclidean reconstruction objective with a rendering-aware quadratic metric. Let I(x) denote an image rendered from Gaussian attributes x, and let J=∂I/∂x. For a small attribute perturbation δ,

    ∥I(x+δ)-I(x)∥₂²≈δ^⊤Hδ, H=J^⊤J.

    		(5)

    The full matrix H is too large to construct. We therefore estimate only its per-Gaussian diagonal blocks within each attribute group by stochastic probing [(Hutchinson, 1989; Bekas et al., 2007)] (Appendix A). The estimate for attribute group a, normalized to unit mean trace per channel, is denoted as Ĥₐ. Applying the same procedure to the landmark positions instead of the image gives Ĥₐˡᵐᵏ. We define the metric of attribute group a as

    Mₐ=αI+βĤₐ+γĤₐˡᵐᵏ.

    		(6)

    The term βĤₐ weights attribute errors by their effect on the rendered image, the ridge term αI with α>0 retains sensitivity to directions that are weakly observed by the renderer, and the optional landmark term (γ>0) adds geometric supervision. Each local basis U_a,j is then obtained by PCA of the residuals of block j in the metric M_a,j (Appendix A). Setting β=γ=0 recovers the simple PCA of Section 3.2.1 within each attribute group and block. Evaluating with projected coefficients c_a,j^⋆=U_a,j^⊤M_a,jr_a,j isolates the approximation quality of the basis from errors introduced by coefficient prediction.

    Memory-budgeted component allocation.

    To maximize visual fidelity under a fixed memory budget, we select the numbers of components K_a,j jointly across attribute groups and spatial blocks. Let λ_a,j,k be the kth squared singular value in the PCA of block j (Appendix A). Since the PCA is computed in the metric M_a,j, λ_a,j,k measures the variation of the residuals explained by component k weighted by its effect on the rendered image. Undoing the per-group normalization of Ĥₐ and the weight β turns it into a value v_a,j,k that is comparable across attribute groups, namely the estimated reduction of the squared image error of Eq. 5 summed over the samples (Appendix A). Given a basis memory budget B and b bytes per stored value, we maximize ∑_a,j∑ₖ₌₁^K_a,jv_a,j,k subject to b∑_a,jnⱼdₐK_a,j≤B, and solve this allocation greedily by adding components in the order of their value per byte, v_a,j,k/(bnⱼdₐ), until the budget is exhausted. This allocates capacity according to estimated visual benefit and storage cost without manually specifying ranks for individual attributes or regions, uses the precomputed spectra and requires no additional rendering.

    3.2.3 Regressing blendshape coefficients

    Projecting a residual of the host model onto the extracted basis provides accurate blendshape coefficients but requires evaluating the original animation network. To avoid this computation at inference time, we train a lightweight predictor

    ĉ=f_φ(w,θ)∈ℝ^K, K=∑_a,jK_a,j,

    		(7)

    which maps animation parameters θ and an identity descriptor w to coefficients of the fixed basis. We optimize parameters φ of a shallow MLP network f_φ, which we refer to as the coefficient network, by minimizing the distillation loss L_dist=∥ĉ-c^⋆∥₂² on the same samples (wᵢ,θᵢ) we use for the basis construction. Appendix E details the architecture and training of the coefficient networks. Identity conditioning allows the same expression or pose to produce subject-specific deformations despite sharing the basis across subjects.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Host models.

    We apply our method to three host models with distinct architectures. AGORA [(Fazylov et al., 2025)] generates heads with a GAN and animates canonical Gaussians with a separate convolutional deformation branch conditioned on FLAME expression and jaw parameters. FlexAvatar [(Kirschstein et al., 2026)] reconstructs a head from a single image and regenerates the attributes of all Gaussians at every frame with a transformer decoder conditioned on a FLAME-derived expression code. DynaAvatar [(Kwon et al., 2026)] reconstructs a full-body avatar with clothing dynamics from a single image and regenerates the Gaussians at every frame with a dynamic transformer conditioned on the current and 15 preceding SMPL-X poses. See Appendix B for more details.

    Implementation details.

    The coefficient network of every host model is a shallow MLP, and for DynaAvatar it also depends on the window of preceding SMPL-X poses that the host model reads. The evaluation protocol of FlexAvatar fits the identity representation w to the input images of every test subject, and our model follows it with a per-subject enrollment that fine-tunes the coefficient network on outputs of the host model. We measure speed as the CPU time of one animation step, i.e. the computation of the Gaussian attributes Ĝ from the animation parameters θ without rendering, on the same desktop CPU for all methods. Appendix D and Table 5 give the settings of every host model.

    Training data.

    Our method generates training data by running host models on samples of their inputs (wᵢ,θᵢ). We take these samples from a subset of the training data of the corresponding host models and use them both to construct the basis and to train the coefficient network. For FlexAvatar we use 1,200 training identities with 8 expressions each, and for DynaAvatar we use frames sampled from its training sequences. AGORA is a generative model, hence we sample 10,000 identities from its latent space and combine each of them with 6 expressions of its training set FFHQ [(Karras et al., 2019)]. The results in Tables 2–4 and Figure 4 are reported for identities excluded from this data.

    4.2 Results

    Comparison to the state of the art.

    We evaluate every distilled model on the benchmark of its host model [(Fazylov et al., 2025; Kwon et al., 2026; Kirschstein et al., 2026)] and denote a host model distilled by our method with +GALA. We adopt metrics from previous publications and measure image quality (FID, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS), the accuracy of expressions, poses and keypoints (AED, AED-jaw, APD, AKD) and the preservation of identity (ID, CSIM). Appendix F defines the metrics and the evaluation protocols.

    Table 2 shows that all three distilled models closely follow their host models and outperform the competing methods on most metrics. For AGORA, FID increases from 3.17 to 3.47, while the animation and identity metrics remain within 0.023 of the host model and are the best (AED-jaw, ID, APD) or second best (AED) among the other animatable models. For DynaAvatar, our model has a 0.64 dB lower PSNR than its host and outperforms all competing methods on all three quality metrics, e.g. by more than 1.9 dB in PSNR. For FlexAvatar, our model obtains the best results on 8 of the 12 quality metrics, including one tie. Only LAM is competitive on portrait animation, where it has a 0.34 dB higher PSNR and the same LPIPS in self-reenactment. On Ava256 single-shot, our model stays within 0.03 dB PSNR of its host, which outperforms the compared one-shot methods by more than 3.8 dB PSNR under its published protocol [(Kirschstein et al., 2026)]. The distilled model therefore retains this lead. With respect to its host, our model stays within 1 dB PSNR in self-reenactment and within 0.03 dB (single-shot) and 0.2 dB (few-shot) on Ava256.

    At the same time, for the three tested host models our method reduces CPU time of their animation steps as 154→5.5ms, 234→4.4ms and 42.9s→6.1ms (16.1ms with skinning included) respectively (Table 5). This corresponds to speed-ups of about ×28, ×54 and ×7,000 times, or ×2,700 times for DynaAvatar when its skinning is included. With an animation step below 7ms on a desktop CPU for all three host models, our method enables real-time animation, even on a mobile phone, for host models that were not capable of it before. AGORA runs at 1 frame per second on the phone, and DynaAvatar, which models garment dynamics, reaches only 0.3 frames per second even on a desktop GPU, whereas our distilled models run at 60 frames per second on the phone (mFPS in Table 2). The video on our project page demonstrates all three distilled models running in the web browser of a mobile phone (Appendix C).

    Qualitative results.

    Figure 3 compares renderings of our method and of the host models for two examples per host model with pronounced facial expressions and body motion, and shows where the errors of our method are located. Our method faithfully reproduces both the facial expressions and the garment motion. With projected coefficients, it reproduces the host models with hardly visible errors in these examples. With predicted coefficients, which add the error of coefficient prediction, the remaining errors are small and localized at thin structures and at the outlines of the silhouettes, such as teeth and glasses for AGORA, mouth interior and hair boundary for FlexAvatar, and garment boundaries for DynaAvatar, and are mainly revealed by the error maps. Appendix J visualizes the local motions captured by individual blendshapes, and Appendix I presents more difficult examples, including a subject for which the coefficient network fails.

    4.3 Ablation Study

    Design choices of the basis construction.

    We evaluate the representation power of our basis, i.e. how well it reconstructs the output of the host model independently of coefficient prediction, by the PSNR between the renderings of our model with projected coefficients c^⋆ and of the host model on held-out identities, at the same memory budget for all compared variants. Table 3a compares our full method with simple PCA, the single global basis of Section 3.2.1 with the rank given by the budget, and with variants that revert one design choice while the others are kept. Simple PCA is 9.7, 11.5 and 13.2 dB below our full method for AGORA, FlexAvatar and DynaAvatar. Most of this gap comes from the two design choices that decide how the memory is spent: a joint basis over all attributes of a block costs 4.7, 3.6 and 8.8 dB, since a joint component stores all d channels instead of dₐ and couples attributes with different scales, and scoring the components by explained variance instead of the value v_a,j,k costs 5.3, 2.7 and 13.3 dB, since explained variance is not comparable between attribute groups with different units and spends most of the memory on attributes with little effect on the image. Rendering-aware PCA itself improves the directions of the basis by a further 0.25, 0.35 and 0.58 dB over Euclidean PCA (β=γ=0) with the same numbers of components.

    Allocation of components.

    Table 4 evaluates the need for allocating the numbers of components K_a,j individually. We compare our greedy allocation (Section 3.2.2) with two simpler rules for the same bases and memory budget: one rank K shared by all attribute groups and blocks, and one rank Kₐ per attribute group shared by all blocks. Table 3a changes the values of the components, whereas here the values are fixed and only the constraints on the ranks change. A single rank reduces PSNR by 6.2, 1.2 and 8.5 dB, since it assigns the same number of components to every attribute group and to every block irrespective of their motion. Individual ranks per attribute group recover a large part of this gap. Our allocation per attribute group and block improves PSNR by a further 3.4, 0.1 and 0.7 dB. Given the values of the components, the greedy allocation requires no tuning and no rendering, and takes a few seconds.

    Number of spatial blocks.

    Table 3b varies the number of spatial blocks B for a fixed basis size. Compared with a global basis per attribute group (B=1), B=32 local blocks improve PSNR by 8.2, 6.9 and 8.6 dB. A component of a local basis stores nⱼdₐ instead of ndₐ values, hence more components fit into the same memory and they can be concentrated in the regions with complex motion. PSNR increases monotonically with B over the tested range, and we use B=32 in all other experiments. For larger B we observed no consistent improvement with predicted coefficients, since more components make the coefficients harder to regress.

    Comparison to alternative distillation.

    To further demonstrate the value of our linear blendshape distillation approach, we compare it to a generic method for neural network distillation. Knowledge distillation [(Bucilă et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015)] trains a smaller student network to reproduce the outputs of a frozen teacher on the inputs of the teacher. We distill students that are thinner and shallower copies of the animation network of corresponding host models. We train students of multiple sizes using the same training data as we use for training our method. Figure 4 compares this standard distillation with GALA for a range of memory budgets. For all three host models, none of the distilled networks approaches our method in terms of speed and accuracy. Additional details of this study are available in Appendix G.

    5 Limitations and Future Work

    While GALA already shows excellent results, its coefficient prediction leaves room for improvement. With projected coefficients c^⋆ our models reproduce their host models closely, whereas with predicted coefficients their PSNR with respect to the host model is lower by 5.7 dB for AGORA and by 12.3 dB for FlexAvatar at a memory budget of 48 MB, and a larger budget mainly improves the results with projected coefficients (Figure 4). Another direction for improvement concerns the spatial partition, which is currently fixed to B=32 blocks for all host models. Meanwhile an optimal partition may depend on the motion and could be selected jointly with the numbers of components K_a,j. Finally, our method inherits the limitations of host models, and our results suggest that avatar models could be trained directly with an identity-shared blendshape basis, which we leave for future work.

    6 Conclusion

    We introduced GALA, which replaces per-frame neural decoding of pretrained Gaussian avatar models with a shallow coefficient network and a linear combination of blendshapes. To the best of our knowledge, GALA is the first method to extract and leverage a blendshape basis shared across identities, whereas previous Gaussian blendshape methods require a separate basis for every subject. We apply GALA to three diverse avatar models for head and full-body animation and demonstrate excellent computational gains while closely preserving the quality of original models and outperforming recent baselines. GALA requires no retraining of original models, it accelerates CPU execution up to three orders of magnitude and enables animation to run at 60 fps on a mobile phone. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and broad applicability of proposed Gaussian blendshape distillation for efficient, high-fidelity on-device avatar animation.

    Appendix

    Appendix A details the estimation of the rendering-aware metric and the construction of the basis in this metric space. Appendix B describes the three host models and Appendix C our mobile demos. Appendix D gives the implementation details of our method, Appendix E describes the coefficient networks, and Appendix F provides the evaluation details, including the evaluation of FlexAvatar on Ava256. Appendix G compares our method with distilled networks. Appendix H compares the distilled FlexAvatar and DynaAvatar models with per-subject blendshape avatars. Appendix I adds qualitative results, and Appendix J visualizes the motions of individual blendshapes. Please refer to the video on our project page for more.

    Appendix A Rendering-Aware Metric and Basis Construction

    Estimation of the rendering Hessian.

    The rendering-aware metric of Section 3.2.2 is based on the Gauss–Newton Hessian H=J^⊤J of the rendered image with respect to the Gaussian attributes, which is too large to construct. We approximate it by its per-Gaussian diagonal blocks within each attribute group, which preserve the interactions among the channels of one Gaussian and one attribute group and discard the interactions between Gaussians and between attribute groups. We estimate these blocks with a stochastic estimator in the spirit of the trace and diagonal estimators of [Hutchinson (1989)] and [Bekas et al. (2007)]. For a random vector ε in image space with entries ±1 of equal probability, one backward pass through the renderer gives

    g=J^⊤ε, 𝔼[gg^⊤]=J^⊤𝔼[εε^⊤]J=J^⊤J.

    		(8)

    For every Gaussian and attribute group a we therefore accumulate the dₐ×dₐ block of gg^⊤ that belongs to the dₐ channels of this Gaussian, and average over identities, animation parameters and cameras of the training samples, with 16 probes per frame. The estimate is symmetrized and normalized to unit mean trace per channel within each attribute group, which gives Ĥₐ. The normalization constant h̄ₐ, the mean trace per channel before normalization, is used again by the allocation of components. The landmark matrix Ĥₐˡᵐᵏ is estimated in the same way, with the Jacobian of the landmark positions in place of J.

    PCA in the metric space.

    For attribute group a and block j, let M_a,j be the restriction of Mₐ of Eq. 6 to the nⱼ Gaussians of the block, and let R_a,j∈ℝ^nⱼdₐ×N contain the corresponding residuals as columns. The local basis is the solution of

    \min_U_a,j,{c_i,a,j}∑ᵢ₌₁^N∥r_i,a,j-U_a,jc_i,a,j∥_M_a,j², ∥z∥_M²=z^⊤Mz, U_a,j^⊤M_a,jU_a,j=I.

    		(9)

    Substituting y=M_a,j^1/2r turns the objective into the Euclidean objective of Eq. 3, hence the problem is solved by uncentered PCA of

    Y_a,j=M_a,j^1/2R_a,j.

    		(10)

    If V_a,j contains the top K_a,j left singular vectors of Y_a,j, the basis and the projected coefficients are

    U_a,j=M_a,j^-1/2V_a,j, c_a,j^⋆=U_a,j^⊤M_a,jr_a,j,

    		(11)

    so that U_a,j^⊤M_a,jU_a,j=I. Since M_a,j is block diagonal with one dₐ×dₐ block per Gaussian, M_a,j^1/2 and M_a,j^-1/2 are computed per Gaussian. Setting β=γ=0 gives M_a,j=αI and reduces the construction to the simple PCA of Section 3.2.1 applied to the block.

    Value of a component.

    The allocation of Section 3.2.2 scores component k of attribute group a and block j by

    v_a,j,k=(h̄ₐ)/(β)λ_a,j,k,

    		(12)

    for β>0, where λ_a,j,k is the kth squared singular value of Y_a,j and h̄ₐ is the mean trace per channel of Ĥₐ before normalization. Since Ĥₐ is normalized separately for every attribute group, the singular values of different groups are not directly comparable, and the factor h̄ₐ/β undoes the normalization and the weight β of the rendering term. The value then combines the estimated reduction of the squared image error with the weighted reductions of the squared attribute error and, if γ>0, of the landmark error, summed over the samples. Since the values are non-increasing within each local basis, the greedy allocation by value per byte retains the components of every local basis in spectral order.

    Appendix B Host Models

    We apply our method to three host models, spanning different architectures, training objectives, and animation mechanisms. Together, these state-of-the-art models cover dedicated deformation networks, decoders with integrated expression conditioning, and temporally conditioned full-body animation. Table 5 lists the numbers of Gaussians and the attribute groups of the host models together with the settings of our distilled models.

    AGORA [(Fazylov et al., 2025)] is a Gaussian avatar GAN trained adversarially on unstructured images of human heads. It follows the dual-branch design of Next3D [(Sun et al., 2023)] and GAIA [(Yu et al., 2025)], using GGHead’s UV-space Gaussian representation [(Kirschstein et al., 2024)]. A mapping network produces an identity code w, and an identity branch generates canonical Gaussian attributes on a UV grid aligned with FLAME. A separate deformation branch, conditioned on w and FLAME expression and jaw parameters θ, predicts attribute residuals. The identity branch is evaluated once per subject, whereas the deformation branch is evaluated at every frame. Identities can be generated by latent sampling or obtained by image inversion.

    FlexAvatar [(Kirschstein et al., 2026)] reconstructs an animatable head from a single image using an encoder–decoder trained with rendering losses on monocular and multi-view portrait videos. The encoder produces an identity representation in template UV space. A FLAME-derived expression code conditions the decoder through cross-attention. Each animation frame therefore requires evaluating the full decoder to regenerate the attributes of all Gaussians. This model tests whether distillation remains effective when animation is integrated into the decoder rather than implemented by a separate deformation branch.

    DynaAvatar [(Kwon et al., 2026)] reconstructs an animatable full-body avatar with clothing dynamics from a single image. Image encoders and a static transformer produce identity features on the SMPL-X template once per subject. A dynamic transformer, conditioned on a window of the current and 15 preceding SMPL-X poses, regenerates the attributes of template-anchored Gaussians at every frame, which are then posed by linear blend skinning. This model tests our method on full-body motion with garment dynamics that depend on the pose history. Its neural animation is by far the most expensive of the three models (Table 5).

    Appendix C Mobile Browser Demo

    Our real-time demos run in a web browser on desktop and mobile devices (Figure 5). They are built on the open-source WebGL Gaussian splat viewer of [Kwok (2023)], whose depth sort and splat rasterizer we keep and whose static point cloud we replace by our animated avatar. The neutral avatar and the blendshape basis are loaded once as textures. At every frame, the browser reads the animation parameters of the driving sequence, evaluates the coefficient network as fragment-shader passes on the GPU, forms the Gaussian attributes as the neutral avatar plus the coefficient-weighted sum of the blendshapes in a second pass, and hands the result to the sort and the rasterizer of the viewer. No host network runs in the browser. The FlexAvatar and DynaAvatar demos can show several avatars at once. The AGORA and FlexAvatar demos use the same viewer and differ only in the animation parameters they read, the FLAME expression and jaw parameters and the tracked expression code respectively, and in the sizes of the basis and the network (Table 5). The video on our project page shows the demos in action.

    Appendix D Implementation Details

    Basis construction.

    We use the same configuration of our method for all host models unless stated otherwise. The Gaussians are partitioned into B=32 spatial blocks, and a separate basis is constructed for every attribute group and block (Section 3.2.2). The rendering-aware metric Mₐ (Eq. 6) uses α=1 and β=16, with β=64 for DynaAvatar, and is estimated with 16 random probes per frame (Appendix A). The landmark term is used only for the positions of FlexAvatar (γ=24), which is itself trained with a landmark loss. The numbers of components K_a,j are allocated under a memory budget B on the storage of the basis (Section 3.2.2), which is listed in Table 5. The basis is stored in half precision (b=2) for the two head models and in single precision (b=4) for DynaAvatar.

    Coefficient network.

    The architecture and training of the coefficient network f_φ (Section 3.2.3) are given in Appendix E. Table 5 lists its size for every host model.

    Enrollment for FlexAvatar.

    The evaluation protocol of FlexAvatar fits the identity representation w to the input images of every test subject. Our model follows this protocol with a per-subject enrollment: given the fitted w and the expressions of the input images, we estimate a constant correction of the neutral avatar and fine-tune the coefficient network for 200 steps on outputs of the host model. The enrollment uses no target frames and no rendering.

    Timing.

    We measure speed as the CPU time of one animation step, i.e. the computation of the Gaussian attributes Ĝ from the animation parameters θ without rendering. All methods are timed on the same CPU, an Intel Core Ultra 9 285K, with eight threads and batch size one. For DynaAvatar, the linear blend skinning of 10 ms per frame is excluded from the animation step in Table 5 and included for all methods in Figure 4, whose time axis is cut before the host model at 43 s.

    Appendix E Coefficient Networks

    Table 6 summarizes the coefficient networks f_φ (Section 3.2.3) of the three distilled models of Table 2.
